en: Vālmīki,
the ascetic, questioned Nārada, the best among sages and the foremost of those skilled in speech, who was devoted to austerity and the study of the Vedas.
Who in this world at present is virtuous, and who is heroic?
Who knows the Dharma, who is grateful, whose speech is truthful, and who is firm in his vows? And who is endowed with good conduct, and who is a benefactor to all beings?
Who is learned, who is capable, and who possesses a singularly pleasing appearance? Who is self-possessed, who has conquered anger, who is wise, and who is free from malice?
And with whom, when his wrath is aroused in battle, do even the gods stand in fear?
"I desire to hear this, for my curiosity is great;
O Great Sage, you are capable of knowing such a man.
Having heard these words of Vālmīki, Nārada, the knower of the three worlds, [replied].
"Listen," he said, addressing him with joy, and spoke these words:
"O Sage, regarding those many qualities you have described as difficult to find, I shall speak after having reflected upon them; listen to how a man may be endowed with them."
Born of the Ikṣvāku lineage, he is known among people by the name Rāma;
he is self-controlled, of great heroism, radiant, steadfast, and master of his senses.
He is wise, possessed of statesmanship, eloquent, glorious, and the destroyer of enemies.
Broad-shouldered, mighty-armed, with a neck like a conch shell and large jaws;
broad-chested, a great archer, with hidden collarbones, a subduer of enemies; his arms reaching to his knees, with a fine head, a beautiful forehead, and noble stride.

He was symmetrical, with well-proportioned limbs, a smooth complexion, and great majesty; he had a broad chest, large eyes, was endowed with fortune, and possessed auspicious marks. He was a knower of dharma, true to his word, and devoted to the welfare of his subjects.

He was illustrious, endowed with wisdom, pure, self-controlled, and possessed of meditative concentration; he was the protector of the world of living beings and the guardian of righteousness (dharma). He knew the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, and was thoroughly proficient in the science of archery (dhanurveda).
He knew the true essence of the meaning of all scriptures, possessed a retentive memory and ready wit;
he was beloved by all the world, virtuous, high-minded, and discerning. Like the ocean by the rivers, he was always sought after by the righteous.
He is noble and truly equal toward all, always pleasing to behold;
endowed with every virtue, he increases the joy of Kausalyā. In depth he is like the ocean, and in steadfastness he is like the Himalayas.
Equal to Viṣṇu in prowess, as pleasing to behold as the moon,
like the fire of time in wrath, and equal to the earth in forbearance;
he was equal to Kubera in generosity and like another Dharma in truthfulness.
King Daśaratha, out of affection, desired to invest his eldest son Rāma— who was endowed with such virtues, possessed of true prowess, and distinguished by the most excellent qualities—
with the position of heir apparent.
Then, seeing the preparations for his consecration, Queen Kaikeyī—
having previously been granted boons by the king— asked for these two boons:
the exile of Rāma and the consecration of Bharata.
Bound by the noose of dharma through his word of truth, King Daśaratha banished his beloved son Rāma. Keeping his promise, that hero went to the forest.
At his father’s command and for the sake of pleasing Kaikeyī,
as he was departing, his beloved brother Lakṣmaṇa followed him—
endowed with humility and increasing the joy of Sumitrā out of affection.

Endowed with every auspicious mark, Sītā— the most excellent of women— followed Rāma, just as Rohiṇī follows the Moon. Followed for a long distance by the citizens and by his father Daśaratha, he departed.
At Śṛṅgaverapura, he dismissed the charioteer on the bank of the Gaṅgā.
Having gone from forest to forest and crossed many rivers of abundant water,
they reached Citrakūṭa by the command of Bharadvāja.

Having constructed a delightful dwelling, the three of them, resembling gods and gandharvas, lived there happily, sporting in the forest. When Rāma had gone to Citrakūṭa, [Daśaratha], then afflicted by grief for his son, [passed away].
King Daśaratha went to heaven while lamenting for his son. When he had died, the mighty Bharata, though being urged toward the kingship by the twice-born led by Vasiṣṭha, did not desire the kingdom.
That hero went to the forest to propitiate the feet of Rāma;
having repeatedly entrusted his sandals as a trust for the sake of the kingdom,
the elder brother of Bharata then caused Bharata to turn back.

Without having attained his desire, he touched the feet of Rāma and ruled in Nandigrāma out of longing for Rāma’s return. But Rāma, perceiving once again the [longing] of the city folk, [acted accordingly].
Arriving there with one-pointed focus, he entered the Daṇḍaka forest.
Having slain the Rākṣasa Virādha, he beheld Śarabhaṅga,
as well as Sutīkṣṇa, Agastya, and Agastya’s brother.
At the word of Agastya, he took up Indra’s bow,
a sword, and two quivers with inexhaustible arrows, being exceedingly pleased;
while Rāma was dwelling in the forest together with the forest-dwellers.
All the ṛṣis arrived there for the sake of slaying the asuras and rākṣasas.
While he was dwelling right there, the rākṣasī Śūrpaṇakhā— who could assume any form at will— was disfigured by the inhabitants of Janasthāna.
Then, following the words of Śūrpaṇakhā, Rāma slew in battle all the rākṣasas who had mobilized—
namely Khara, Triśiras, and the rākṣasa Dūṣaṇa,
as well as their followers.
Fourteen thousand *rakṣasas* had been slain.
Then, hearing of the slaughter of his kinsmen, Rāvaṇa, overwhelmed with rage,
sought out a companion in the form of a *rakṣasa* named Mārīca.
Though he was repeatedly restrained by Mārīca, Rāvaṇa did not heed those words; for it is not fitting for you, O Rāvaṇa, to oppose one who is more powerful than yourself.
Yet, impelled by Time, Rāvaṇa disregarded that speech.
Then, together with Marīca, he went to that hermitage. Having lured the two princes far away by means of his illusory power,
that master of magic killed the vulture Jaṭāyu and carried off Rāma’s wife.
Having seen that the vulture had been slain and having heard that Maithilī had been carried away,
Rāghava, tormented by grief and with his senses distraught, lamented.
Then, out of that very sorrow, he cremated the vulture Jaṭāyu.
While searching for Sītā in the forest, he encountered a Rākṣasa named Kabandha,
who was deformed in appearance and terrible to behold;
having slain him, the mighty-armed one cremated him, and he (Kabandha) ascended to heaven.
"And he said to him,
'O Rāghava, you should go to Śabarī, a practitioner of dharma, an ascetic woman skilled in the dharma.
Then that one of great splendor, the slayer of enemies, approached Śabarī."
Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, having been duly honored by Śabarī on the banks of the Pampā,
was joined there by the monkey Hanumān;
and at the word of Hanumān, he met with Sugrīva.
The mighty Rāma related all of that to Sugrīva.
Then, out of affection and in his distress, the king of the monkeys recounted the entire narrative of his enmity to Rāma.
There, the monkey described the strength of Vālin,
and Rāma’s promise regarding the slaying of Vālin; meanwhile,
Sugrīva remained constantly apprehensive of Rāghava’s prowess.
To inspire confidence, Rāghava kicked the massive body of Dundubhi with his big toe, flinging it a full ten yojanas away;
he then pierced seven sala trees with a single great arrow.
Then, creating confidence by causing the mountain and even the subterranean realm (rasātala) to tremble,
that great monkey, with a pleased mind and full of trust,
went together with Rāma to the cave-city of Kiṣkindhā.
Then Sugrīva, the best of monkeys, tawny as gold, let out a roar;
by that great sound, the lord of monkeys emerged.
Then, at the word of Sugrīva, having slain Vālī in battle—
Rāghava then reinstated Sugrīva himself in that kingdom.
And that bull among monkeys, having summoned all the monkeys together,
dispatched them to the various quarters, desiring to find the daughter of Janaka.
Then, at the word of the vulture Saṃpāti, the mighty Hanumān leaped across the salt ocean, which was a hundred yojanas in width;
having reached there, he arrived at the city of Laṅkā, protected by Rāvaṇa.
He beheld Sītā, who had gone to the Aśoka grove and was lost in thought;
having presented the token of recognition and announced the news,
and having comforted Vaidehī, he crushed the archway.
Having slain five army commanders and even seven sons of ministers, and having crushed the heroic Akṣa, he was taken captive;
for he recognized himself as being invulnerable by means of a weapon due to the boon of his grandfather.
Enduring those captive Rākṣasas at his own will,
the hero then burned the city of Laṅkā, with the exception of Sītā, the princess of Mithilā; thereafter,
the great monkey returned once more to deliver the pleasant news to Rāma.
Having approached that high-souled one and circumambulated Rāma, he of immeasurable soul reported the truth: "Sītā has been seen.
Then, accompanied by Sugrīva, he went to the shore of the great ocean.
He agitated the ocean with arrows resembling the sun.
Then the ocean, the lord of rivers, revealed himself;
and at the word of the ocean, Nala caused a bridge to be built.
Having gone to the city of Laṅkā by means of that [bridge] and having slain Rāvaṇa in battle,
he consecrated Vibhīṣaṇa as the lord of the rākṣasas in Laṅkā.
By that great deed, the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, [were transformed].
The assembly of great-souled Rāghava, along with the hosts of gods and sages,
was gratified. Thus honored by all the deities who were themselves supremely satisfied, Rāma, having accomplished his purpose and freed from his feverish anxiety, rejoiced.
Having obtained boons from the deities and restored the monkeys to life,
he then ascended that Puṣpaka chariot and went to Nandigrāma.
In Nandigrāma, the sinless one, together with his brothers, cast off his matted locks.

1.001.070c Having recovered Sītā, Rāma regained his kingdom once more. 1.001.071a The world was exceedingly joyful and delighted; it was contented, well-nourished, and profoundly righteous. It was free from calamity and disease, and devoid of the fear of famine.

Nowhere shall any men behold the death of a son, and women shall never be widows, remaining eternally devoted to their husbands. There shall be no fear arising from the wind, nor shall living beings drown in water.
There was not the slightest fear of enemies, just as it was in the Kṛta Yuga. Having performed hundreds of horse sacrifices and many sacrifices involving abundant gold,
he gave ten billion cows to the learned according to the prescribed rites.
Rāghava shall establish royal lineages a hundredfold and shall establish the four castes in this world, each fixed in its own duty,
for ten thousand and one thousand years.
Having served the kingdom, Rāma will go to the world of Brahmā.
This [account] is purifying, destructive of sin, meritorious, and equal to the Vedas;
whoever recites the life-story of Rāma is liberated from all sins.
A man who recites this narrative, the *Rāmāyaṇa*, which bestows long life,
is honored in heaven after death along with his sons, grandsons, and his retinue.
A twice-born man who recites it shall attain the status of a bull among speakers.
A kṣatriya might attain the status of a lord of the earth; a merchant might attain the fruit of his trade;
and even a person who is a śūdra might attain greatness.
Having heard those words of Nārada, the great sage, whose soul was devoted to dharma and who was skilled in speech, honored him along with his disciples. Then,
having been duly honored by him, the celestial sage Nārada—
Having been permitted after being asked, he departed through the sky. When that sage had gone for a moment toward the world of the gods,
he then proceeded to the bank of the Tamasā, not far from the Jāhnavī.
Having reached the bank of the Tamasā, the great sage,
seeing a ford free from mud, spoke to his disciple standing at his side:
"Bharadvāja, behold this ford that is free from mud."
"Delightful with its clear waters, like the mind of a virtuous man— O dear one, let the water-pot be set down and give me my bark garment;
I shall bathe right here in this supreme bathing place on the banks of the Tamasā."
Thus addressed by the high-souled Vālmīki, Bharadvāja,
being self-restrained, offered the bark garment to his guru, the sage.
Taking the bark garment from the hand of his disciple, he, whose senses were controlled, [donned it].
He wandered about, beholding that vast forest on every side. In its vicinity, the venerable one saw a pair of cranes moving together, never parting from one another, emitting their beautiful cries.
But from that pair,
a Niṣāda, a dwelling-place of enmity and of evil intent, slew one male while he was looking on.
His limbs drenched in blood, he writhed upon the surface of the earth.
But seeing her husband slain, his wife uttered piteous cries.
And seeing that twice-born man thus struck down by the Niṣāda,
compassion arose within that righteous-souled seer.
Then, out of compassion, that twice-born man, perceiving that this was unrighteous,
spoke these words upon hearing the Krauñca bird crying out:
"O Niṣāda, may you find no firm footing for eternal years!"
"Because you have slain one of this pair of curlews while it was infatuated by passion"—
as he spoke thus, a reflection arose in his heart as he looked on:
"What was this that I have uttered to this bird who is so afflicted with grief?"
Reflecting thus, that highly wise and intelligent one formed a resolution;
and that bull among sages spoke these words to his disciple:
"It is composed in metrical feet with equal syllables, and endowed with the rhythm of stringed instruments."
"May this verse proceed from me as one afflicted by grief, and not otherwise.
As the sage spoke these unsurpassed words, his disciple received them with great joy, and the teacher was well-pleased with him.
Then, having performed his ablutions at that sacred ford according to the prescribed rites,
the sage returned while reflecting upon that very same matter.
Bharadvāja was then a disciplined disciple of his preceptor, well-versed in sacred learning.
Taking a full water-pot, he followed behind;
having entered the hermitage with his disciple, that knower of dharma sat down and, remaining in meditation, engaged in other conversations.

Then Brahmā, the creator of the worlds, the self-sovereign lord, four-faced and of great splendor, arrived to see that bull among sages. Upon seeing him, Vālmīki then rose up suddenly, restraining his speech.
With palms joined in reverence and becoming composed, he stood there filled with supreme wonder. He honored that god with water for the feet, the arghya offering, a seat, and salutations;
having bowed down according to the rules, he inquired after his eternal well-being.
Then, having sat down upon a most honored seat, the Blessed One offered a seat to the great seer Vālmīki. When that Grandfather of the World himself had thus taken his seat, [the Lord spoke].
With his mind fixed on that very [incident], Vālmīki entered into meditation:
"A grievous deed has been committed by this evil-souled one, whose intellect is gripped by enmity— he who,
for no reason, should slay such a krauñca bird of such lovely song."
Grieving repeatedly for the female crane, his mind turned inward and devoted solely to sorrow, he sang this verse once again.
Then Brahmā, smiling, spoke to that bull among sages.

"O Brahmin, you have already composed the *śloka* itself; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter. By my very will, O best of sages, this Sarasvatī has begun to flow through you; compose the entire life-story of Rāma."
"Relate the conduct of the wise Rāma, whose soul is dharma and who is endowed with virtue in this world— just as you heard it from Nārada—
including both his secret and his public deeds."
Whatever has occurred regarding Rāma together with Saumitri, and concerning the Rākṣasas in every respect, as well as Vaidehī— whether in public or in private—
all that which was previously unknown shall become known to you.
"Not a single word of yours shall ever prove false in this poetic work. O Rāma, compose a holy and delightful narrative bound in verses,
which shall endure as long as the mountains and rivers remain upon the surface of the earth."
The story of the Rāmāyaṇa shall circulate among the worlds for as long as the tale of Rāma composed by you continues to spread;
for that duration, you shall dwell in my worlds, both above and below.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Brahmā vanished on the spot.
Thereupon, the sage Vālmīki, together with his disciples, was filled with wonder.
Then all of his disciples sang this verse once again.
Delighted and greatly amazed, they spoke again and again:
"That which was sung by the great seer in four lines of equal syllables has,
through its being recited, further attained the state of a *śloka* (verse) because of its increasing sorrow."
This thought arose in the mind of that Vālmīki, whose soul was purified:
"I shall compose the entire poem of the Rāmāyaṇa with such verses, possessing noble conduct, meaning, and words, and being delightful to the mind."
Then the illustrious sage of noble intellect composed for the famous Rāma a fame-enhancing poem consisting of hundreds of verses of equal syllables.
Having heard that entire account concerning dharma, the righteous-souled one clearly sought further information regarding the conduct of that wise man.
Having sipped water, the sage stood with self-restraint and joined palms in reverence.
Upon darbha grass with its tips pointing eastward, he sought by means of dharma the course of Rāma’s birth— his exceedingly great heroism, his universal favorability,
his popularity among the people, his forbearance, his gentleness, and his character of truthfulness.
Therein are various and diverse other stories concerning Viśvāmitra’s assistance,
the marriage of Jānakī, the shattering of the bow,
the dispute between Rāma and Rāma, and likewise the virtues of the son of Daśaratha.
Thus [he described] the consecration of Rāma, the wicked disposition of Kaikeyī,
the obstruction of Rāma’s consecration, his exile,
the king’s grief and lamentation, and his departure to the other world.
The dejection of the subjects and the dismissal of the subjects;
the conversation with the lord of the Niṣādas and likewise the return of the charioteer; the crossing of the Gaṅgā and the meeting with Bharadvāja.
1.003.008c Upon Bharadvāja’s permission, the sight of Citrakūṭa; 1.003.009a the construction of the dwelling and the arrival of Bharata;
1.003.009c the propitiation of Rāma and the performance of the water-libation for his father.
The consecration with the most excellent sandals, the dwelling in Nandigrāma,
the departure for the Daṇḍaka forest, the meeting with Sutīkṣṇa,
the conversation with Anasūyā, and the offering of the cosmetic ointment.
The conversation with Śūrpaṇakhā, as well as the disfigurement [of her], the slaughter of Khara and Triśiras, the emergence of Rāvaṇa,
the killing of Mārīca, and likewise the abduction of Vaidehī.
The lamentation of Rāghava, the slaying of the king of vultures, the sight of Kabandha, the sight of Lake Pampā,
the sight of Śarabhaṅga, and likewise the sight of Hanumān.
The lamentation of the high-souled Rāghava at Pampā;
the journey to Ṛṣyamūka and the meeting with Sugrīva; the production of confidence, the alliance, and the conflict between Vālin and Sugrīva.
The slaying of Vālin and the installation of Sugrīva; the occasion of Tārā’s lamentation and the dwelling during the rainy nights;
the wrath of the lion among the Rāghavas and the gathering of the forces.
The dispatching [of messengers] to the various directions, the announcement regarding the earth,
the giving of the ring, the showing of the bear's cave,
the fasting unto death, and the vision of Saṃpāti.
The climbing of the mountain and the leaping across the ocean,
the entry into Laṅkā at night— even the mere thought of these— along with the journey to the drinking grounds and the sight of the inner harem.
The sight of the Aśoka grove and of Sītā; the giving of tokens of recognition and the conversation with Sītā; the intimidation by the rākṣasīs and the vision of Trijaṭā’s dream.
The presentation of the jewel to Sītā, the breaking of the trees, the flight of the rākṣasīs, the slaughter of the kiṃkaras,
the capture of the son of the Wind-god, and the roaring that preceded the burning of Laṅkā.
Then, the crossing back over [the ocean], as well as the seizing of the honey;
the consolation of Rāghava, as well as the recovery of the jewel; the encounter with the ocean, and the construction of the bridge by Nala.
The crossing of the ocean, the siege of Laṅkā at night,
the alliance with Vibhīṣaṇa, the announcement of the means for slaughter,
the death of Kumbhakarṇa, and the destruction of Meghanāda.
The destruction of Rāvaṇa, the recovery of Sītā in the enemy’s city,
the consecration of Vibhīṣaṇa, the appearance of the Puṣpaka chariot,
the journey to Ayodhyā, and the reunion with Bharata.
The auspicious consecration of Rāma, the dismissal of the entire army, the pleasing of his own kingdom, the departure of Vaidehī,
and whatever else was yet to come for Rāma upon the surface of the earth.

The venerable seer Vālmīki composed that in his subsequent poem; the self-possessed and venerable seer Vālmīki composed the entire life-story of Rāma, who had attained the kingdom, in verses of wonderful phrasing.
Having composed that work, together with its future history and its sequel, the highly wise and powerful lord reflected: "Who indeed might employ this?
While that great seer of purified soul was thus reflecting, [the following occurred].
Then Kuśa and Lava, dressed as ascetics, grasped his feet. The illustrious princes, Kuśa and Lava, who were knowers of dharma,
brothers endowed with beautiful voices, were seen by him dwelling in the hermitage.
Seeing that those two were intelligent and well-versed in the Vedas,
the Lord had them master the entire *Kāvya*, the *Rāmāyaṇa*, and the great life-story of Sītā for the purpose of augmenting the Vedas.
Having fulfilled his vow, he composed [the work] titled "The Slaying of Paulastya" (Rāvaṇavadha),
which was sweet in both recitation and song, endowed with the three measures (pramāṇa),
possessed the seven musical scales (jāti), and was accompanied by stringed instruments and rhythmic tempo (tāla).
They sang this poem, which was endowed with the sentiments (rasas) of humor, the erotic, the pathetic, the furious, the heroic, the terrifying, the loathsome, and so forth;
for those two were experts in the principles of music and skilled in the musical scales (sthāna) and modulations (mūrcchanā).
The two brothers were endowed with beautiful voices like Gandharvas in bodily form; they were perfect in beauty and auspicious marks, speaking with sweet voices,
appearing like two reflections drawn forth from a mirror, or like two other bodies produced from the body of Rāma.
Those two blameless princes, having fully mastered that supreme and righteous narrative— the entirety of that poetic composition which is subject to verbal expression—
in the assembly of sages, the twice-born, and the virtuous.

Those two high-souled and highly fortunate ones, who knew the truth according to the teachings and were composed toward the world, were marked by every auspicious characteristic. Once, they [were present] among the assembled sages of purified souls.
Standing near those who were seated, they sang this poem.
Hearing it, all the sages, their eyes clouded with tears, spoke to them, "Excellent! Excellent! having been struck by the utmost wonder.
1.004.015 All those sages, who were fond of righteousness, with hearts full of joy,
praised Kuśa and Lava, who were worthy of praise as they sang.
1.004.016 "Oh, what sweetness there is in the song, and especially in these verses!"
Although this had occurred long ago, it was shown as if it were before one's eyes.
Then, having entered [the performance], the two of them sang that emotion with great skill; together, they sang sweetly, passionately, and perfectly endowed with the excellence of tone.

While they were being thus praised by the great seers who extolled their asceticism, the two sang with voices exceedingly sweet and deeply impassioned. A certain sage, pleased with them, stood there and gave them a water-jar.
A certain highly illustrious man, being pleased, gave bark garments to the two of them. This wonderful narrative, proclaimed by the sage,
which is the supreme foundation for poets, has been completed in due order.
Once, on the city streets and royal highways, the elder brother of Bharata saw those two singers being praised everywhere;
he then brought the two brothers, Kuśa and Lava, to his own residence.
Rāma, the destroyer of enemies, honored those two who were worthy of honor; that lord,
the scorcher of foes, sat upon a divine golden throne together with his ministers and brothers seated nearby.
Having seen those two, endowed with beauty and holding lutes,
Rāma then spoke to Lakṣmaṇa, Śatrughna, and Bharata:
"Listen to this narrative concerning these two who possess the splendor of gods."
These two sages, Kuśīlava and Lava, who possess great ascetic power and bear the marks of royalty, sing perfectly with sweet voices in verses of diverse meaning.
"That too, they say, brings me prosperity;
learn now of my deeds of great power.
Then, urged by the words of Rāma, those two—
They sang with the perfection of the prescribed method,
and Rāma, seated in the assembly, gradually became one whose mind was intent on the desire to hear.
For all those victorious kings beginning with Prajāpati, this entire earth was something never before possessed by anyone else;
among them was he named Sagara, by whom the ocean was dug out.
Sixty thousand sons followed him as he went forth. In the lineage of those great-souled kings of the Ikṣvākus,
this great narrative known as the Rāmāyaṇa has arisen.
I shall now set forth all of this in its entirety from the beginning;
it should be heard with a mind free from malice, as it pertains to virtue, pleasure, and wealth.
There was a great, joyful, and prosperous kingdom named Kosala.
Situated on the bank of the Sarayū and abounding in wealth and grain,
there was a city renowned throughout the world named Ayodhyā,
which had been built by Manu himself, the lord of men.
That magnificent great city is twelve yojanas in length and three yojanas in width; it is beautifully laid out with well-proportioned great highways and graced by a vast,
well-ordered royal road.
King Daśaratha, the enhancer of the great kingdom, constantly caused that city to be sprinkled with water and strewn with loose flowers,
just as the Lord of the Gods dwells in heaven.
It possessed gates and archways, with well-arranged market-stalls; it was equipped with all kinds of machines and weapons, and provided with artisans of every craft;
it was crowded with bards and panegyrists, glorious, and of incomparable splendor.
The city was filled with high towers and banners, crowded with hundreds of *śataghnī* weapons; it was joined on all sides by troupes of dancing women,
possessed of gardens and mango groves, and girdled by great *sāla* trees.
It had deep and formidable moats, was difficult to approach and inaccessible to others, and was filled with horses, elephants, cattle, camels,
and donkeys; it was likewise surrounded by hosts of neighboring kings who paid tribute.
It was graced by merchants residing in various lands,
adorned with palaces fashioned from jewels like mountains,
and filled with gabled chambers, resembling Indra’s city, Amarāvatī.
It was variegated, shaped like a checkerboard, and filled with throngs of excellent women;
it was strewn with all kinds of jewels and adorned with celestial palaces and mansions,
densely packed with houses and situated upon level ground.
Filled with polished rice grains and water flavored with the juice of sugarcane stalks,
it resounded intensely and exceedingly with kettledrums, clay drums, lutes, and cymbals— truly unsurpassed on this earth.
It was like a celestial chariot of the Siddhas attained in heaven through ascetic power,
with its inner chambers well-arranged and filled with the best of men;
and those who do not pierce one another with arrows when they are alone and secluded.
Skilled and dexterous, they could pierce even a sound by sight alone;
they were slayers of roaring lions, tigers, and boars in the forest,
using both sharp weapons and the sheer strength of their arms.
Then King Daśaratha caused that city to be inhabited by thousands of such great chariot-warriors;
it was filled with virtuous men who maintained the sacred fires.
By the best of the twice-born, who had mastered the Vedas and their six auxiliary branches, who were givers of thousands, devoted to truth, high-souled,
resembling great seers, and by sages who were pure;
In that city of Ayodhyā lived one who was a knower of the Vedas, a collector of all [learning],
far-sighted, possessed of great splendor, beloved by the people of both the city and the countryside,
a great chariot-warrior among the Ikṣvākus, a performer of sacrifices, devoted to dharma, and self-controlled.
A royal sage equal to a great seer, renowned throughout the three worlds,
powerful, having destroyed his enemies, possessed of friends, and with his senses conquered;
he was like Śakra and Vaiśravaṇa in wealth and other accumulated riches.

Just as Manu of great splendor was the protector of the world, so King Daśaratha, while dwelling [in his kingdom], protected the universe. By him, who was true to his word and who pursued the three goals of life, [the world was governed].
That preeminent city was protected by him, just as Amarāvatī is by Śakra;
in that best of cities, the people were joyful, righteous-souled, and deeply learned,
content with their respective wealth, free from greed, and speakers of truth.
In that supreme city, there was no householder whatsoever who did not possess abundant stores, nor one whose aims were unaccomplished, nor one lacking cattle, horses, wealth, or grain;
nor was there anywhere a man who was lustful, miserly, or cruel.
In Ayodhyā, it is impossible to find anyone who is ignorant or an atheist;
all men and women are virtuous in character and well-restrained. Joyful in their conduct and behavior, they are as stainless as great seers.

There was no one without earrings, no one without a crown, no one without a garland, and no one with meager enjoyments; there was no one who had not groomed himself, no one whose limbs were not anointed, and no one who lacked fragrance.
There was no one who ate unrefined food, no one who was not generous, and no one who did not wear armlets and golden neck-ornaments.

In Ayodhyā, there was no one seen without ornaments on his hands, nor anyone lacking self-control; there was no Brahmin who had not maintained the sacred fires, none who had not performed sacrifices, and none who had not given thousands in charity, nor was there anyone who had neglected the rules against the intermixture of castes.

The Brahmins were constantly devoted to their own duties, having conquered their senses; they were habituated to giving and study, and were restrained in accepting gifts. There was no atheist, no liar, and no one who was not deeply learned.
At that time, there was no one who was envious, nor incapable, nor unlearned;
nor was there anyone who was dejected, distracted in mind, or afflicted.
Among men or women, there was none who was lacking in prosperity or lacking in beauty.
In Ayodhyā, it is impossible to find anyone who lacks devotion to the king;
even among the four castes, those who worship the gods and guests are all long-lived and devoted to righteousness and truth.

The ruling power had the Brahmins at its head, while the Vaiśyas were devoted to the Kṣatriyas; the Śūdras, intent on their own duties, served the three higher castes. That city was well protected by that lord of the Ikṣvākus.
Just as in former times by the wise Manu, the lord of men,
[were appointed] warriors who were like fire, refined yet impatient,
whose learning was complete, and who were like lions in their dens.

It was filled with the finest horses born in the land of Kamboja and those of Bahlika; with those from Vanayu and those bred by the rivers, resembling the steeds of Indra; and it was full of rutting steeds born on the Vindhya mountains and the foothills, as well as those from the Himalayas.
That city was filled with exceedingly powerful elephants in rut, resembling mountains;
with elephants descended from Añjana and Vāmana;
and with those of the Bhadra-mandra, Bhadra-mṛga, and Mṛga-mandra breeds.
It is always filled with ever-intoxicated nāgas who resemble mountains;
for two more yojanas, it shines forth under its true name. Having seen that city of true name, with its firm gate-arches and bolts;

The lord of the earth, equal to Śakra, ruled over the auspicious city of Ayodhyā, which was adorned with diverse mansions, crowded with thousands of men, and filled with hundreds of thousands of people.
That hero had eight illustrious ministers who were pure and devoted, always intent upon the affairs of state:
Dhṛṣṭi, Jayanta, Vijaya, Siddhārtha, and Arthasādhaka.
Aśoka was the mantra-guardian, and Sumantra was the eighth. He had two esteemed officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the best of sages:
Vasiṣṭha and Vāmadeva, as well as other ministers.

They were illustrious, high-souled, learned in the scriptures, and possessed of firm prowess; they were renowned, disciplined, and obedient to their commands; they had attained brilliance, forbearance, and fame, and always spoke with a smile.
Out of anger, or for the sake of desire or wealth, they would never speak an untruth. Among them, there is nothing unknown— whether among their own people or among others—
be it what is currently being done, what has already been done, or even what is intended to be done, all of which is known through their spies.

Skilled in legal affairs and tested in their friendships, they should administer punishment at the appropriate time even toward their own sons; they must be intent on the accumulation of the treasury and the maintenance of the army.
Even toward a man who has acted harmfully, they should not inflict injury if he is innocent;
for these heroes, whose energy is constant, abide by the royal science and are ever the protectors of the pure inhabitants of their realm.
Without harming the Brahmins and Kṣatriyas, they filled the treasury,
having observed the strength and weakness of men and applying very severe punishments;
they were all pure, of one mind, and possessed of full discernment.
In that city or kingdom, there was never anywhere a man who spoke falsehood;
nor was there any man there who was wicked or devoted to another’s wife. That entire kingdom and that preeminent city were completely tranquil.
They were all well-dressed, well-adorned, and possessed of excellent character;
they remained vigilant with the eye of policy for the welfare of the lord of men,
devoted to their preceptor, and renowned for their heroic exploits.
Renowned even in foreign lands due to their universal certainty of intellect,
King Daśaratha, the sinless one, governed the earth together with such ministers who were endowed with every virtue.
Observing his subjects through his spies and pleasing them with righteousness,
he found no one superior to him, nor any equal, much less an enemy.
He remained thus, supported by those ministers who were well-disposed toward his counsel and firmly established in their duties.
Surrounded by those who were devoted, skillful, and capable,
that king attained brilliance,
like the risen sun endowed with its rays of light.
Although that great-souled one, who possessed such power and was a knower of dharma,
performed austerities for the sake of a son, he had no son to perpetuate his lineage.
As that great-souled one was reflecting in this way, this thought arose in him:
"For the sake of my daughter, why should I not perform a horse sacrifice?
Having thus formed a firm resolve that he must sacrifice,
the wise and righteous king consulted with all his ministers, who were likewise self-disciplined.
Then the king spoke thus to Sumantra, the best of ministers:
"Quickly bring all my elders along with the family priests.
Having heard this in private, the charioteer spoke these words to the king.
"This ancient account was taught by the officiating priests and heard by me; formerly,
the blessed Sanatkumāra related this story in the presence of the sages, O King, concerning the arrival of your son."
Kāśyapa has a son known as Vibhāṇḍaka;
he will have a son famous as Ṛṣyaśṛṅga. Having been raised entirely in the forest, that sage will always be a forest-dweller.

The lord of Brahmins knows no other [duty] because he constantly follows his father; O King, this twofold nature of the high-souled one’s student life (brahmacarya) shall be celebrated throughout the worlds and always recounted by the Brahmins.
As he was living in this manner,
attending upon the sacred fire and his illustrious father, time passed by.
At that very time, however, the powerful Romapāda—
A king of great strength shall reign, renowned throughout the Aṅgas. Due to that king’s transgression,
there will arise a most terrible and dreadful drought, bringing fear to all living beings.
When a drought has occurred, the king, filled with sorrow,
will summon Brahmins who are advanced in Vedic learning and bring them together, saying: "Sirs, you are learned in the Dharma and know the conduct of the world."
"Let them prescribe the rule for whatever atonement should be performed.
O protector of the earth, those Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas will speak to the king:
'O King, bring the son of Vibhāṇḍaka here by every possible means.'"
"O protector of the earth, having summoned Ṛṣyaśṛṅga and honored him well,
bestow the maiden Śāntā upon him according to the prescribed rites with a composed mind.
Having heard their words, the king will fall into deep reflection.
"By what means indeed can that powerful one be brought here?
Then the self-possessed king, having deliberated with his ministers,
will send forth the family priest and the counselors, duly honored.
Having heard the king’s words, they were distressed and their faces became pale;
fearing the sage, they will not go, but will instead entreat the king.
Having reflected, they will suggest to him those expedients that are appropriate.
"We shall bring the brahmin, and no fault will arise.
Thus, by the King of Aṅga himself, the son of the ṛṣi was brought by means of courtesans;
the god rained, and Śāntā was given to him.
"Rishyashringa, as your son-in-law, will provide you with sons.
This much that was spoken by Sanatkumara has been related by me.
Then, delighted, Dasharatha replied to Sumantra:
"Tell me in detail how Ṛṣyaśṛṅga was brought here.
Thus urged by the king, Sumantra then spoke these words:
"Listen along with the ministers to how Ṛṣyaśṛṅga was brought."
The family priest, together with the ministers, said this to Romapāda:
"We have devised a plan that is free from danger.
Ṛṣyaśṛṅga is a forest-dweller devoted to austerity and the study of the Vedas."
"He is ignorant of women, of sense-objects, and of pleasure.
Let us lead him to the city by means of desirable objects of the senses that agitate the minds of men; let it be resolved upon quickly."
"Let beautiful courtesans, well-adorned, go there;
having enticed him by various means, they shall bring him back here with due honor.
Having heard this, the king replied "So be it" to the domestic priest.
Then the family priest and the ministers did exactly as they were told.
Upon hearing this, the chief courtesans entered the great forest and made every effort to catch sight of him not far from that hermitage.

He was constantly content with his father, the son of the sage Ghora, who dwelt perpetually in the hermitage; indeed, that ascetic had never before seen anything outside of the hermitage since the time of his birth.
Whether it be a woman, a man, or any other creature born in that city or kingdom,
once upon a time, the son of Vibhāṇḍaka arrived at that region by chance; there he beheld those beautiful women.
Those women, dressed in colorful garments and singing with sweet voices, approached the son of the sage and all spoke these words:
"Who are you, O Brahmin, and what are you doing? We wish to know."

"You wander alone in this desolate and terrible forest; tell us who you are. Because those women of lovely form had not been seen by him before, a thought arose in his heart out of affection to reveal his own father.
"My father is Vibhāṇḍaka, and I am his legitimate son.
My name and my deed are known on earth as Ṛṣyaśṛṅga. O ladies of auspicious appearance, our hermitage is here, close by."
"I shall indeed perform worship for all of you here according to the prescribed rites.
Having heard the words of the sage’s son, the minds of them all were indeed resolved;
and they all went with him to see that hermitage.
Then the son of the seer performed an offering for those who had departed:
"This is the *arghya*, this is the water for the feet, and these are our roots and fruits.
Having accepted that entire offering, they were all filled with eagerness.
Terrified of the sage, they quickly set their minds on departing.
"O twice-born one, these fruits of ours are indeed excellent; accept them—may you be blessed—and eat them without delay."
Then, all of them, filled with joy, embraced him and gave him sweetmeats (*modaka*) and various auspicious foods. Having tasted them, the radiant one thought they were merely fruits.
Never tasted before by those who dwell eternally in the forest,
they then took leave of the brahmin and informed him of their observance of vows; then,
out of fear of his father, those women departed under some pretext.
When they had all departed, the twice-born son of Kāśyapa became uneasy at heart and wallowed in sorrow. Then,
on the following day, that powerful man returned to that place.
There, those beautiful courtesans were seen, well-adorned. Upon seeing the brahmin approaching, their hearts were filled with joy;
then, all of them drew near and spoke these words to him.
"Come, gentle one, to our hermitage," they said;
"there too, this glorious rule shall apply with even greater distinction.
Having heard those words of all of them, which were so heart-touching, [he replied].
He made up his mind to depart, and then the women led him away.
While that high-souled brahmin was being led there,
the god suddenly sent down rain, gladdening the world at that time.
When the brahmin had arrived in his own kingdom after exactly one thousand years,
the lord of men went out to meet the sage, bowed low, and touched the ground with his head; then,
with great composure, he offered him the guest-offering (arghya) according to the prescribed rule.
He requested a favor from the best of brahmins: "May no anger enter this brahmin.
Having entered the inner apartments and given the maiden Śāntā to him according to the prescribed rites, the king, with a peaceful mind, attained great joy.
Thus did the highly effulgent Ṛṣyaśṛṅga dwell there with his wife Śāntā, well-honored by all objects of desire. Furthermore,
O Indra among kings, listen again to my beneficial words.
Just as that wise and foremost of gods had declared:
"In the lineage of the Ikṣvākus, there will be born a most righteous king named Daśaratha, illustrious and true to his promise."
That king shall form a friendship with the King of Aṅga, and he shall have a highly fortunate daughter named Śāntā. Furthermore, the son of the King of Aṅga is known as Romapāda.

The highly illustrious King Daśaratha will go there [to him]. "O righteous-souled one, I am childless; let Śāntā perform a sacrifice for me, commanded by you, for the sake of the continuity of my lineage."
Then, having heard those words of the king and reflected upon them in his mind,
that self-possessed man will give Śāntā a husband who possesses sons. And having received that brahmin, the king will be freed from his feverish distress.

He will perform that sacrifice with a joyful inner soul. And King Daśaratha, desiring to sacrifice and knowing the dharma, will— with palms joined in reverence— choose Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, the best of the twice-born, as his officiant.
For the sake of sacrifice, for the sake of progeny, and for the sake of heaven, that lord of men,
the ruler of the people, shall obtain his desire from the foremost of the twice-born;
and he shall have four sons of immeasurable prowess.
"Establishers of the lineage, renowned throughout all the worlds"—
thus did the lord Sanatkumāra, the foremost of gods and the master of old, relate this story in the former age of the gods.
Therefore, O tiger among men, O great king, go yourself with your army and vehicles, bring him here after having honored him well;
do this after having obtained the consent of Vasiṣṭha and having heard the words of the Sūta.
Accompanied by his harem and his ministers, he proceeded to where that twice-born man was;
gradually traversing forests and rivers,
he reached the region where that bull among sages resided.
Having approached that best of the twice-born who was near Romapāda,
he first beheld the son of the ṛṣi, blazing like fire.
Then the king performed a special worship toward him according to the prescribed rules.
Out of friendship for that king, with a heart full of joy,
Romapāda related [the matter] to the wise son of the ṛṣi;
and he, in turn, honored him for their friendship and kinship.
Having been thus hospitably entertained by him and having stayed for seven or eight days, that bull among men, the king, spoke these words to the king:
"O King, O lord of the people, Śāntā, your daughter, is here together with her husband."
"Let him go to my city, for a great task is at hand. Having agreed to the departure of that wise man, saying "So be it," the king spoke these words to the brahmin: "Go, together with your wife."
The son of the seer, having replied "So be it" to the king,
then departed with his wife, permitted by the king.
Having joined their palms to one another and embraced each other with affectionate hearts, they went forth.
Daśaratha and the heroic Romapāda both rejoiced. Then, having taken leave of his friend, the joy of the Raghus set out and dispatched swift-moving messengers to the citizens.
"Let the entire city be quickly and beautifully decorated.
Then, hearing that the king had arrived, those citizens were overjoyed;
they carried out everything exactly as the king had commanded at that time.
Then the king entered the well-adorned city,
preceded by the sounds of conchs and drums, with that bull among the twice-born at his head. Then all the citizens were indeed filled with joy upon seeing the brahmin.
Being ushered in with honor by the king, whose deeds were like those of Indra,
and having been led into the inner apartments and honored according to the scriptures,
he then considered himself to have accomplished his purpose through that reception.

1.010.028a When all the women of the inner apartments saw Śāntā, who was so like the Tathāgatā, 1.010.028c that large-eyed lady, they approached her with joy and delight along with her husband. 1.010.029a She was honored by them and especially by the king himself.
She dwelt there happily for some time with the twice-born man. Then,
after a considerable period had passed, at a certain most enchanting time when spring had arrived, the king’s mind was set upon performing a sacrifice.
Then, having propitiated that brahmin who resembled a god with his head bowed,
he chose him for the sacrifice for the sake of the lineage's continuity.
And being highly honored, he said "So be it" to the king.
"Let the sacrificial requisites be gathered and let the horse be released.
Then the king spoke these words to Sumantra, the best of ministers:
"Sumantra, summon quickly the officiating priests who are exponents of the Vedas."
Then Sumantra, moving with swift prowess,
went quickly and brought together all those brahmins who had mastered the Vedas:
Suyajña, Vāmadeva, Jābāli, and Kāśyapa.
Having honored the family priest Vasiṣṭha and those other best of the twice-born, the righteous King Daśaratha then spoke these gentle words, consistent with both dharma and worldly purpose:
"1.011.008a While I lament for the sake of my son, there is indeed no happiness.

1.011.008c For that purpose, it is my intention that I shall sacrifice with a horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha). 1.011.009a Therefore, I desire to perform that sacrifice according to the rites prescribed in the scriptures."
"By the power of the son of the seer, I too shall obtain my desires. Then all the brahmins, headed by Vasiṣṭha, honored those words as they issued from the mouth of the king, exclaiming, "Excellent!"
Then those led by Ṛṣyaśṛṅga replied to the king:
"Let the sacrificial materials be gathered and let the horse be released;
in every way, you shall obtain four sons of immeasurable prowess."
"Since you possess this righteous intention regarding my sons who have come here for their sake," the king became joyful upon hearing those words spoken by the twice-born man. Then,
with words auspicious with joy, the king spoke thus to his ministers:
"By the word of my elders, let the sacrificial materials be gathered for me quickly;
let the horse, supervised by capable men and accompanied by its preceptor, be released;
and let the sacrificial ground be prepared on the northern bank of the Sarayū."
"May the propitiatory rites increase according to the ritual manual and according to the prescribed rule.
This sacrifice can be performed by any king;
let no grievous offense occur in this most excellent of sacrifices."
For the learned *brahmarākṣasas* search for a flaw here;
the performer of a sacrifice devoid of ritual rules perishes instantly.
Therefore, let this sacrifice of mine first be completed according to the prescribed rule.
"Let such arrangements be made; you are capable in these matters.
Then all the ministers honored those words of the lord of kings, saying "So be it," and carried out exactly as they were commanded.
Then those twice-born ones praised that bull among kings, who was conversant with dharma;
having received his permission, they all returned the way they had come.
Once the twice-born had departed, the lord of men [addressed] those ministers.
Having dismissed him, the one of great splendor entered his own residence.
When spring returned once more, a full year had elapsed;
having saluted Vasiṣṭha and honored him according to custom, [he departed].
He spoke these humble words to the best of the twice-born for the sake of offspring:
"O Brahmin, O bull among sages, let my sacrifice be performed according to the injunctions;
let it be so ordained that no obstacle arises regarding the components of the sacrifice."
"You are my affectionate friend and you are my supreme preceptor;
moreover, the burden of the sacrifice now undertaken must indeed be borne by you. "So be it," that best of the twice-born replied to the king.
"I shall do all of this exactly as you have proposed.
Then he spoke to the aged twice-born ones who were experts in sacrificial rites,
and to the elderly and most righteous masters of architecture.
He [summoned] laborers, artisans, carpenters, and diggers;
likewise accountants and craftsmen, as well as actors and dancers;
and also pure men, learned in the scriptures and highly erudite.
"By the king's command, let you all strive to perform the sacrificial rites;
let many thousands of bricks be brought quickly. And let guest-houses be constructed for the kings, endowed with every excellence."
Hundreds of auspicious dwellings for Brahmins must be constructed,
well-built and fully supplied with abundant food, snacks, and drinks;
likewise, extensive quarters must also be provided for the city-dwellers.
1.012.011a "The dwellings indeed abound with food and are provided with all desired objects; 1.012.011c likewise, much that is beautiful should be given to the people of the countryside as well.
1.012.012a Food should be given according to the rules, having honored them, and not merely in jest."
1.012.012c So that all castes may receive honor and be well-respected,

1.012.013a one must not show contempt toward them, even under the influence of desire or anger; 1.012.013c likewise, those men who are diligent in sacrificial rites and the artisans [should be honored].
1.012.014a You must also perform worship for them specifically, in the proper order,
1.012.014c so that everything is well-arranged and nothing is omitted;
1.012.015a let your honors do this with hearts full of affection and tenderness.

Then, having all assembled together, they said this to Vasiṣṭha: "We shall do exactly as you have said; nothing at all will be omitted. Thereupon, having summoned Sumantra, Vasiṣṭha spoke these words.
Invite the kings upon the earth who are righteous,
as well as thousands of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras;
bring together men from all lands, treating them with due honor.
Bring here, with great honor, that illustrious lord of Mithilā, Janaka, the hero of true prowess, who is perfected in all the scriptures as well as in the Vedas.

"Knowing him to have been your relative in a former life, I shall therefore tell you about him first. Bring here yourself that affectionate lord of Kāśī, who always speaks kindly, is of virtuous conduct, and resembles a god."
Likewise, bring here the aged King of Kekaya, who is supremely righteous,
that father-in-law of the lion among kings, together with his son;
and the highly fortunate Romapāda, the lord of Aṅga, having honored him well.
"Bring that illustrious comrade of the lion among kings.
Bring also the kings of the eastern lands, the Sindhusauvīras, and the Saurāṣṭreyas;
and bring all the lords of men from the southern regions."
"Bring here all those other kings upon the face of the earth who are affectionate toward us, along with their followers and kinsmen, as quickly as possible.
Having heard those words of Vasiṣṭha, Sumantra then acted with haste.
He then commanded auspicious men there to bring the kings; for the righteous-souled one himself set out at the sage’s command,
while Sumantra hurried to summon the rulers of the earth.
And all those laborers reported everything that had been prepared for the sacrifice to the wise Vasiṣṭha.
Then the best of the twice-born, being pleased, spoke again to them all.
One should not give anything to anyone out of contempt, nor even in jest;
for what is given with contempt destroys the giver—of this there is no doubt.
Then, after some days and nights had passed, the lords of the earth arrived.
Having brought many jewels for King Daśaratha,
Vasiṣṭha, being well-pleased, then spoke these words to the king:
"O tiger among men, by your command the kings have arrived."
"O best of kings, all those monarchs have been honored by me as was their due;
and the preparations for the sacrifice, O King, have been completed by men who were highly attentive. May you now proceed from this vicinity to the sacrificial ground to perform the sacrifice."
It was provided on all sides with every kind of desirable object brought forth;
then, according to the words of both Vasiṣṭha and Ṛṣyaśṛṅga,
the lord of the world set out on an auspicious day and under a favorable constellation.
Then all those best of the twice-born, headed by Vasiṣṭha,
placed Ṛṣyaśṛṅga at their forefront and commenced the sacrificial rites. Then,
when a full year had passed and that horse had arrived,
On the northern bank of the Sarayū, the king’s sacrifice commenced;
placing Ṛṣyaśṛṅga at their head, the best of the twice-born performed the rites for this great-souled king’s grand Horse Sacrifice.
The officiating priests, masters of the Vedas, perform the rites according to the rules;
they proceed according to the ordinances, in accordance with justice, and as prescribed by the scriptures.
Having performed the *pravargya* rite according to the scriptures, the twice-born likewise perform the *upasada*.

And they performed all the additional rites according to the rules and the scriptures. Then, having honored [the guest], all those bulls among sages, being joyful, performed the rituals beginning with the morning libation (prātaḥsavana) according to the prescribed injunctions.

Not a single oblation was omitted there, nor was there any lapse whatsoever; indeed, everything was performed with such security that it appeared as if created by Brahmā himself. During those days, no one was seen who was weary or even hungry.
There was no unlearned Brāhmaṇa there, nor likewise any who did not follow the hundred-fold path. Brāhmaṇas ate constantly, as did those who had protectors;
ascetics ate, and likewise the śramaṇas ate.
The elderly, the diseased, women, and likewise children—there is no satiety found for those who eat incessantly. "Give food! Give food! they cry, "and various kinds of garments!"

Thus urged, they performed those acts there many times. And on day after day, numerous mounds of food were seen there, resembling mountains, prepared according to the prescribed rites for the perfected one.
"For the bulls among the twice-born praise food that is delicious and served according to the rules.
Rāghava heard them say, "Oh, we are satisfied! Blessings upon you!
And well-adorned men were serving the Brāhmaṇas.
And others, adorned with polished jeweled earrings, waited upon them;
at intervals during the ritual, those wise and eloquent Brahmins spoke many reasoned arguments, desiring to defeat one another.
Day after day, on that sacrificial ground, those twice-born ones,
skilled in their duties and urged by the scriptures, performed all the rites according to the sacred texts.
There was no one there who did not know the six Vedāṅgas, nor anyone who lacked vows, nor anyone who was not deeply learned.
At that time, there was a twice-born man serving as the sacrificial assistant (*sadasya*) for that king who was not skilled in the ritual;
when the time for erecting the sacrificial posts arrived, there were six made of *bilva* wood and likewise six of *khadira*,
as many more joined with *bilva*, and others made of *parṇa*.
One was prescribed to be made of *śleṣmātaka* wood, and likewise one of *devadāru* wood;
these two alone were ordained there with their arms extended for grasping.
All of these were caused to be fashioned by those learned in the scriptures and experts in sacrifice.
For the sake of the beauty of that sacrifice, all the pillars— decorated with gold,
well-constructed, and firmly set by the artisans according to rule—
were eight-sided and possessed a smooth appearance.
Covered with garments and adorned with flowers and perfumes, those radiant Seven Sages shone as if in the heavens. And the bricks were constructed according to rule and in the proper proportions.
1.013.022c There, the fire-altar was piled by Brahmins skilled in the art of cord-measurement (śulbakarma). 1.013.022e That altar, for the lion among kings, was constructed by the learned twice-born;
1.013.023a it was indeed in the form of Garuḍa with golden wings, triplefold and consisting of eighteen parts.
1.013.023c Animals were assigned there, dedicated to this or that deity;
1.013.024a serpents and birds likewise were directed according to the scriptures.
1.013.024c At the place of immolation (*śāmitra*) was the horse, as well as those creatures that dwell in the water.
Then, all of this was performed by the officiating priests according to the scriptures; at that time,
three hundred animals were bound there to the sacrificial posts,
including that most excellent jewel of a horse belonging to King Daśaratha.
Having attended to that horse there from all sides, Kausalyā,
with a steady mind, slaughtered it with three excellent knives with the greatest joy, together with the bird.

Kausalyā, desiring to act in accordance with dharma, stayed for one night. Then the Hotṛ, Adhvaryu, and Udgātṛ priests prepared the queen, surrounded by her attendants, as well as the junior wife, Vāvātā, to be yoked to the horse.

Having extracted the omentum of that bird, the officiating priest, who was self-controlled and highly accomplished, cooked it according to the scriptures. Then the lord of men smelled the fragrance of the smoke from the omentum.
1.013.030c Purifying his own sin according to the time and according to the rule,

1.013.031a all sixteen officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) shall, in accordance with the ritual injunctions, cast all the limbs of the horse into the fire. 1.013.031c All the *brāhmaṇas* together shall perform this.

For other sacrifices, the oblation is prepared upon branches of the *plakṣa* tree; however, for the single *aśvamedha*, a portion made of *vetasa* reeds is prescribed. The *aśvamedha* is reckoned by the Brahmins according to the *Kalpasūtra* as lasting for three days.
The Catuṣṭoma day was ordained as its first;
the Ukthya was reckoned as the second, and likewise the Atirātra as the final one. Many rites were performed there, as prescribed according to the vision of the scriptures.
The Jyotiṣṭoma and Āyuṣ sacrifices, as well as the two Atirātras,
the Abhijit and Viśvajit, and the great Aptoryāma sacrifice were established.
Then the king, the enhancer of his own lineage, gave the eastern quarter to the Hotṛ priest.
To the Adhvaryu she gave the western direction, but to the Brahman the southern quarter;
likewise, to the Udgātṛ she gave the northern—
this was the sacrificial fee ordained in ancient times by the Self-Existent One for the great Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Having completed the sacrifice according to the prescribed rites, that bull among men,
the king who increased the merit of the sacrifice, then bestowed that earth upon the officiating priests.
All the priests, however, spoke to the king, who was now cleansed of all taint:
"Only you, sir, are worthy to protect the entire earth alone.
We have no need for land, for we are not capable of protecting it;
O lord of the earth, we are indeed constantly devoted to the practice of Vedic study."
"May your majesty grant us some small recompense here," they said.
To them the king gave ten hundred-thousand cows,
ten crores of gold, and four times as much silver.

Then all the officiating priests together bestowed wealth upon the sage Ṛṣyaśṛṅga and the wise Vasiṣṭha. Thereupon, those best of the twice-born, having performed the distribution according to rule, [departed].
With hearts full of joy, they all replied with great delight.
Then the king, his mind pleased, having completed that unsurpassed sacrifice—
which destroys sin, leads to heaven, and is difficult for other bulls among kings to achieve— [attained his goal].
Then King Daśaratha spoke to Ṛṣyaśṛṅga at that time:
"O you of noble vows, you ought to perform that which will cause the lineage to flourish.
And that best of the twice-born replied to the king, "So be it."

"O King, you shall have four sons who will perpetuate your lineage. Then Medhātithi, having reflected upon this supreme matter, regained his composure and, being a knower of the Vedas, spoke thus to the king:
"I shall perform for you the *putrīyā* sacrifice for the sake of obtaining a son—
a perfected rite according to the rules using the mantras proclaimed in the *Atharvaśiras*.
Then he began that *putrīyā* sacrifice for the sake of a son."
The radiant one offered oblations into the fire according to the ritual prescribed by the seers of the mantras.
Then the gods, along with the gandharvas, the siddhas, and the supreme ṛṣis,
assembled according to the rules for the purpose of receiving their shares.
Having assembled according to protocol in that assembly hall, those deities addressed these significant words to Brahmā, the creator of the worlds:
"O Blessed One, by your grace, there is a Rākṣasa named Rāvaṇa..."
"He oppresses us all with his prowess; we are unable to subdue him.
O Blessed One, in the past you were pleased and granted him a boon. Out of respect for that boon, we always forgive everything he does."
That evil-minded one terrifies the three worlds and hates those who are exalted;
he desires to assault Śakra, the king of the thirty-three gods,
as well as the ṛṣis, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, and brahmins.
Deluded by the granting of the boon, he is invincible and transgresses all bounds. The sun does not scorch him, nor does the wind blow at his side;
even the ocean, garlanded with moving waves, does not tremble upon seeing him.
"Therefore, we have no fear of that Rakshasa of terrible appearance. O Blessed One, you ought to devise a means for his destruction.
Thus addressed by all the gods, he reflected and then spoke.
"Ah! This is the ordained means for the slaughter of that evil-minded one.
Because he said, 'I am unslayable by Gandharvas, Yakṣas, gods, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas,' and I replied to him, 'So be it.'"
Out of contempt, that Rakṣasa did not mention humans at that time;
therefore, he is to be slain by a human, and no other death exists for him.
Having heard these pleasing words uttered by Brahmā, [the gods were delighted].
At that time, all the gods and great seers were filled with joy.
In the meantime, Viṣṇu of great splendor arrived;
having met with Brahmā, he stood there composed in meditation.
All the gods, having offered praise and bowing down, said to him:
"O Viṣṇu, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds, we shall appoint you as the sovereign of King Daśaratha, the ruler of Ayodhyā."

O Viṣṇu, assume the state of a son within his three wives— who resemble Modesty, Prosperity, and Fame— by dividing yourself into four parts, for he is a knower of dharma, generous, and equal in splendor to a great ṛṣi.
"There, O Viṣṇu, having become a human, slay in battle Rāvaṇa, who has grown into a thorn to the world and cannot be slain by the gods.
For he [defeats] the gods, along with the Gandharvas, the Siddhas, and the best of the Ṛṣis."

The foolish Rākṣasa Rāvaṇa oppresses [the world] with the arrogance of his prowess. That haughty Rāvaṇa, possessed of increased splendor, swollen with pride, and an enemy of the Lord of the Thirty-three gods— [he must be subdued].
"Let there be a cry of triumph! Uproot that thorn in the side of the ascetics, that source of terror to the practitioners of austerity!
Then Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa was thus commissioned by the best of the gods.
Even though he knew [the answer], he spoke these gentle words to the gods:
"O gods, what means is there for the slaying of that lord of the Rākṣasas,
employing which I might destroy that thorn in the side of the sages?"
Thus addressed, all the gods replied to the imperishable Viṣṇu:
"Assuming a human body, slay Rāvaṇa in battle.
For he, O subduer of enemies, performed intense austerities for a long period of time."
By this [act], Brahmā, the creator of the world and honored by the worlds, became pleased;
being well-satisfied, the Lord granted a boon to that Rākṣasa:
"You shall have no fear from various kinds of beings, except from humans."
"In former times, human beings were treated with contempt by him because of the granting of that boon;
therefore, O scorcher of foes, his slaughter is ordained to be at the hands of humans. Having heard these words of the gods, the self-possessed Viṣṇu—
At that time, he sought to win over his father, King Daśaratha.
And at that time, that king of great splendor,
the slayer of enemies, being childless and desiring sons, performed a sacrifice for the sake of obtaining progeny.
Then, from that purifier of the sacrificer, there appeared a great being of incomparable splendor, possessing immense heroism and great strength—
dark-complexioned, wearing red garments, with a red face and a voice like the sound of a drum.
With glossy, tawny-brown hair, beard, and excellent locks;
endowed with auspicious marks and adorned with divine ornaments;
possessing a height like a mountain peak and the prowess of a proud tiger.
Resembling the sun in appearance and like the crest of a blazing fire,
it was a vessel made of refined gold with a silver rim,
filled with divine milk-rice, appearing like a beloved wife.
Having grasped that vast [bow] with both arms as if it were a product of his own illusory power (*māyā*),
he looked upon King Daśaratha and spoke these words:
"O King, know me to be a son of Prajāpati who has come here."
Then, with palms joined in reverence, the king replied:
"O Blessed One, welcome to you! What may I do for you?
Thereupon, the man born of Prajāpati spoke these words once more.

"O King, by worshipping the gods, this has been attained by you today. O tiger among men, take this milk-rice (pāyasa), fashioned by the gods, which produces progeny, is auspicious, and increases health."
"Give food, indeed, to your worthy wives;
through them you shall obtain the sons for whose sake you perform this sacrifice, O King.
"So be it," the king replied joyfully, accepting his command with his head bowed.
Having saluted that wondrous and pleasing being, he— filled with supreme joy— performed a circumambulation of the golden vessel given by the gods, which was completely full of divine food.
Then Daśaratha, having obtained the milk-rice prepared by the gods,
became supremely delighted, like a pauper who has acquired great wealth.
Then that being, of wondrous appearance and supreme radiance—
Having completed that task, he vanished right there.
His inner apartments shone with the radiance of his rays of joy,
like the sky illuminated by the beams of the delightful autumnal moon.
Having entered the inner apartments, he spoke thus to Kausalyā:
"Accept this milk-rice, which is for the sake of obtaining a son for yourself.
Then the lord of men gave half of that milk-rice to Kausalyā.
The lord of men gave half of that half to Sumitrā;
he gave the remaining half to Kaikeyī for the sake of obtaining sons,
and he gave the final remaining half of the milk-rice, which was like nectar, [to herself].
Having reflected thus, the lord of the earth once again gave that payasa separately to each of his wives, including Sumitrā.
Having received this payasa from the king, those excellent women—
With their hearts overflowing with joy, they all considered it a great honor. But when Viṣṇu had thus attained the status of son to that high-souled king,
the blessed Lord Svayambhū spoke these words to all the deities.
"Create for us powerful assistants who can assume any form at will— helpers for the hero Viṣṇu, who is true to his promise and seeks the welfare of us all—
and who are skilled in illusion, heroic, and equal to the wind in speed."

They were skilled in policy, endowed with wisdom, and possessed of prowess equal to Viṣṇu; they were incorruptible, experts in strategic means, and gifted with divine physiques; they were perfected in the mastery of all weapons, like those who have tasted the nectar of immortality.
Among the foremost apsarases and the bodies of gandharva women; among the daughters of yakṣas and pannagas, and among the ṛṣikas and vidyādharīs;
and upon the limbs of kinnarīs and the bodies of vānarīs.
"Procreate sons of equal prowess in the form of monkeys.
Having been thus addressed by the Blessed One and having promised to carry out that command,
they accordingly begot sons in the form of monkeys.
The high-souled ṛṣis, along with the siddhas, vidyādharas, uragas,
and cāraṇas, created heroic sons who were wanderers of the forest.
Once created, they numbered many thousands and were intent on the slaying of the ten-necked Rāvaṇa.

Those heroes of immeasurable strength, courageous and capable of assuming any form at will, possessing bodies like elephants and mountains and endowed with great power, were born with the forms of bears, monkeys, and cow-tailed macaques. They appeared very quickly.
Whatever was the form, the attire, and the prowess of each god,
from all of that combined, a son was born individually for each of them.
And some were born among the female langurs, possessing highly esteemed valor.
Likewise, those born of female bears and female kinnaras became monkeys;
all of them used rocks as weapons, all fought with trees,
all had claws and teeth as their arms, and all were experts in every weapon.
They could shake the lords of mountains, split firm trees,
and agitate with their speed the ocean, the lord of rivers;
they could tear the earth with their feet and leap across the great sea.
They could enter the vault of the sky and even seize the clouds;
they could capture wild elephants roaming intoxicated in the forest,
and with their roar, they could strike down the birds as they shrieked.
From such [monkeys] were born hundreds of thousands of great-souled troop-leaders, monkeys capable of changing their form at will;
these best of troop-leaders, in turn, fathered heroic monkeys.
1.016.018a Others took their positions by the thousands upon the plateaus of Mount Ṛkṣavat;
1.016.018c others occupied various mountains and forests.
[They sought] Sugrīva, the son of the Sun, and Vālin, the son of Śakra.
All those lords of monkeys attended upon the two brothers,
who were accompanied by those powerful leaders of monkey troops whose bodies resembled masses of clouds and mountains.
The earth became covered with beings of terrifying forms for the sake of assisting Rāma;
and when that horse sacrifice of the high-souled one had been completed.
Having accepted their shares, the gods departed as they had come.
Having completed the rules of his initiation, the king, accompanied by his group of wives, entered the city together with his servants, army, and vehicles.
Having been honored by that king according to their merit, those lords of the earth departed for their respective countries, joyful, after bowing down to the bull among sages.
When the lords of the earth had departed, King Daśaratha once again—
The illustrious one entered the city, placing the best of the twice-born at his head;
highly honored, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga proceeded together with Śāntā,
followed by the wise king and his retinue.
Kausalyā gave birth to Rāma, who was endowed with divine marks— the highly fortunate son who delights the Ikṣvākus and is half of Viṣṇu. Kausalyā shone with that son of immeasurable splendor.
Just as Aditi was favored by the god who wields the thunderbolt,
so too was Bharata, whose prowess was truth, born of Kaikeyī;
he was a direct fourth part of Viṣṇu, endowed with all virtues.
Then Sumitrā gave birth to two sons, Lakṣmaṇa and Śatrughna—
two heroes skilled in all weapons, who were endowed with half of Viṣṇu’s essence. Thus, four high-souled sons were born separately to the king.
Virtuous, worthy, and pleasing like the Proṣṭhapada stars,
he performed the naming ceremony (*nāmakarman*) after the eleventh day had passed;
[he named] the eldest, the high-souled Rāma, and Bharata, the son of Kaikeyī.
Then Vasiṣṭha, being exceedingly pleased, bestowed names upon them: he named the son of Sumitrā Lakṣmaṇa, and the other Śatrughna;
he then had all their birth rites and other ceremonies performed.
Among them, Rāma was the eldest, like a banner, and brought joy to his father;
he was held in high esteem by all living beings, like the Self-born Creator himself.
All were knowers of the Vedas and heroes; all were devoted to the welfare of the world.
All were endowed with wisdom and all were perfected in virtues; yet among them, the highly energetic Rāma, whose prowess is truth,
was exceedingly affectionate toward Lakṣmaṇa from childhood, and Lakṣmaṇa, the increaser of prosperity, [was likewise devoted to him].

Lakṣmaṇa, endowed with auspicious fortune, was always the doer of all that was pleasing to his elder brother Rāma, who delights the world; indeed, he was like another life-breath external to Rāma’s own body.

Without him, that best of men finds no sleep; indeed, he does not eat even the finest food brought before him without him. For when Rāghava mounts his horse and goes out on a hunt, [he cannot do so without him].
Then, with his bow, he followed behind him, guarding him;
for Śatrughna, the younger brother of Lakṣmaṇa, was always dearer to Bharata than his own life, and Bharata was likewise ever dear to him.
With his four highly fortunate and beloved sons, Daśaratha became supremely delighted,
like the Grandfather with the gods. When they were all endowed with wisdom and possessed of every excellence, [he was filled with joy].
Modest, renowned, all-knowing, and far-sighted—
then the righteous King Daśaratha, together with his preceptors and kinsmen, reflected upon the marriage of those [princes].

While that high-souled king was thus reflecting in the midst of his ministers, the great sage Viśvāmitra, possessed of immense splendor, arrived. Desiring an audience with the king, he spoke to the gatekeepers.
"Quickly announce that I have arrived— Kauśika, the son of Gādhi!
Hearing those words of his, they all ran toward the royal palace,
their minds agitated, impelled by his speech.

Having gone to the royal palace, they then announced to King Ikṣvāku that the seer Viśvāmitra had arrived. Upon hearing those words of theirs, the king, together with his domestic priest, remained composed.
He went out to meet him with great joy, as Vāsava goes to meet Brahmā. Seeing that ascetic of rigid vows blazing with splendor,
the king, his face beaming with delight, then offered him the guest-offering (arghya).
Having accepted the water-offering (*arghya*) from the king according to the rites prescribed in the scriptures, he inquired after the welfare and health of the lord of men. Then,
having approached Vasiṣṭha, that bull among sages likewise inquired after his well-being.
And he spoke to those highly blessed ṛṣis according to the proper custom. With delighted minds, they all entered the king’s residence, and being honored there, they sat down according to their rank.
Then, with a joyful mind, the most noble king, delighted and honoring him, spoke to the great sage Viśvāmitra:
"It is like the attainment of nectar, like rain in a land without water."
Just as the birth of a son to one who is childless with a worthy wife, or as the recovery of what was lost, or as the joy at a great success—
just so do I regard your arrival; welcome to you, O Great Sage!
"What supreme desire of yours shall I fulfill? Why are you so joyful?
O Brahmin, you have become a worthy recipient for me; by good fortune you have arrived, O righteous one!
Today my birth has borne fruit, and my life is well-lived."
Formerly, by the title of royal seer (*rājarṣi*), your splendor was illuminated by asceticism;
having now attained the status of a celestial seer (*brahmarṣi*), you are worthy of my manifold worship. Therefore, O Brahmin, this [gift] is a wonder to me and a supreme purifier.
"O Lord, by the sight of you, I have been placed in an auspicious field.
Tell me what you desire; for what purpose have you come? I wish to be favored so that I may increase your welfare."
"O Kauśika, you ought not to hesitate regarding this task;
for I am the doer in its entirety, since you are indeed my deity. Having heard these words, which were pleasing to the heart;
Having spoken words that were pleasant to hear, self-restrained, and humble, the supreme seer— renowned for his virtues and distinguished by his qualities—
attained the highest joy.
