Having heard those words of the lion among kings, which were so wonderful in their detail, the highly effulgent Viśvāmitra, his hair standing on end with joy, addressed him:
"O tiger among kings, this is worthy of you; it could not come from anyone else on earth."
"O tiger among kings, you who are born of a great lineage and are designated as a Vasiṣṭha— make a firm resolve regarding this matter that is in my heart; be one whose promise is true."
"O bull among men, I was observing a vow for the sake of attaining perfection. However, there were two Rākṣasas capable of assuming any form at will who acted as obstacles to it.
Even after my vow had been performed many times, these two Rākṣasas appeared at its conclusion."
Mārīca and Subāhu, both heroic and well-trained,
rained down a torrent of flesh and blood upon that sacrificial altar. When that firm resolve for the ritual observance had thus been desecrated, [the sages departed].
Having exerted my efforts in vain and being devoid of enthusiasm, I departed from that place.
O King, it was not my intention to release my anger;
for such was the nature of that practice that no curse could be uttered there.
"O tiger among kings, you ought to give me your own son, the heroic Rāma, whose valor is truth; he is my eldest son, still wearing the side-locks of youth.
For he is capable, being protected by me through my own divine splendor."
"In the destruction even of those Rākṣasas who are destroyers,
I shall grant him manifold blessings, of this there is no doubt;
by which he shall attain renown throughout all the three worlds."
Having encountered Rāma, those two are not able to stand their ground in any way whatsoever;
nor does any man other than the descendant of Raghu dare to slay them.
For those two wicked ones, though arrogant in their prowess, have now fallen under the power of the noose of Time.
"O tiger among kings, those two are no match for the high-souled Rāma.
O monarch, you should not harbor such affection for your son.
I give you my word: know that those two Rākṣasas are already slain."
"I know the high-souled Rāma, whose prowess is truth;
so too does Vasiṣṭha of great splendor, as well as these others who are established in asceticism.
If you desire the attainment of dharma and supreme fame upon this earth,"
"O Indra among kings, if you desire stability, you ought to grant me Rāma.
O descendant of Kakutstha, if all your ministers,
headed by Vasiṣṭha, give their consent, then send forth Rāma."
"You ought to grant me your beloved, unattached son,
the lotus-eyed Rāma, for ten nights of the sacrifice;
O Rāghava, let not this time of my sacrifice pass by."
"Act accordingly; may prosperity be yours, and do not set your mind on grief.
Having spoken these words, which were consistent with dharma and artha, the great sage Viśvāmitra, possessed of immense luster and a righteous soul, fell silent.
Having heard those words of the sage, which so utterly tore at his heart and mind,
the king was seized with great fear.
His mind distressed,
he moved from his seat upon hearing those words spoken by Viśvāmitra, O tiger among kings;
for a moment he was as if unconscious, but then regaining his senses, he spoke this.
"Rāma, the lotus-eyed one, is less than sixteen years of age;
I do not see in him the fitness for battle with the rākṣasas.
Here is this full akṣauhiṇī army, of which I am the lord and master."
"Surrounded by these night-stalkers, I shall go as a warrior;
these servants of mine are brave, valiant, and skilled in weapons. They are fit to fight the hosts of Rākṣasas, so you ought not to take Rāma."
"I myself, bow in hand, shall be the protector at the head of the battle.
As long as I draw breath, I shall fight against the night-stalkers. That excellent vow shall be fulfilled without obstacle, being well-protected."
"I shall go there myself; you ought not, Rāma, to take him. For he is but a child, unlearned, and does not know the relative strength [of forces];
he is neither endowed with the power of divine weapons nor skilled in battle."
"And he is no match for the Rākṣasas, for they certainly fight with deceit. Separated from Rāma, O tiger among sages, I cannot bear to live even for a moment; you ought not to take Rāma away."
"O Brahmin of noble vows, if you wish to lead Rāghava away,
then take him with me and his fourfold army.
O Kauśika, sixty thousand years have passed since my birth."
This one was obtained through great hardship; you ought not to take Rāma away.
For among my four sons, my love for him is supreme. You ought not to take away Rāma, the eldest and the foremost in righteousness.
1.019.012a What is the prowess of those Rākṣasas, whose sons are they, and who are they? 1.019.012c Of what stature are they, and who protects them, O bull among sages?
1.019.013a And how should Rāma counteract those Rākṣasas?

"O Brahmin, tell me everything by my own forces or by my stratagems against those who fight with deceit. O Blessed One, how must I stand in battle against those of wicked intent? For the Rākṣasas are indeed arrogant in their prowess."
Having heard those words of his, Viśvāmitra replied:
"There is a Rākṣasa named Rāvaṇa, born of the lineage of Pulastya.
Having been granted boons by Brahmā, he oppresses the three worlds intensely."
Surrounded by many rākṣasas, he is possessed of great strength and great heroism.
Indeed, it is heard that Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas, is of immense prowess;
he is the brother of Vaiśravaṇa himself and the son of the sage Viśravas.
When that one of great strength does not himself create an obstacle to the sacrifice,
then those two Rākṣasas of immense power,
Mārīca and Subāhu, being incited by him, will cause an obstruction to the sacrifice.
Thus addressed by that sage, the king then said to the sage:
"I am indeed not able to stand in battle against that evil-minded one;
therefore, O knower of dharma, show favor toward my son."
Gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, birds,
and serpents are not able to withstand Rāvaṇa in battle, much less human beings;
for that rākṣasa seizes away the prowess of the powerful in combat.
"O best of sages, whether accompanied by my own forces or joined by my sons, I am not able to fight him or his armies—
him who resembles an immortal, yet remains unskilled in battles."
"O Brahmin, my son is but a child; I will certainly not give up this little son of mine.
Furthermore, those two sons of Sunda and Upasunda are like Death itself in battle;
since they would cause obstacles to your sacrifice, I will by no means give up my son."
"Mārīca and Subāhu are both powerful and well-trained;
with either one of them, I would fight along with my circle of friends.
Having heard those words of his, spoken with syllables choked by affection, [Rāvaṇa replied:]
1.020.001c Samānyu, the son of Kuśika, replied to the lord of the earth:
1.020.002a "Having previously promised this matter, you now wish to abandon your vow. This reversal is unbecoming of this lineage, which is prone to passion."
"O King, since this is what is appropriate for you, I shall depart as I came. O descendant of Kakutstha, having failed in your promise, may you remain happy along with your kinsmen.
[Thus spoke] the wise Viśvāmitra, who was overcome with rage.

The entire earth trembled, and fear entered the gods. Perceiving the whole world to be in a state of terror, the great seer Vasiṣṭha— steadfast and firm in his vows— addressed these words to the king.
Born in the lineage of the Ikṣvākus, you are like another Dharma incarnate;
steadfast, firm in your vows, and glorious, you ought not to abandon righteousness. O Rāghava, you are renowned throughout the three worlds as a soul devoted to dharma.
"Follow your own duty; you ought not to bear the burden of unrighteousness.
O Raghava, for one who has promised 'I shall do this' but then fails to act, there occurs the destruction of the merit of sacrifices and charitable works. Therefore, O Rama, release me."

Whether he has mastered the weapons or not, the Rākṣasas will not be able to overcome him, for he is protected by the son of Kuśika as the nectar of immortality is guarded by fire. He is righteousness incarnate; he is the foremost among the valiant.
1.020.010c He is preeminent in wisdom in this world and the ultimate refuge of asceticism.
1.020.011a He knows the various weapons throughout the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile; 1.020.011c no other man knows him, nor shall any ever know him.
Neither any gods nor ṛṣis, nor asuras, nor rākṣasas,
nor the foremost of gandharvas and yakṣas, along with the kiṃnaras and mahoragas [could prevail],
for all the weapons belonged to the sons of Kṛśāśva, who were supremely righteous.

Long ago, when he was ruling the kingdom, they were given to Kauśika. Those sons of Kṛśāśva, born from the daughter of Prajāpati, were shaped like elephants, possessed of great heroism, radiant, and bringers of victory.
Jayā and Suprabhā, the slender-waisted daughters of Dakṣa,
gave birth to a hundred most radiant missiles and weapons;
formerly, Jayā obtained fifty excellent sons.
And Suprabhā also gave birth to another fifty sons, named Saṃhāras, who were immeasurable, able to assume any form at will, invincible,
difficult to assail, and exceedingly powerful for the destruction of the Asura armies.
This son of Kuśika knows those weapons exactly as they are;
moreover, he is capable of creating unprecedented ones, for he is a knower of dharma.
Such is the heroism of Viśvāmitra, who possesses great splendor and performs mighty austerities.
"O King, you ought not to entertain any doubt regarding Rāma’s departure.
While Vasiṣṭha was speaking thus, King Daśaratha, with a joyful countenance, summoned his son Rāma along with Lakṣmaṇa.
Having performed the rites for auspiciousness by his mother and his father Daśaratha,
and having been consecrated with auspicious mantras by the family priest Vasiṣṭha,
King Daśaratha kissed his beloved son on the head.
With a deeply pleased inner soul, he gave [the bow] to the son of Kuśika. Then, seeing the lotus-eyed Rāma focused upon Viśvāmitra, a wind blew that was pleasant to the touch and free from dust.
There was a great rain of flowers and the sounding of celestial drums;
as the Great-Souled One set forth, there arose the resounding blast of conchs and kettledrums.
Viśvāmitra went at the front, and then followed the highly illustrious Rāma.
Wearing side-locks of hair like those of a crow and bearing bows, the son of Sumitrā followed him;
both carrying quivers and holding bows in hand, they illuminated the ten directions like two three-headed serpents following the high-souled Viśvāmitra.
Those two noble ones followed him like the Aśvins following the Grandfather [Brahmā]; with their hands protected by leather finger-guards and wearing swords,
those two of great splendor were like the two sons of Agni following the inconceivable god Sthāṇu.
Having traveled one and a half yojanas on the southern bank of the Sarayū, Viśvāmitra addressed Rāma in sweet words:
"My child, take this water; let there be no further delay."
"Accept this collection of mantras, as well as Balā and Atibalā.
You shall have neither fatigue nor fever, nor any alteration of your form;
and the Nairṛtas shall not overpower you, whether you are asleep or heedless."

1.021.012a There is no one on earth equal to you in the strength of arms; 1.021.012c nor, O Rāma, could there be anyone equal to you in the three worlds. 1.021.013a Neither in good fortune, nor in courtesy, nor in knowledge, nor in the certainty of intellect, [is there anyone your equal].
"O sinless one, no one in the world is to be considered your equal.
Once these two sciences have been acquired, there shall be no one equal to you.
For Bala and Atibala are indeed the mothers of all knowledge."
"O Rāma, best among men, hunger and thirst shall not afflict you while you recite the *Balā* and *Atibalā* on the road, O descendant of Raghu;
for one who studies these two sciences, there shall also be incomparable fame upon the earth."
"O descendant of Kakutstha, these two sciences, endowed with splendor, were indeed given to my grandfather; for you, O righteous one, are his equal to receive them.
Truly, all these many virtues reside in you; of this there is no doubt."
"Through asceticism, these two shall become endowed with many forms.
Then Rāma, having touched water, pure and with a joyful countenance,
received those two sciences from the great seer of purified soul.
1.021.018e Endowed with knowledge, Rāma, possessed of great prowess, shone resplendently.
1.021.019a Having entrusted all his weighty duties to the son of Kuśika,
1.021.019c the three of them dwelt there by the Sarayū that night in great happiness.
When the night had turned to dawn, the great sage Viśvāmitra addressed Rāma, the descendant of Kakutstha, as he lay upon a bed of leaves:
"O Rāma, you who have brought noble offspring to Kausalyā, the morning twilight is now beginning."
"Arise, O tiger among men; the daily rites ordained by destiny must be performed.
Hearing those most noble words of the sage, the two heroic princes bathed, offered water libations, and recited the supreme prayer.
Having performed their daily rites, the two of great prowess, being greatly delighted, saluted Viśvāmitra, whose wealth is asceticism, and stood ready to depart.
As those two of great prowess set out, they reached the divine river that flows through the three paths.
Then, at that auspicious confluence of the Sarayū,
they beheld a holy hermitage belonging to sages of fierce splendor who had been performing supreme austerities for many thousands of years.
Seeing that holy hermitage, the two Raghavas were filled with supreme joy;
they spoke these words to the high-souled Viśvāmitra:
"To whom does this holy hermitage belong, and what man dwells here?"
"O Blessed One, we wish to hear this, for our curiosity is great.
Having heard those words of theirs, the bull among sages smiled and said,
"Listen, O Rāma, to whose hermitage this was in former times."
1.022.010a Kandarpa was embodied; he is called Kāma by the wise.

1.022.011a [He approached] Sthāṇu, who was performing austerities here, composed and restrained by his vows, 1.022.011c as the Lord of the Gods, having performed his marriage, was departing accompanied by the hosts of Maruts.
The evil-minded one assailed him, but was rebuked with a roar by the Great-Souled One.
O descendant of Raghu, as that wicked-minded one was being consumed by his fierce gaze,
all the limbs of his body shattered apart.
1.022.013 His body was destroyed there as he was being consumed by the high-souled one;
indeed, Kāma was rendered bodiless out of anger by the Lord of the Gods. 1.022.014 From that time forth, O Rāghava, he became renowned as Anaṅga ("the Bodiless").
And that glorious region of Aṅga is where he released his body.
This is his sacred hermitage, O hero; these sages were formerly his disciples, devoted to dharma, and no sin is found in them.
"O Rāma of auspicious appearance, let us dwell here tonight between these two holy rivers; tomorrow we shall cross them.
As they were conversing there, he [perceived it] with his long-sighted vision of asceticism.
Having understood this, the sages were supremely delighted and experienced great joy. Having offered the guest-offering, water for the feet, and hospitality to the son of Kuśika,
they subsequently performed the rites of hospitality for Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
Having received hospitable treatment and delighting them with their conversation,
they dwelt there very happily at that time in Kāmāśramapada.
Then, when the morning was clear, those two subduers of enemies performed their daily rites.
Placing Viśvāmitra at their head, they approached the bank of the river.
Then all those high-souled sages, firm in their vows,
having brought forward a beautiful boat, spoke to Viśvāmitra.
"May your lordship board the boat, preceded by the prince;
go upon your path safely, lest there be a lapse of time.
Having said "So be it," Viśvāmitra honored those sages.
Accompanied by those two, he crossed the river that flows toward the ocean.
Then, in the middle of the river, Rāma asked the bull among sages:
"What is this tumultuous sound of the water being split asunder?"
Having heard the words of Rāghava, which were filled with curiosity,
the righteous-souled one explained the certainty regarding that sound:
"O Rāma, on Mount Kailāsa there is a lake created by Mānasa."
O tiger among men, because it was created by Brahmā, this lake is called Mānasa;
from that lake flowed forth the river Sarayū, which embraces Ayodhyā,
being sacred as it issues from the lake of Brahmā.

"O Rāma, this incomparable sound approaching the Jāhnavī is born from the agitation of the waters; perform your salutation with self-restraint. Then those two, being exceedingly righteous, offered their salutations to both of them.
Having reached the southern bank, those two of swift stride proceeded onward.
Seeing that forest of terrifying appearance, which had never been entered before, the son of the best of kings, a scion of Ikṣvāku, questioned the bull among sages.
"Oh, how difficult this forest is! It resounds with the chirping of swarms of crickets, is strewn with terrifying beasts of prey, and filled with birds of dreadful cry;
it is filled with various kinds of birds warbling with fearsome sounds."
Adorned with lions, tigers, boars, and elephants, and crowded with *dhava*, *aśvakarṇaka*, *kakubha*, *bilva*, *tinduka*,
and *pāṭala* trees, as well as *badarī* shrubs— what indeed is this dreadful forest?
The great sage Viśvāmitra, possessed of great splendor, said to him:
"Listen, O child, descendant of Kakutstha, as to whose dreadful forest this is.
O best of men, these two districts were formerly prosperous."
1.023.016c Malada and Karūṣa were fashioned by the creation of the gods.
1.023.017a Long ago, O Rāma, when Vṛtra was slain,
the thousand-eyed Indra was overwhelmed by impurity and entered by the sin of killing a Brahmin due to hunger.
The gods and the sages whose wealth is asceticism bathed that Indra;
they bathed him with jars and cleansed away his impurity.
Having repeatedly cast his impurity and that of Kāruṣa upon this earth, [they purified him].
Then they experienced great joy born of the body of Indra,
when Indra became stainless, free from blemish, and pure;
well-pleased, the Lord granted an unsurpassed boon to that region.
"These two regions shall remain established and attain renown in the world as Malada and Karūṣa, for they have borne the impurities of my body.
"Excellent! Excellent! the gods said to that subduer of Pāka.
Having seen that worship performed for the region by the wise Śakra,
O subduer of enemies, these two provinces— Maladā and Karūṣa— have remained established for a long time, rejoicing in wealth and grain.
Then, after some time, there was a Yakṣī capable of assuming any form at will,
who possessed the strength of a thousand elephants;
her name was Tāṭakā— may you be blessed— and she was the wife of the wise Sunda.
"O Raghava, this wicked Tāṭakā, whose son is the Rākṣasa Mārīca who possesses the prowess of Śakra, constantly destroys these two regions,
Malada and Karūṣa."
She dwells here, blocking the path at a distance of more than half a yojana;
therefore, you must proceed to the forest where Tāṭakā resides. Relying on the strength of your own arms, slay this woman of evil conduct.
"By my command, make this region free once more of its thorns;
for no one is able to enter such a place,
O Rāma, which has been devastated by a terrible and unbearable Yakṣiṇī."

1.023.030a All this has been told to you regarding how this dreadful forest was completely devastated by the Yakṣī, and even today it does not recover. 1.024.001a Then, the supreme words of that immeasurable sage—
Having heard this, that tiger among men replied with auspicious words:
"O bull among sages, since it is heard that yakṣas possess little prowess,
how is it that this weak woman sustains the strength of a thousand nāgas?"
Viśvāmitra spoke these words: "Listen to how she became superior in strength;
how this woman, though weak, maintains her power through the heroic energy granted by a boon.
Formerly, there was a great yakṣa of great prowess named Suketu."

Childless and of virtuous conduct, he performed great austerities. Then, O Rāma, the Grandfather (Brahmā), being well-pleased with that lord of the Yakṣas, gave him a jewel of a daughter known by the name Tāṭakā.
The Grandfather granted her the strength of a thousand elephants,
yet the highly illustrious Brahmā did not grant a son to the Yakṣa. When she was born and grew up, endowed with beauty and youth, [he gave her to him].

He gave his illustrious daughter as a wife to Sundā, the son of Jambha. Then, after some time, the Yakṣī gave birth to a son named Mārīca, who was difficult to overcome; he became a Rākṣasa due to a curse.
O Rāma, when Sunda had been slain, Tāṭakā desired to assault Agastya, the best of sages,
together with her son.
He addressed Mārīca, saying, "Assume the form of a rākṣasa."
1.024.010c Agastya, being extremely enraged, cursed Tāṭakā as well:
1.024.011a “O great Yakṣī, man-eater, deformed and with a distorted face! 1.024.011c Abandoning this form, let there be a dreadful form for you!”
"This very Tāṭakā, filled with indignation caused by the curse and overwhelmed by rage,
is destroying this auspicious region frequented by Agastya.
O Rāghava, [subdue] this wicked Yakṣī, who is most cruel."
"For the sake of the welfare of cows and Brahmins, slay her who possesses wicked prowess;
for indeed, in the three worlds, no man other than you, O delight of the Raghus, dares to strike her who is possessed by a curse."
"O best of men, you should not feel compassion for the sake of killing a woman;
a prince must act for the benefit of the four social orders. This is the eternal duty of those appointed to bear the burden of sovereignty."
"O Kākutstha, abandon this unrighteous woman, for no dharma exists in her.
Indeed, O King, it is heard that in ancient times Śakra slew Mantharā, the daughter of Virocana,
when she desired to destroy the earth."

O Rāma, in ancient times, Viṣṇu destroyed the wife of Bhr̥gu, who was firm in her vows, because she desired a world without Indra; she was the mother of Kāvya. By these and many other high-souled princes, [the earth has been protected].
"The women who were devoted to unrighteousness have been slain by the best of men.
Having heard the sage’s words, which were free from weakness, Rāghava— the son of the foremost of men and firm in his vows— joined his palms in reverence and replied.

"By the instruction of my father's word, out of reverence for my father's command, the word of Kauśika must be carried out without hesitation. I have been instructed thus by the high-souled one in the midst of my elders in Ayodhyā."
"My father Daśaratha must not disregard those words of his;
therefore, having heard my father's speech and by the command of that knower of Brahman,
I shall carry out the supreme slaying of Tāṭakā— of this there is no doubt."
"For the sake of the welfare of cows and Brahmins, for the happiness of this land,
and to carry out the command of you, the immeasurable one, I am prepared.
Having spoken thus, the subduer of enemies gripped his bow by the middle with his fist.
He let out a fierce twang of his bowstring, filling the quarters with the sound. Terrified by that noise, Tāṭakā and the forest-dwellers were struck with fear;
and Tāṭakā herself, provoked to great anger, was bewildered by that sound.
Reflecting upon that sound, the Rākṣasī, overwhelmed with rage,
heard it and rushed with speed toward the place from which the sound had issued.
Seeing her— enraged, deformed, and with a distorted face— Rāghava [stood firm].
And seeing her exceedingly increased in size by that magic power, he addressed Lakṣmaṇa:
"Behold, Lakṣmaṇa, the terrifying and dreadful form of this Yakṣiṇī;
at the mere sight of her, the hearts of the timid would surely shatter."
"Behold her, invincible and endowed with the power of illusion.
Today I shall turn her back, having deprived her of the tips of her ears and her nose;
for I cannot bring myself to kill her while she is protected by her feminine nature."
"It is my intention that I shall destroy both her prowess and her course.
While Rāma was speaking thus, Tāṭakā, overwhelmed with rage,
raised her arms and, roaring, rushed directly toward Rāma.
As she was rushing forward with speed, like a leaping thunderbolt, he pierced her in the chest with an arrow; she fell down and died.
Then, seeing her slain—she who was of terrifying appearance—the Lord of the Gods [was struck with wonder].
"Excellent! Excellent! the gods cried out as they honored the descendant of Kakutstha.
Then Purandara, the thousand-eyed Indra, being supremely pleased, spoke;
and all the gods, filled with joy, addressed Viśvāmitra.
"O Sage Kauśika, may it be well with you! All the hosts of Maruts, together with Indra, have been gratified by this deed. Show your affection toward Rāghava.
[Bring] the sons of Prajāpati Bhṛśāśva, whose prowess is truth."
"O Brahmin, announce those who possess the power of asceticism to Rāghava.
O Brahmin, he is a worthy recipient for you and is resolved to follow you;
moreover, a great task for the gods must be performed by the prince."

Having spoken thus, all the gods, delighted, departed as they had come after honoring Viśvāmitra; then the twilight began. Thereupon, the best of sages was filled with joy, gratified by the slaying of Tāṭakā.
Smelling the crown of Rāma’s head, he spoke these words:
“O Rāma of auspicious appearance, let us stay here tonight;
tomorrow at dawn we shall go to that hermitage of mine.”
Then, having spent that night, the highly illustrious Viśvāmitra smiled and addressed Rāghava in sweet-sounding words:
"I am well-pleased; may prosperity be yours, O prince of great renown."

"Endowed with supreme affection, I give you all these weapons by which you shall conquer and bring under your control your enemies in battle, even the hosts of gods and asuras, along with the gandharvas and uragas."

"May you be blessed; I shall give you all those divine weapons in their entirety. O Rāghava, I will give you the great divine Staff-wheel (Daṇḍacakra), and likewise, O hero, the Wheel of Dharma (Dharmacakra) and the Wheel of Time (Kālacakra)."
O best of men, O Rāghava, [he received] the exceedingly fierce discus of Viṣṇu, as well as the discus of Indra,
the thunderbolt weapon, the excellent trident of Śiva,
and also the Brahmaśiras weapon and the Aiṣīka weapon.
"O mighty-armed one, I give to you the unsurpassed Brahma-weapon; and also,
O descendant of Kakutstha, both maces— Modakī and Śikharī— blazing and fierce, O tiger among men, I bestow them upon you, O prince."
"O Rāma, I give you the noose of Dharma and likewise the noose of Time;
I give you the supreme weapon, the noose of Varuṇa. O delighter of the Raghus, I bestow upon you two thunderbolts, the dry and the wet."
I give you the Paināka weapon and likewise the Nārāyaṇa weapon;
I give you the beloved Āgneya weapon known by the name Śikhara, and the first Vāyavya weapon, O Rāghava.
"O sinless descendant of Kakutstha, I give to you the weapon named Hayaśiras, as well as the Krauñca weapon, two Śaktis,
the Kaṅkāla, the terrible Musala, the Kāpāla, and the Kaṅkaṇa."
"O mighty-armed son of the best of men, I give you all these which the Asuras possess: the great Vaidyādhara weapon known by the name Nandana, and the jewel among swords."
"O Rāghava, I give you the beloved Gāndharva weapon known by the name Mānava, as well as the Saura weapon for inducing sleep and pacifying,
and the Darpaṇa, Śoṣaṇa, Saṃtāpana, and Vilāpana weapons."
"O tiger among men, O prince of great renown, accept this invincible *madana* weapon, beloved of Kandarpa, as well as the favorite *paiśāca* weapon known by the name *mohana*."
O tiger among men, [he gave him] the Tāmasa weapon and the Saumana of great power;
O son of a king, [he gave him] the invincible Saṃvarta and the Mausala;
O mighty-armed one, [he gave him] the Satya weapon as well as the supreme Māyādhara.
The weapon named Ghoratejaḥprabha, which draws away the energy of others; the Soma-weapon named Śiśira; the Tvaṣṭra-weapon named Sudāmāna;
the terrible Śīteṣu of Bhaga; and then the Mānava weapon.
"O mighty-armed son of a king, accept these most noble ones, who can assume any form at will and possess great strength; do so immediately.
Having purified yourself and being self-restrained, stand facing the east."
Being well-pleased, he bestowed upon Rāma that unsurpassed collection of mantras. As the wise sage Viśvāmitra was chanting them,
all the highly precious weapons presented themselves before the descendant of Raghu.

Then, all of them, filled with joy, spoke to Rāma with palms joined in reverence: "O most noble one, O Rāghava, here we are, your servants. And Kākutstha, having accepted this, touched them with his hand.
"Be present in my mind," he urged them.
Then, with a joyful heart, the immensely radiant Rāma paid homage to the great sage Viśvāmitra and prepared to depart.
Having received the weapons, his face beaming with joy and purified, the descendant of Kakutstha spoke to Viśvāmitra even as he was departing:
"O Blessed One, I have now acquired the weapons; I am invincible even by the gods."
"O bull among sages, I desire the withdrawal of these weapons.
When the descendant of Kakutstha had spoken thus, the great sage Viśvāmitra— steadfast, firm in his vows, pure, and highly disciplined— then explained the method of their withdrawal.
Satyavān, Satyakīrti, Dhṛṣṭa, and Rabhasa;
Pratihāratara by name, Parāṅmukha, and Avāṅmukha;
Lakṣākṣa and Viṣama, as well as Dṛḍhanābha and Sunābhaka.
Daśākṣa and Śatavaktra, Daśaśīrṣa and Śatodara; Padmanābha and Mahānābha, Dundunābha and Sunābhaka;
Jyotiṣa and Kṛśana, and both Nairāśya and Vimala.
Yaugandhara and Haridra, as well as Daityapramathana; Saumanasa and Vidhūta, both of whom have the form of makaras; Karavīraka, and Dhanadhānya, O Rāghava.
O Rāma, [the sons of Bhṛśāśva were] Kāmarūpa, Kāmaruci, Moha, Āvaraṇa,
Jṛmbhaka, Sarvanābha, Santāna, and Varaṇa—
all radiant and able to assume any form at will.
"Accept them from me; may it be well with you, for you are a worthy recipient, O Rāghava.
Then those beings, possessing divine and radiant bodies, embodied and bestowing happiness, spoke sweet words to Rāma with palms joined in reverence.
"O tiger among men, here we are; command us, what shall we do for you?
To them, the joy of the Raghus replied, "You may go as you please;
however, at times of need, you who dwell in Lake Mānasa must provide me with assistance."
Then, having taken leave of Rāma and circumambulated him,
they said to the descendant of Kakutstha, "So be it," and departed as they had come.
And that Rāghava, having learned of them, [approached] the great sage Viśvāmitra.
As he was walking along, he then spoke these sweet and gentle words:
"What is this that appears like a cloud not far from the mountain? This grove of trees shines forth from here; indeed, my curiosity is great."

"O best of sages, we have emerged from this hair-raising wilderness, which is beautiful to behold, teeming with deer, exceedingly enchanting, and adorned with various kinds of birds that warble sweetly."
"By this very state of well-being in the region, I understand;
O Blessed One, tell me everything: whose hermitage is this, where those sinful slayers of Brahmins and evildoers have arrived?"
Then, as that immeasurable one was questioning him about that forest,
the immensely radiant Viśvāmitra began to explain:
"O Rāma, this is the former hermitage of the high-souled Vāmana."
It is renowned as Siddhāśrama, for it was here that the great ascetic attained perfection.
At that very time, however, King Bali, the son of Virocana,
having conquered the hosts of gods along with Indra and the Maruts, [ruled the earth].
Renowned throughout the three worlds, he caused that kingdom to be governed. While Bali was performing the sacrifice, the gods, led by Agni,
assembled together and spoke to Viṣṇu himself here in this hermitage.
"O Viṣṇu, Bali the son of Virocana is performing a supreme sacrifice. Before that ritual is completed, let him attain his own purpose—
those supplicants who approach him from here and there."

Whatever is required, wherever it is needed, and in whatever manner— all that you bestow upon them. Therefore, O Viṣṇu, for the sake of the welfare of the gods, having resorted to the yoga of illusion and assumed the form of a dwarf, perform this supreme auspicious deed.
"By your grace, this shall become known as Siddhāśrama. O Lord of Gods, once the task is accomplished, arise, O Blessed One, from here.
Then Viṣṇu, of great splendor, was born of Aditi.
Assuming the form of a dwarf, he approached the son of Virocana; then,
having begged for three paces of land and received them with respect,
the Soul of the World— who delights in the welfare of all beings— struck across the worlds.
Having subdued Bali by his might,
he of great splendor once again made the three worlds subject to Śakra. By him, this hermitage, which destroys all fatigue, was formerly occupied.
"By me also, out of devotion, this [hermitage] of Vāmana is being enjoyed.
Rakshasas who cause obstacles come to this hermitage;
here, O tiger among men, those evildoers must be slain by you."
"O Rāma, today we shall go to the unsurpassed Siddhāśrama.
That hermitage, dear one, belongs to you just as it does to me.
Having seen him, all the sages dwelling in Siddhāśrama [welcomed him].
Rising up again and again, they suddenly paid homage to Viśvāmitra;
they performed worship for the wise Viśvāmitra according to his merit,
and likewise performed the rites of hospitality for the two princes.
Then, having rested for a moment, the two princes, subduers of their enemies and joy of the Raghus, spoke with joined palms to that tiger among sages:
"O bull among sages, may you be blessed; enter upon the initiation this very day."

"May this Siddhāśrama become perfected; let your word be true. Thus addressed, the great sage Viśvāmitra, possessed of great splendor, entered upon the initiation, self-restrained and with his senses controlled.
The two princes also, having spent that night with great composure,
rose at the time of dawn and paid homage to Viśvāmitra.
Then those two princes, subduers of their enemies, who were knowledgeable of place and time, [proceeded].
Knowing the proper place and time for speech, the two of them addressed these words to Kauśika:
"O Blessed One, we wish to hear at what time those two night-stalkers are to be guarded against; O Brahmin, that moment must not be allowed to pass."
As the two descendants of Kakutstha were speaking thus, eager for battle,
all those sages joyfully praised the two princes:
"O Raghavas, from this day forth, protect [us] for six nights."
"For this sage has entered upon initiation and will observe silence.
Having heard those words, the two illustrious princes remained sleepless for six days and nights, guarding the penance grove.
Those two heroes, supreme archers and subduers of enemies, remained vigilant and kept watch; they protected Viśvāmitra, the best of sages. Then, as time passed, the sixth day arrived.
Rāma said to the son of Sumitrā, "Be vigilant and composed.
As Rāma was speaking thus, eager for battle,
the sacrificial altar, along with the teachers and domestic priests, suddenly blazed up.
And that sacrifice proceeded according to rule with the chanting of mantras;
and a great, terrifying sound manifested in the sky,
like a cloud emerging in the rainy season and covering the heavens.
1.029.010c Thus, manifesting their illusory powers (*māyā*), the two Rākṣasas rushed forward.
1.029.011a Mārīca and Subāhu, as well as their followers, 1.029.011c approaching with terrifying forms, discharged torrents of blood.
Seeing those two suddenly rushing toward him,
the lotus-eyed Rāma looked at Lakṣmaṇa and spoke these words:
"Behold, Lakṣmaṇa, these wicked flesh-eating rākṣasas."
Like clouds driven away by the wind,
Rāghava, filled with supreme rage, discharged at Mārīca the most exalted and brilliantly radiant Mānava weapon, O Rāma.
Struck by that supreme weapon, the Mānava,
he was cast a full hundred yojanas into the surging ocean,
unconscious, reeling, and tormented by the power of the cold-tipped arrow.
1.029.016c Having seen the illusory Mārīca cast down, Rāma said to Lakṣmaṇa:
1.029.017a "Behold, Lakṣmaṇa, this Śīteṣu arrow, endowed with the power of Mānava;
it carries him away after bewildering him, yet he is not deprived of his life."
"I shall also slay these merciless,
evil-doing Rākṣasas— who abide in sinful deeds, who destroy sacrifices, and who feed on blood.
Having seized that exceedingly great Āgneya weapon, the joy of the Raghus [prepared to strike].

Subāhu hurled [the weapon], and being pierced, he fell to the earth. Taking up the Vāyavya weapon, the highly illustrious Rāghava, most noble, struck down the remaining [demons], bringing joy to the sages.
1.029.021a Having slain all those Rākṣasas who were destroyers of the sacrifice, the joy of the Raghus was honored there by the sages, just as Indra was in ancient times upon his victory.
1.029.022a Then, when the sacrifice was completed, the great sage Viśvāmitra—
Seeing the quarters of the sky free from calamity, she spoke thus to the descendant of Kakutstha:
"O mighty-armed one, I have achieved my purpose; you have fulfilled the word of your elder.
O illustrious Rāma, this Siddhāśrama has truly been made real."

Then, having accomplished their purpose, the two heroic brothers Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa spent that night there, joyful and delighted in their innermost hearts. When the night had turned to dawn, they performed their morning rites.
Together they approached Viśvāmitra and the other sages. Having saluted the best of munis, who was blazing like a fire,
those two sweet-spoken ones addressed him with words that were both sweet and noble.
"O tiger among sages, here we two, your servants, have arrived.
Command us as you wish; what instruction shall we carry out?
When they had spoken thus, all the great seers [responded] to them.
Placing Viśvāmitra at their head, they spoke these words to Rāma:
"O best of men, there will be a most righteous sacrifice for Janaka, the King of Mithilā; we shall go there."
"And you too, O tiger among men, shall go there with us;
you ought to behold that wonderful jewel of a bow,
for it was formerly bestowed upon that assembly by the gods, O best of men."

It possessed immeasurable power, was formidable, and shone most brilliantly at the sacrifice. Neither gods, nor gandharvas, nor asuras, nor rākṣasas were able to string it, much less any humans, by any means whatsoever.
1.030.010a For, desiring to test the power of that bow, the rulers of the earth—
1.030.010c even those princes of great strength— were unable to string it.
1.030.011a O tiger among men, that was the bow of the high-souled King of Mithilā.
"There, O descendant of Kakutstha, you shall behold a sacrifice of wondrous appearance.
For it was as the fruit of that sacrifice, O tiger among men, that Maithila requested from all the gods that supreme bow with its beautiful central ring."
Having spoken thus, the best of sages then set forth, accompanied by the assembly of seers and the descendant of Kakutstha, after taking leave of the forest deities:
"May it be well with you; having accomplished my purpose, I shall depart from Siddhāśrama."
On the northern bank of the Jāhnavī, having circumambulated the Himavat mountain range and the unsurpassed Siddhāśrama,
he then set out toward the northern direction.
As that best of sages departed, about a hundred carts of those who followed him and were exponents of the Veda accompanied him on his journey;
likewise, there were flocks of beasts and birds dwelling in the Siddhāśrama.
They followed the high-souled Viśvāmitra, the great sage.
Having traveled a long distance as the sun was hanging low,
those groups of sages, composed in mind, took up residence on the bank of the Śoṇa.
When the sun had set, those of immeasurable luster bathed, offered oblations into the fire,
and sat down with Viśvāmitra at their head.
Rāma also, together with the son of Sumitrā, having honored those sages, [sat down].
Then he sat down in front of the wise Viśvāmitra.
Then Rāma, endowed with great splendor and filled with curiosity, questioned the great sage Viśvāmitra, that tiger among munis.
"O Blessed One, what region is this, adorned with such flourishing forests? I wish to hear it; may you be blessed; you should tell me the truth.
Thus urged by Rāma's words, he of noble vows began to speak.
In that region, among the assembly of sages,
there was a great ascetic of immense penance named Kuśa, born of Brahmā,
who begot four sons equal to himself upon the princess of Vidarbha.
To Kuśāmba, Kuśanābha, Ādhūrtarajas, and Vasu— those endowed with brilliance and great energy, who desired to fulfill the duty of the Kṣatriya—
Kuśa spoke to his sons, who were most righteous and speakers of truth.
Having heard the words of Kuśa, all four of those foremost among men, esteemed by the world,
then established their cities.
The highly energetic Kuśāmba, for his part, founded the city of Kauśāmbī.
The righteous Kuśanābha brought about a supreme and great prosperity; O Rāma, the lord of the earth Ādhūrtarajas made Dharmāraṇya his capital,
and King Vasu made Girivraja his excellent city.
1.031.006a This is the earth belonging to that high-souled Vāsava, O Rāma;
1.031.006c these five excellent mountains shine forth on all sides.
1.031.007a The delightful river Sumāgadhī, renowned among the Magadhas, has flowed here.
She shines like a garland in the midst of these five principal mountains.
O Rāma, this is indeed the Māgadhī river belonging to that high-souled Vāsava; it has been frequented by him since ancient times, O Rāma, and is a fertile field adorned with rows of crops.
O descendant of Raghu, the righteous royal sage Kuśanābha begot one hundred peerless daughters upon Ghṛtācī. Adorned with fine ornaments, they were beautiful and endowed with the bloom of youth.
Having arrived at the garden grounds, like flashes of lightning during the rainy season,
O Raghava, they sang, danced, and played instruments;
adorned with excellent ornaments, they attained the highest delight.
Then those women, whose every limb was beautiful and who were peerless in form upon the earth,
arrived at the garden grounds like stars amidst the clouds;
they were endowed with all virtues and possessed of beauty and youth.
Seeing them, Vāyu, whose self is in all things, spoke these words:
"I desire you all; you shall become my wives. Abandon this human disposition, and you shall obtain long life."
Having heard those words of Vāyu, whose actions are effortless,
the hundred maidens then laughed at his speech and said:
"O best of gods, you move within all living beings."
"O best of gods, all of us know your power; why do you disregard us? O god, all the daughters of Kuśanābha are capable of displacing you from your station; let us rather protect our ascetic merit."

"Let there not be such a time for that fool; do not disregard your father, who speaks the truth. Let us attend to the *svayaṃvara* according to dharma, for our father is our master and he is indeed our supreme deity."
"Whichever of us our father gives to shall be our husband.
Hearing those words of theirs, the Lord Vāyu, the powerful master, became exceedingly enraged; entering all their limbs, he broke them.

1.031.021a Those maidens, shattered by the wind, entered the king’s palace. 1.031.021c Seeing them thus broken, the king, greatly agitated, spoke this: 1.031.022a "What is this? Tell me, my daughters! Who is it that disregards righteousness?"
"By whom have all these women been made hunchbacked, that you stand encircling me yet do not speak?
Hearing those words of the wise Kuśanābha,
the hundred maidens touched his feet with their heads and spoke.
"O King, Vāyu, who is the soul of all, desires to violate her;
following an evil path, he does not regard righteousness. We are under the protection of our father—blessings be upon you—we do not stand at our own will."
"Choose our father yourself, if he will give you to us.
Because he would not accept their words due to that persistent attachment to sin,
they all spoke thus and were violently struck down by the wind.
Having heard those words of theirs, the most righteous king, possessed of great splendor, replied to his hundred incomparable daughters:
"O daughters, you who possess forgiveness have shown forbearance; a very great service has been performed."
"Having reached a unanimous decision, my family has been spared by you.
For while forgiveness is indeed an ornament for women, it is also for men; yet that which was difficult to achieve has been endured by you, especially since you are among the gods."
"O daughters, as much forbearance as you all possess without distinction— O daughters, forbearance is charity, forbearance is sacrifice, and forbearance is truth;
forbearance is fame, forbearance is dharma, and the entire world is established upon forbearance."
Having dismissed the maidens, O descendant of Kakutstha, the king, whose prowess equaled that of the gods, being skilled in counsel,
deliberated with his ministers regarding the bestowal [of Sītā] at a time and place appropriate for such a gift.
At that very time, however, a great sage named Cūlī,
who was a perpetual celibate (ūrdhvaretas) of virtuous conduct, engaged in Brahmanic austerity.
While that ṛṣi was performing penance there, a Gandharva woman attended upon him.
"May you be blessed; at that time, she was the daughter of Ūrmilā, named Somadā.
Having bowed down before him, she dwelt there for a time, devoted to his service; being most virtuous, her preceptor became pleased with her."
And in the course of time, O descendant of Raghu, he spoke to her:
"I am well-pleased; may prosperity be yours! What pleasing service may I do for you?
Perceiving that the sage was satisfied, the Gandharvī spoke in a sweet voice:
Extremely pleased, she who was skilled in speech addressed him who was an expert in speech:
"Endowed with Brahmanic splendor, having become one with Brahman, and possessed of great ascetic power,
I desire a righteous son joined with Brahmanic austerity."
"I am without a husband—blessings be upon you—and I am not the wife of anyone. Since I have approached you through the *brāhma* rite, you ought to grant me a son.
Pleased with her, the brahmin seer gave her an unsurpassed son.
The son of Cūlin was known as Brahmadatta, born of his mind (mānasa). That King Brahmadatta then resided in the city of Kāmpilyā with supreme splendor, just as the King of the Gods dwells in heaven.

O descendant of Kakutstha, that most righteous King Kuśanābha then formed the intention to give his hundred daughters to Brahmadatta. Having summoned that Brahmadatta, the king of great splendor, the lord of the earth—

With a heart full of joy, the king gave him a hundred maidens; then, O descendant of Raghu, the protector of the earth, Brahmadatta, took their hands in marriage one after another, just as the Lord of the Gods did for his own daughters.
Then, as soon as their hands were touched, those hundred maidens—formerly hunchbacked—were freed from their affliction; endowed with supreme beauty, they shone forth at that time.
King Kuśanābha, seeing them thus liberated by Vāyu, [was filled with wonder].
He became supremely pleased and experienced joy again and again. Then the lord of the earth sent King Brahmadatta, who had completed his marriage, along with his wife and the assembly of preceptors.
1.032.026a Somadā too, being greatly delighted by her son’s worthy deed, 1.032.026c and those Gandharva daughters-in-law, according to custom, welcomed him.
1.033.001a O Rāghava, when the marriage was completed and Brahmadatta had departed,
Being childless, he performed the *pautrī* sacrifice for the sake of obtaining a son. While that sacrifice was being performed, Kuśa, the son of Brahmā, then spoke with great joy to King Kuśanābha:
"O son, you shall have a son who is your equal and deeply righteous;
through him, you will obtain Gādhi and eternal fame in the world.
Having spoken thus, O Rāma, Kuśa [dismissed] King Kuśanābha.
Entering the sky, he went to the eternal world of Brahmā. Then, after some time, to the wise Kuśanābha was born a son most devoted to dharma, known by the name Gādhi.
"O descendant of Kakutstha, that Gādhi was my father, most righteous in conduct.
O joy of the Raghus, I am born of the lineage of Kuśa and am known as Kauśika. And I have an elder sister, O Rāghava, who is devoted to her vows."
Named Satyavatī, she was bestowed upon Ṛcīka;
following her husband, she went to heaven in her physical body. That most noble woman became the great river Kauśikī.
Divine, with its holy waters and delightful, it rests upon the Himavat;
for the sake of desiring the welfare of the world, my sister has set out [upon it]. Therefore, I dwell happily and with self-restraint on the slopes of the Himavat.
Filled with affection for his sister Kauśikī, O delighter of the Raghus,
that virtuous and holy Satyavatī remained established in truth and righteousness; devoted to her husband, highly fortunate, she became the Kauśikī, the best among rivers.
"O Rāma, it was indeed by my own ascetic discipline that I abandoned her and came here;
having reached Siddhāśrama, I have attained perfection through your splendor. O Rāma, this is the account of my own birth and my lineage that I have proclaimed."
"O mighty-armed one, regarding that region about which you question me—midnight has already passed, O descendant of Kakutstha, as I have been telling these stories.
Go to sleep; may prosperity be yours, and let there be no obstacle to our journey here."
All the trees are motionless, and the beasts and birds are hidden;
the quarters of the sky are pervaded by the darkness of night, O delighter of the Raghus. Gradually the twilight fades away, and the sky appears as if covered with eyes.
The dense mass of constellations and stars shines with their lights;
and the cool-rayed moon, the dispeller of the world’s darkness, rises up,
O Lord, gladdening the minds of living beings in the world with its radiance.
"Then all nocturnal beings roam here and there—
the hosts of yakṣas and rākṣasas, and the fierce eaters of flesh.
Having spoken thus, the great sage of immense splendor fell silent.
"Excellent! Excellent! all the sages exclaimed, honoring him. Rāma, along with the son of Sumitrā, his wonder somewhat aroused, praised that tiger among sages and then retired to sleep.
Having spent the remainder of the night on the banks of the Śoṇa with the great seers, when the night had turned into a beautiful dawn, Viśvāmitra addressed them:
"O Rāma, the night has well dawned; the morning twilight is now proceeding."
"Arise, arise! May it be well with you; resolve to depart.
Having heard those words of his and performed his morning rites, he resolved to go and spoke these words.
"This Śoṇa river has auspicious waters, it is shallow and adorned with sandbanks;
O Brahmin, by which path shall we cross over?
Thus addressed by Rāma, Viśvāmitra spoke as follows.
"This is the path pointed out by me, by which the great seers travel. Having traveled a long distance on that road when half the day had passed,
they then beheld the Jāhnavī, the best of rivers, frequented by sages.
Seeing that river of meritorious waters, frequented by swans and cranes,
all the sages together with Rāghava became joyful;
they then established their camp upon its bank.
Then, having bathed according to the prescribed rule, having satiated the ancestors and the gods,
having offered the Agnihotra oblations, and having consumed the sacrificial food like nectar,
they entered the pure bank of the Ganges with joyful minds.
Surrounding the high-souled Viśvāmitra on all sides,
Rāma, with a joyful heart, then spoke to Viśvāmitra:
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear about the river Gaṅgā, which flows through the three paths."
"How did she, having traversed the three worlds, reach the lord of rivers and streams?
Thus urged by Rāma's words, the great sage Viśvāmitra began to recount the origin and the growth of Gaṅgā.
1.034.012a There is a great mountain-king named Himavat, a vast mine of minerals. 1.034.012c He has two daughters, O Rāma, whose beauty is peerless on earth.
1.034.013a The daughter of Meru, O Rāma, was the slender-waisted mother of those two.
1.034.013c By name Menā, she was indeed the charming and beloved wife of Himavat. 1.034.014a From her was born this Gaṅgā, the eldest daughter of Himavat;
1.034.014c his second daughter, O Rāghava, was named Umā.
Then all the gods, desiring to accomplish the purpose of the deities, requested the Lord of Mountains for his eldest daughter, Gaṅgā, the river that flows through the three paths.
Himavat gave his daughter, the purifier of the worlds, according to the law.
Out of a desire for the welfare of the three worlds, they accepted the Gaṅgā as she flowed according to her own will;
and for the sake of the three worlds, those who bring benefit to the three worlds took up the Gaṅgā and departed with hearts that felt their purpose was fulfilled.
O descendant of Raghu, there was another daughter of the mountain who,
having undertaken a severe vow, practiced asceticism as one whose wealth is her penance. To her,
who was engaged in such fierce austerity, the best of mountains gave his daughter.
To the peerless Rudra, [he gave] Umā, who is honored by the worlds. O Raghava, these two daughters of the King of Mountains, Gaṅgā— the best of rivers— and the goddess Umā, are honored by the worlds.

"1.034.021a This dharma has been declared to you, O dear one, best among those who possess movement, regarding how the river that flows through three paths first went to the sky. 1.035.001a When that sage had finished speaking these words, both Rāghava and Lakṣmaṇa— "
Having rejoiced at the discourse, the two heroes spoke to the bull among sages:
"O Brahmin, this supreme teaching endowed with dharma has been narrated by you.
You ought to speak further regarding the eldest daughter of the King of Mountains."
1.035.003 You are the knower of details; you know in detail how [the Gaṅgā] originates from the divine and the human realms.
By what cause does she, the purifier of the world, sanctify the three paths? 1.035.004 How did the Gaṅgā become renowned as the "Three-Path-Goaer," the supreme river?
"O knower of dharma, endowed with what deeds does one attain [this] in the three worlds?
When the descendant of Kakutstha had spoken thus, Viśvāmitra, whose wealth is asceticism,
related the entire story in its full detail in the midst of the sages.
Long ago, O Rāma, the great ascetic Śitikaṇṭha, having performed his marriage,
beheld the goddess with longing and proceeded to engage in sexual union.
A hundred divine years passed for the god Śitikaṇṭha.

"And yet, O Rāma, scorcher of enemies, no son was born to him from her. Thereupon, the gods, led by the Grandfather (Brahmā), became deeply anxious, thinking: 'What being will be produced here that shall withstand [him]? "
Having approached and prostrated themselves, all the gods spoke as follows:
"O God of gods, O Mahādeva, you who are devoted to the welfare of this world; it behoves you to show favor in response to the prostration of the gods."
"O best of gods, the worlds will not be able to sustain your splendor.
Endowed with Brahmanic ascetic power, perform penance together with the goddess;
for the sake of desiring the welfare of the three worlds, restrain your splendor within your own splendor."
"Protect all these worlds; you ought not to bring them to ruin.
Having heard the words of the deities, the Great Lord of all the worlds replied to them all, "So be it," and spoke this further:
"I shall maintain my splendor within my own splendor together with Umā;
let the thirty gods and the earth attain peace,
for this unsurpassed splendor of mine has been shaken from its place."
"O best of gods, tell me who will sustain that [mass] for me?
Thus addressed, the gods then replied to the bull-bannered one:
"The Earth shall indeed sustain this energy that has been agitated."
Thus addressed, the Lord of the Gods released [his seed] upon the surface of the earth,
by whose splendor the earth, including its mountains and forests, was pervaded.
Then the gods spoke again thus to the Consumer of Oblations (Agni):
"Enter that place of fierce energy, O one of great splendor, accompanied by Vāyu. Then,
pervaded again by fire, it became the White Mountain (Śvetaparvata) and the divine forest of reeds (Śaravaṇa), resembling both fire and the sun."
1.035.018e Where the greatly effulgent Kārttikeya, born from Agni, was born; 1.035.019a then the gods, together with the hosts of sages, [approached] Umā and Śiva,
and thereafter, with hearts full of joy, they worshipped them exceedingly.
Then, O Rāma, the daughter of the Mountain, filled with indignation and her eyes bloodshot with rage, spoke thus to all the gods:
"Since I have been prevented from uniting with him out of my desire for a son," [she cursed them all].
"You ought not to procreate offspring from your own wives;
from this day forward, let your wives be childless.
Having spoken thus to all the gods, he cursed the earth as well.
"O Avani, you shall have many forms and many husbands;
and because you did not desire my son, O woman of evil intellect, you shall not obtain the joy derived from having sons, for you have been defiled by my wrath."
Seeing all those gods thus ashamed, the Lord of the Gods then set out for the direction protected by Varuṇa.
Having gone there, he performed austerities on the northern side of that mountain.
On the peak arising from the Himalayas, Maheśvara dwells together with the Goddess.
This detailed account of the Daughter of the Mountain has been related to you, O Rāma;
now listen to me, along with Lakṣmaṇa, concerning the origin of the Gaṅgā.
In ancient times, while the god was performing austerities, the gods together with the hosts of sages approached the Grandfather, desiring a commander-in-chief.
Then all the gods spoke to the blessed Grandfather.
Having prostrated themselves, Indra and the other gods, led by Agni, spoke these auspicious words:
"O Lord, that general who was formerly granted to us by your holiness is now performing supreme asceticism together with Umā."

"O knower of ordinances, please provide whatever must be done hereafter for the welfare of the worlds, for you are our supreme refuge. Having heard these words of the deities, the Grandfather of all the worlds—
Consoling the gods with sweet words, he spoke this to them:
"That which was spoken by the daughter of the mountain—that you shall not procreate through your wives—is her unerring word; it is indeed the truth, there is no doubt."
"This is the Ganges flowing through the sky, in whom the Consumer of Oblations (Agni) shall beget a son,
a subduer of enemies, who will become the commander-in-chief of the gods. The eldest daughter of the Lord of Mountains shall honor that son."
"That will be highly esteemed by Umā, of this there is no doubt.
Having heard those words of his, O descendant of Raghu, all the gods, feeling their purpose fulfilled, prostrated themselves and honored the Grandfather.
1.036.010a Having gone to Mount Kailāsa, O Rāma, which is adorned with minerals,
1.036.010c all the gods appointed Agni for the sake of obtaining a son. 1.036.011a "O God, O Consumer of Oblations, accomplish this task of the gods!"

"O you of great splendor, discharge your seed into Gaṅgā, the daughter of the mountain. Having made this promise to the gods, Pāvaka approached Gaṅgā and said: "O Goddess, do indeed bear this embryo; it is a source of joy to the gods."
Having heard these words, he assumed a divine form;
beholding her majesty, he was scattered all around her.
Then the Fire-god consecrated the goddess from every side.
"O descendant of Raghu, all the channels of the Gaṅgā are full.
Then Gaṅgā spoke to him, the priest of all the gods:
"O Lord, I am unable to bear your uplifted splendor."
Being consumed by that fire, his consciousness deeply distressed,
the consumer of the oblations of all the gods then spoke this to Gaṅgā:
"Let this embryo be deposited here on the Himalayan foothill."
Having heard Agni’s words, O sinless one, Gaṅgā, possessed of great majesty, then released that exceedingly radiant embryo from her currents;
for that which issued forth from her shone with the luster of molten gold.
Gold reached the earth as pure and auspicious *hiraṇya*;
copper and black iron were likewise produced from its very intensity. Tin and lead became its impurities there.

Having reached the earth, this [seed] grew into various minerals. As soon as the embryo was deposited, the entire forest, though covered with mountains, became resplendent with splendors and turned entirely golden.
From that time forth, O Rāghava, tiger among men, that which was known as *jātarūpa* became gold, possessing a brilliance equal to fire. Then,
when that boy was born, Indra and the hosts of Maruts [approached him].
For the purpose of providing milk, the Kṛttikās made an agreement;
having established this supreme covenant regarding the newborn, they gave him their milk,
being resolved that "he is the son of us all."
Then all the deities said, "He shall be called Kārttikeya;
he will become a son renowned throughout the three worlds, of this there is no doubt.
Having heard those words of theirs, [the seed] fell during the discharge of the embryo.
Bathing him with supreme splendor, as if he were a blazing fire,
the gods called the highly fortunate Kārttikeya— who was like a flame to the descendant of Kakutstha— “Skanda,” because he had fallen from the flow of the womb.
Then, unsurpassed milk appeared for the Kṛttikās;
becoming six-faced, he drank the milk from their breasts. Having taken that milk in a single day, his body then became delicate.

By his own prowess, the Lord conquered the hosts of the Daitya armies. Then, having assembled with Agni at their head, the hosts of gods consecrated him of stainless luster as the commander-in-chief of the celestial forces.
"O Rāma, this detailed account of the Gaṅgā has been related by me to you,
as well as the auspicious and meritorious story of the Birth of Kumāra. Having thus narrated that tale in sweet words to Rāma, Kauśika—
Once again, he spoke these further words to the descendant of Kakutstha:
"In former times, there was a heroic lord of men, the ruler of Ayodhyā, named Sagara. He was a righteous soul who desired offspring, yet he remained childless."
O Rāma, the daughter of the King of Vaidarbha was named Keśinī;
she was the eldest wife of Sagara, most righteous and truthful in speech. She was the daughter of Ariṣṭanemi, peerless in beauty upon the earth.
Sagar’s second wife was named Sumati. Then,
having reached the Himavat mountain at the Bhṛgu-prasravaṇa peak, the king performed austerities together with those two wives.
Then, when a hundred years had been completed, the sage Bhṛgu— the best among the truthful— having been propitiated by his asceticism, granted a boon to Sagara:
"O sinless one, you shall obtain a very great number of offspring."
"And you shall attain incomparable fame in the world, O bull among men. "O dear one, one woman shall give birth to a son who will perpetuate your lineage;
another shall give birth to sixty thousand sons."
As that tiger among men was speaking, the two wives of the king, having propitiated him,
then spoke with great joy and palms joined in reverence:
"O Brahmin, whose son will be the one, and which woman will give birth to many?"
"O Brahmin, we wish to hear [this]; let your word be true.
Having heard those words of theirs, Bhṛgu, the most righteous one, spoke these supreme words: "Let your own will be carried out here."
"Whether there be one to perpetuate the lineage, or many who are exceedingly powerful,
renowned, and full of great energy— what [number] or what boon do you desire?
Having heard these words of the sage, O descendant of Raghu, Keśinī [replied].
O Rāma, in the presence of the king, Sumati then accepted as her son a lineage-bearing prince;
likewise, Suparṇa’s sister took sixty thousand sons who were highly energetic and renowned.
Having circumambulated the sage and bowed his head in salutation,
the king, together with his wife, went to his own city, O descendant of Raghu. Then,
after some time had passed, the eldest queen gave birth to a son.
Keśinī gave birth to the son of Sagara known as Asamañjas; but Sumati, O tiger among men, gave birth to a gourd-vessel containing the embryo.
From the breaking of that gourd, sixty thousand sons emerged.
Nurses raised them in jars filled with ghee,
and after a long time, they all attained youth.
Then, after a long period, they became endowed with beauty and youth.
At that time, Sagara had sixty thousand sons.
O best of men, the eldest among those born of Sagara,
O descendant of Raghu, took the children into the waters of the Sarayū.
Constantly laughing as he threw them in and watching them as they drowned, Aṃśumat—
the valiant son of Asamañja— was exiled from the city by his father for being intent on the harm of the citizens.
He was esteemed by all the world and spoke kindly to everyone. Then, after a long time, O best of men, a thought arose in Sagara’s mind, firmly resolved that he would perform a sacrifice.
Having made his decision, the king, who was learned in the Vedas, then proceeded to perform the sacrificial rites together with the assembly of preceptors.
O descendant of Raghu, at the conclusion of the discourse, having heard the words of Viśvāmitra—
Extremely pleased, he spoke to the sage, who was like a blazing fire:
"May you be blessed; I wish to hear this story in detail.
O Brahmin, how did my ancestor indeed perform that sacrifice?"
Viśvāmitra, however, spoke to the descendant of Kakutstha as if smiling:
"O Rāma, hear in detail the account of the high-souled Sagara.
There is a supreme mountain named Himavat, the father-in-law of Śaṅkara."
Having reached the Vindhya mountain, they looked at one another. O best of men, a sacrifice was commenced between them;
for that region, O tiger among men, is praised for sacrificial rites.

O Kākutstha, Aṃśumān, a great car-warrior of firm bow, abiding by the will of Sagara, performed that horse-sacrifice for him; while he was performing that sacrifice on the auspicious lunar day, Vāsava—
Assuming the form of a Rākṣasī, she carried off the sacrificial horse.
While that horse of the high-souled one was being carried away, O descendant of Kakutstha,
all the groups of preceptors then spoke to the sacrificer:
"O descendant of Kakutstha, this sacrificial horse is being carried away with speed during the festival; slay the abductor and let the horse be brought back.
This interruption of the sacrifice will bring misfortune to us all."
"O King, let it be done in such a way that the sacrifice remains free from flaw.
Having heard the words of the preceptor in that assembly, the monarch spoke these words to his sixty thousand sons:

"O bulls among men, I see no way for the sons of the rākṣasas to escape, for this great sacrifice has been undertaken by those highly fortunate ones purified by mantras. Therefore, go and search for them, my sons; may prosperity be yours."
"Follow the entire earth girt by the ocean;
O sons, traverse one *yojana* at a time in width.
Dig into the earth as far as the horse can be seen."
"Seeking that very stealer of my horse by my command,
I myself— having been initiated along with my grandson and the assembly of my preceptors—
shall remain here for your welfare until the horse is found."
Having spoken thus, O Rāma, those princes of great strength, their minds filled with joy yet constrained by their father’s command, descended to the surface of the earth;
each one [covered] a span of one yojana in length and breadth across the ground.
O tiger among men, they pierced [the earth] with their arms that felt like thunderbolts,
with spears resembling lightning, and with most dreadful plows;
as the earth was being split apart, O descendant of Raghu, it let out a roar.
O Raghava, as the Nagas, Asuras, and Rakshasas were being slain, there arose a roar from those creatures that was difficult to withstand,
O delighter of the Raghus, extending for sixty thousand yojanas.
The heroes pierced the earth down to the unsurpassed subterranean realm of Rasātala;
thus, O tiger among kings, the princes wandered everywhere, excavating Jambūdvīpa, which was crowded with mountains.
Then the gods, along with the Gandharvas, the Asuras, and the Pannagas,
all with agitated minds, approached the Grandfather.
With dejected faces, they then propitiated that Great-Souled One.
Extremely terrified, they spoke these words to the Grandfather:
"O Blessed One, the entire earth is being excavated by the sons of Sagara,
and many high-souled aquatic creatures are being slain."
"This destroyer of our sacrifice is carrying away the horse by means of this [deceit]," saying thus,
all those beings began to slay the sons of Sagara.
Having heard the words of the deities, the blessed Grandfather (Brahmā) indeed [spoke].
He replied to those who were greatly terrified and deluded by the power of Death:
"This entire earth belongs to the wise Vāsudeva;
assuming the form of Kapila, he supports the world incessantly."

"The eternal fissure of the earth was indeed witnessed, as was the destruction of the short-lived sons of Sagara. Having heard these words of his grandfather, O subduer of enemies, the thirty-three [sons]— 1.039.003a The eternal fissure of the earth was indeed witnessed; 1.039.003c and the destruction of the sons of Sagara, who did not live long. 1.039.004a Having heard the words of his grandfather, O subduer of enemies, the thirty-three...
The gods, exceedingly delighted, returned the way they had come. And as the earth was being split apart by the sons of the high-souled Sagara, there arose a sound like that of a thunderclap.
Then, having split the entire earth and performed a circumambulation of it,
all the sons of Sagara together spoke these words to their father:
"The whole earth has been traversed, and the beings dwelling within it have been destroyed."
Gods, dānavas, rākṣasas, piśācas, uragas, and kiṃnaras—we do not see that horse, nor indeed the stealer of the horse.
What shall we do? May prosperity be yours; let your wisdom deliberate upon this matter.
Having heard those words of his sons, O descendant of Raghu, Sagara, the best of kings, spoke these words in great anger: "Dig further, may you be blessed; break through the surface of the earth!"
"Having encountered the stealer of the horse, return once your purpose is fulfilled," they said,
as the sixty thousand sons of the high-souled Sagara, adhering to their father’s command, rushed toward the subterranean realm (Rasātala).
Then, as that [pit] was being excavated, they beheld Virūpākṣa, the elephant of the quarter, who resembled a mountain and supported the surface of the earth;
O descendant of Raghu, he held the entire earth with its mountains and forests.

The great elephant Virūpākṣa bore [the mountain] upon his head. O descendant of Kakutstha, whenever that great elephant shakes his head out of weariness for the sake of rest during the change of the moon, an earthquake occurs at that time.

Having circumambulated that great elephant, the guardian of the quarter, and honoring him, O Rāma, they proceeded, having pierced through the netherworld (rasātala). Then, having broken through the eastern direction, they further split open the southern one.
In the southern direction as well, they beheld a great elephant,
Mahāpadma by name, a high-souled being resembling a massive mountain;
seeing him supporting [the earth] with his head, they were struck with the utmost wonder.
Then, having performed a circumambulation of the high-souled Sagara,
the sixty thousand sons split open the western quarter.
Even in the western direction, they encountered one as vast as a mountain.
Those of great strength beheld the elephant of the quarter, Saumanasa;
having circumambulated him and inquired after his well-being,
they then proceeded to dig toward the direction presided over by Soma.
1.039.021a To the north, O best of the Raghus, they beheld one white as snow, 1.039.021c auspicious,
bearing this earth with an auspicious form. 1.039.022a Then, having touched him and performed a circumambulation of him, all [the brothers]—
60,000 sons split open the surface of the earth.
Then, having gone toward the renowned northeastern quarter,
all those sons of Sagara dug into the earth out of rage.
There they beheld Kapila, the eternal Vāsudeva, and the horse of that god wandering not far away. Recognizing him as the destroyer of their sacrifice, their eyes became clouded with rage.
Enraged, they rushed forward and cried out, "Stay! Stay!
"For you have stolen our sacrificial horse," they said. "O evil-minded one, know that we who have arrived here are the sons of Sagara."
O descendant of Raghu, having heard those words of theirs, Kapila was then overcome by great wrath and uttered a roar of defiance (*huṃkāra*). Then,
by that immeasurable and high-souled Kapila—
"O descendant of Kakutstha, all the sons of Sagara have been reduced to heaps of ashes.
Knowing that his sons had been gone for a long time, O delighter of the Raghus, King Sagara spoke to his grandson, who was blazing with his own splendor:
"You are brave and learned, equal to your ancestors in splendor. Seek out the path of your fathers, by which the horse has been carried away.
There are powerful and great beings dwelling within the earth."

"Take up your sword and bow for the purpose of repelling them. Having saluted those who are to be saluted, and having slain even those who create obstacles, return with your purpose accomplished, having reached the completion of my sacrifice."
Thus addressed by the high-souled Sagara, Aṃśumat,
taking up his bow and sword, departed with swift prowess.
He [reached] the subterranean path excavated by his high-souled ancestors.
Urged on by that king, O best of men, he entered [the city].
Possessed of great splendor, he beheld the elephant of the quarter being worshipped by Daityas, Dānavas, Rākṣasas, Piśācas, birds, and serpents.
Having circumambulated him and inquired after his well-being,
he questioned his ancestors as well as the stealer of the horse. Having heard those words of Aṃśumat, the elephant of the quarter spoke with affection.
"You shall accomplish your purpose without conflict; you will return quickly with the horse.
Having heard those words of his, he proceeded to question all the elephants of the quarters in due order and according to the proper rule.

Honored by all those guardians of the quarters, who were skilled in speech and experts in discourse, he was urged, "Go together with your horse. Having heard their words, he departed with swift prowess.
Where his ancestors, the oceans, had been reduced to heaps of ashes,
the son of Asamañja then fell under the sway of grief; overcome with supreme distress and deeply pained by their slaughter, he cried out in lamentation.
1.040.014a There, filled with pain and grief, that tiger among men saw a sacrificial horse wandering not far away.
1.040.015a That tiger among men beheld it, desiring to perform the water-rites.
Seeking water, the one of great splendor did not see any reservoir; then,
casting his keen gaze about,
O Rāma, he beheld Suparṇa, the lord of birds, the maternal uncle of the Pitṛs, who was like the wind.
And that mighty Vainateya spoke these words to him:
"Do not grieve, O tiger among men; this slaughter is approved by the world.
For it was by the immeasurable Kapila that these beings of great strength were consumed."
"O wise one, you ought not to give them ordinary worldly water.
O bull among men, Gaṅgā, the eldest daughter of Himavat,
the purifier of the world, shall sanctify these who have been reduced to heaps of ashes."
"This ash has been moistened by Gaṅgā, the beloved of the world;
she will lead sixty thousand sons to the heavenly realm. Go now, O highly fortunate one, taking the horse with you, O bull among men."
"O hero, you ought to complete the sacrifice of your grandfather. Having heard the words of Suparṇa, the exceedingly powerful and highly illustrious Aṃśumat quickly took the horse and returned.
Then, O descendant of Raghu, having approached the consecrated king,
he reported exactly what had occurred, as well as the words of Suparṇa.
Having heard those words of Aṃśumat, which were of a terrible appearance, the king—

He brought the sacrifice to completion according to the ritual manuals and according to the prescribed rules. Having performed the sacrifice, the illustrious lord of the earth returned to his own city;
yet, regarding the descent of the Gaṅgā, the king could not arrive at a firm decision.
1.040.026a Without having reached a final decision, the great king, after a long time,
1.040.026c having ruled the kingdom for thirty thousand years, departed for heaven. 1.041.001a O Rāma, when Sagara had passed away according to the law of time, the subjects...
They chose the highly virtuous King Aṃśumat.
O descendant of Raghu, that King Aṃśumat was exceedingly great;
he had a son who was known as the mighty Dilīpa.
O descendant of Raghu, having entrusted the kingdom to Dilīpa,
he performed most rigorous asceticism on a delightful peak of the Himavat for thirty-two thousand years, that highly illustrious one.
The king, whose wealth was his asceticism, having gone to the forest of penance, attained heaven.
But Dilīpa, possessed of great splendor, having heard of the slaughter of his grandfather,
could not reach a firm resolve because his mind was stricken with grief.
"How shall there be a descent of the Gaṅgā? How shall the water-rites for them be performed?
And how may I cause them to cross over?"—thus he became consumed by this thought, as he, whose self was known through dharma, reflected constantly.
A son named Bhagīratha was born, who was supremely righteous. Dilīpa, however, possessed great splendor; having performed many sacrifices, he ruled the kingdom for thirty thousand years.
Without reaching a decision regarding their rescue, O tiger among men, the king succumbed to the law of time due to disease;
the king went to the world of Indra by virtue of his own earned deeds.
1.041.010c Having consecrated his son Bhagīratha upon the delightful throne, that bull among men—
1.041.011a the righteous royal sage Bhagīratha, O descendant of Raghu— was childless despite his great splendor, yet he remained desirous of offspring.
O descendant of Raghu, he performed long austerities at Gokarṇa; with arms raised, practicing the "five-fire" penance, subsisting on air for a month, and having conquered his senses,
he remained engaged in that terrible asceticism for thousands of years.
Then the blessed Lord Brahmā, the sovereign and lord of creatures, being well-pleased,
approached together with the hosts of gods and spoke to the high-souled Bhagīratha as he was performing austerities.

"O illustrious Bhagīratha, O lord of men, I am pleased with you because of your well-performed austerities; choose a boon, O observer of noble vows. To him, the one of great splendor spoke to the Grandfather of all the worlds:
The highly fortunate Bhagīratha stood with palms joined in reverence:
"If the Blessed One is pleased with me, and if there is fruit from my asceticism,
may all the sons of Sagara receive water from me."
