"O God, if these remains of my great-souled ancestors were drenched with the waters of the Gaṅgā,
all my great-grandfathers would go to heaven forever;
and offspring should be granted, O Lord, so that our lineage may not perish."
"O God, let this be my supreme boon: that he be born in the lineage of the Ikṣvākus.
To the king who had thus spoken, the Grandfather of all the worlds replied with auspicious words, sweet and composed of melodious syllables.
"O Bhagīratha, great chariot-warrior, this desire of yours is a great one.
'So be it; may prosperity be yours,' [I say], O enhancer of the Ikṣvāku lineage.
This is the Haimavatī Gaṅgā, the eldest daughter of Himavat."
"O King, let Hara be appointed there to sustain her.
O King, the earth will not be able to endure the fall of Gaṅgā;
O hero, I see no one other than the wielder of the trident who can sustain those two."
Having spoken thus to the king and addressed Gaṅgā,
the god who created the worlds departed for heaven together with all the hosts of Maruts.
When that God of gods had gone, he [the king] remained with his thumb-tip pressed against [his nose].

1.042.001c Having made the earth [his wife], O Rāma, he waited upon her for a year. 1.042.002a Then, when the year was complete, the Lord of Umā, Paśupati, who is honored by all the worlds, spoke these words to the king:
"O best of men, I am pleased with you; I shall do what is pleasing to you.
I will bear the daughter of the King of Mountains upon my head.
Then the eldest daughter of Himavat, who is honored by all the worlds, [spoke].
Then, O Rāma, having assumed a form of immense size and an unbearable velocity,
she fell from the sky onto the auspicious head of Śiva; yet,
bewildered by the mass of his matted locks, that streak of light found no exit.
There the goddess wandered for many groups of years;
O descendant of Raghu, she was exceedingly gratified by this,
and then Hara released the Gaṅgā toward Bindusaras.
From the sky, [the water] fell upon the head of Śaṅkara and then reached the earth;
there it spread out, preceded by a fierce sound.
Then the celestial sages, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and hosts of Siddhas likewise [beheld it].
Then they beheld from the sky the earth below,
with celestial chariots shaped like cities, as well as excellent horses and elephants;
and there stood the deities, moving restlessly about.
That most wonderful and supreme descent of the Gaṅgā into the world was such that hosts of gods of immeasurable power gathered there, desiring to behold it;
and by the splendor of the ornaments of those descending throngs of deities, [the sky shone].
The sky, its clouds having vanished, shone like the sun with its hundred rays;
then, with schools of porpoises, serpents, and darting fish,
the atmosphere appeared as if scattered with streaks of lightning.
The sky was covered by white masses of water being scattered in a thousand directions,
like autumnal clouds overspread by flocks of swans;
in some places it moved very swiftly, in some places crookedly, and in some places far-reaching.
In one place it was bent, in another tossed upward, and in some places it moved very slowly;
in one place the water struck against water itself,
and after repeatedly rising toward the sky, it fell again upon the earth.
1.042.016a That water, having fallen from the head of Śaṅkara and then falling again upon the surface of the earth, shone then, stainless and free from impurity.
1.042.017a There, the hosts of ṛṣis and gandharvas, as well as those dwelling on the surface of the earth, [gathered].
They touched the water fallen from the limbs of existence, thinking it to be pure;
and those who had fallen from the sky to the surface of the earth by means of a curse,
having performed their ablutions there, became cleansed of all impurity.
Then, purified of their sins by that brilliantly shining water,
they re-entered the sky and returned to their own worlds. The world rejoiced, delighted by that radiant water.

Having performed his ablutions in the Gaṅgā, he was freed from all fatigue. The royal sage Bhagīratha, endowed with great splendor, mounted a divine chariot and proceeded ahead; the Gaṅgā followed behind him.
O Rāma, all the gods along with the hosts of ṛṣis, the Daityas, Dānavas,
and Rākṣasas, the foremost Gandharvas and Yakṣas, together with the Kiṃnaras and Mahoragas,
and all the Apsarases followed Bhagīratha’s chariot.
1.042.023c All the aquatic creatures followed the Gaṅgā with joy. 1.042.024a Wherever King Bhagīratha went, there the illustrious Gaṅgā,
1.042.024c the best of rivers and destroyer of all sins, followed.

Then King Sagara, followed by Gaṅgā, went and entered the subterranean realm where they had been reduced to ashes. O Rāma, when the ashes were indeed drenched by the waters of Gaṅgā, [the sons rose up].
1.043.002c Brahmā, the lord of all the worlds, spoke this to the king:
1.043.003a "O tiger among men, the sixty thousand sons of the high-souled Sagara have been delivered and have gone to heaven like gods."
"O King, as long as the water of the ocean shall remain in the world,
so long shall the sons of Sagara abide in heaven like gods;
and this eldest daughter of yours shall become the Gaṅgā."
And because of your deed, she shall indeed remain renowned in the world by your name;
she shall be known as Gaṅgā, Tripathagā, and the divine Bhāgīrathī.
Because she sanctifies the three paths, she is therefore remembered as Tripathagā.
"O lord of men, O King, offer water here for all your ancestors and fulfill your vow. For by that highly illustrious ancestor of yours, O King, [the vow was made] at that time."
"Even by that foremost of the righteous, O dear one, this desire was not attained;
likewise, by Aṃśumat, who possessed incomparable splendor in the world,
though he sought to bring the Gaṅgā, his vow was not fulfilled."

O highly fortunate one, by your father Dilīpa— a virtuous royal sage whose splendor was equal to that of the great seers, whose austerity was indeed equal to my own, and who remained steadfast in the dharma of the kṣatriyas— [this earth was protected].
"O sinless one, you have again requested that the Gaṅgā be led down, though she was not previously thought capable of being led; O bull among men, that vow has been fulfilled by you,
and you have attained the highest and most esteemed fame in the world."
"O subduer of enemies, because you have brought down the Gaṅgā, you have attained this great abode of Dharma. O best of men, bathe yourself in these waters that are ever worthy."
"O tiger among men, being pure in these waters, may you obtain the fruit of merit.
Perform the water-libation rites for all your ancestors.
May it be well with you; I shall depart for my own world—farewell, O King!"
Having spoken thus, the Lord of Gods, the Grandfather of all the worlds,
possessed of great glory, departed for the realm of the gods just as he had come.
The royal sage Bhagīratha, too, having offered the supreme water libations, [proceeded].
Having offered water oblations to the oceans in due order and according to the prescribed rule, the highly illustrious and pure king entered his own city;
having achieved all his goals, that best of men ruled over his own kingdom.
And the world rejoiced upon finding that king, O Rāghava;
with its grief destroyed and its purpose fulfilled, it became free from all distress.
This detailed account of the Gaṅgā has been related by me to you, O Rāma.
"May you attain well-being; may it be auspicious for you. The time for twilight is passing away.
This narrative concerning the descent of the Gaṅgā, which bestows merit, fame, long life, heaven, and even sons, has been recounted by me."
Having heard the words of Viśvāmitra, Rāghava, together with Lakṣmaṇa,
was struck with great wonder and then spoke to Viśvāmitra:
"O Brahmin, this most excellent account you have related is truly marvelous."
The descent of the Gaṅgā and the filling of the ocean were meritorious deeds; and for him,
as he contemplated that auspicious account of Viśvāmitra together with the son of Sumitrā, that entire night passed away.
Then, at the clear dawn, Rāghava, the subduer of enemies, having performed his daily rites, addressed these words to the great sage Viśvāmitra:
"The blessed night has passed; that which is most worthy of hearing has been heard."

O you of great asceticism, as I have been reflecting upon this entire narrative of yours in its full detail, this night, though long, has passed away as if it were but a moment. Let us now cross the most excellent of rivers, the sacred stream that flows through the three worlds.
"For this boat is well-spread with comfort for the sages of meritorious deeds;
having learned that the Blessed One has arrived here, it has come swiftly. Having heard those words of the high-souled Rāghava, [he replied].
Together with the assembly of sages and the descendant of Raghu, he caused them to cross over;
having reached the northern bank and likewise honored the host of seers,
they settled on the bank of the Gaṅgā and beheld the city of Viśālā.

Then that best of sages, accompanied by Rāghava, quickly proceeded to the beautiful city of Viśālā, which was divine and like unto heaven. Then the highly wise Rāma [addressed] the great sage Viśvāmitra.
With palms joined in reverence, he asked about the great city of Viśālā:
"O great sage, to which royal lineage does this Viśālā belong?
I wish to hear it—blessings be upon you—for my curiosity is great."
Having heard those words of Rāma, the bull among sages began to relate that ancient account of Viśāla. "Listen, O Rāma, as I tell you the auspicious story of Śakra."
"O Raghava, hear in truth what occurred in this place.
Formerly, O Rama, in the Kṛta Yuga, there were the mighty sons of Diti,
and the highly fortunate, heroic, and most righteous sons of Aditi."
Then, O best of men, this thought arose in those high-souled ones:
"How may we become immortal, free from decay, and indeed free from all affliction?
As they were reflecting thus, O Rāma, an insight occurred to those wise ones.

"By churning the Ocean of Milk, we shall surely obtain the nectar there. Having thus resolved upon the churning, they made Vāsuki the rope and Mount Mandara the churning-stick, and those of immeasurable prowess began to churn.

Then, O best of men, from the very essence produced by the churning of the waters, there arose the one named Dhanvantari and the most radiant Apsarases; because they emerged from that [essence], they became known as Apsarases.
There were sixty crores of those highly resplendent apsarases,
O descendant of Kakutstha, and their attendants were indeed innumerable;
yet none of them— neither all those gods nor the dānavas— would accept them.
And because he did not accept [the gift], they are remembered as being common to all.
Then, O descendant of Raghu, Varuṇa’s daughter, Vāruṇī,
the highly fortunate one, flew up, seeking a husband.
"O Rāma, the sons of Diti did not accept that daughter of Varuṇa;
but the sons of Aditi, O hero, accepted that blameless girl. For that reason, they are called Daityas because of Diti, and Suras because they are the sons of Aditi."
The gods were thrilled and exceedingly joyful at the acquisition of the Vāruṇī wine.
O best of men, the preeminent horse Uccaiḥśravas, the Kaustubha jewel,
and likewise the supreme nectar emerged.
Then, O Rāma, for his sake there occurred a great destruction of the lineage; the sons of Aditi then began to slay the sons of Diti. The heroic sons of Aditi struck down the sons of Diti.
In that terrible and great battle between the Daityas and the Ādityas,
Purandara, having slain the sons of Diti and obtained the kingdom,
joyfully ruled over the worlds together with the assemblies of ṛṣis and Cāraṇas.
When those sons had been slain, Diti, overcome with supreme grief,
O Rāma, spoke these words to her husband, Kāśyapa Mārīca:
"O Blessed One, I am one whose sons have been killed by your exceedingly powerful sons."
"I desire a son, earned through long ascetic penance, who shall be the slayer of Śakra. Therefore, I shall perform austerities; you ought to grant me a conception.
You ought to authorize such a son as the slayer of Śakra."
Having heard those words of hers, the immensely radiant Mārīca Kāśyapa then replied to Diti, who was deeply distressed:
"So be it; may prosperity be yours. Be pure, O lady rich in asceticism."
"You shall give birth to a son, O Śakra, who will be the slayer [of your enemies] in battle,
provided you remain pure for a full thousand years;
from me, you shall give birth to a son who will be the destroyer of the three worlds."
Having spoken thus, the one of great splendor wiped her with his hand;
then, having touched her and said "May it be well," he departed for asceticism.
When he had gone, O best of men, Diti was filled with supreme joy.
Having reached Kuśaplavana, she performed most severe austerities. O best of men, while she was performing those penances, the thousand-eyed Indra served her with supreme excellence of character.
The thousand-eyed Indra offered him fire, kusha grass, wood, water, as well as fruits and roots, and whatever else was desired;
he also served him by massaging his limbs and removing his fatigue.
Śakra attended upon Diti at all times. Then, O descendant of Raghu, when ten years were yet remaining of the thousand-year period,
Diti, being exceedingly pleased, spoke to the thousand-eyed one.
"O best among the powerful, ten years remain for you who have been performing austerities—blessings upon you; after that, you shall see your brother.
O son, for your sake, I shall restore him who is eager for victory."
"O son, free from all feverish anxiety, you shall enjoy the conquest of the three worlds together with me.
Having spoken thus to Śakra, when the sun had reached its meridian, the goddess Diti was overcome by sleep, placing her feet where her head should have been.
Seeing her impure, with her hair hanging down from her feet and her feet placed where her head should have been, Śakra laughed and rejoiced;
then Purandara entered the opening of her body.
O Rāma, the possessor of the supreme self split the embryo into seven parts. As the embryo was being pierced by the hundred-jointed thunderbolt,
it cried out with a clear voice, O Rāma, and then Diti woke up.
"Do not weep, do not weep," Śakra said to the embryo;
yet the immensely powerful Vāsava split it even as it was crying out.
"He must not be killed, he must not be killed! thus Diti cried.
Then Śakra, out of respect for his mother’s words, stepped forth.
With palms joined in reverence and holding his thunderbolt, Śakra addressed Diti:
"O Goddess, you were impure when you slept, having placed your hair at your feet."

"O Goddess, having found that opportunity, I split him who was the slayer of Śakra in battle into seven pieces; you ought to forgive me for that. When the embryo had been divided into seven parts, Diti was overcome with supreme grief."
She spoke these words with conciliation to the thousand-eyed, invincible one:
"O Lord of Gods, O Destroyer of Bala, it is through my own fault that this embryo has been rendered fruitless in seven ways; there is no fault of yours in this matter."
"I desire that a favor be done for me regarding the transformation of my womb:
let these seven become the guardians of the abodes of the seven Maruts.
Let these sons of mine roam in the sky as these seven Vātaskandhas."
"My sons, renowned as the Mārutas, possess divine forms.
Let one wander in the world of Brahmā, and likewise another in the world of Indra;
the third, of great fame, shall be known in heaven as Vāyu."
"O best of gods, may it be well with you; by your command, these four sons of mine, having become gods, shall roam through the quarters.
They shall be renowned as the Mārutas, named after you alone."
Having heard those words of hers, the thousand-eyed Purandara, the slayer of Bala, spoke these words with palms joined in reverence to Diti:
"All this shall happen exactly as you have said; of this there is no doubt."

"May it be well with you; your sons shall roam about as gods. Having thus made this resolution in the forest of asceticism, O Rāma, the mother and son departed for the third heaven, having accomplished their purpose—so we have heard.

"This is that region, O descendant of Kakutstha, which was formerly inhabited by Mahendra; it is there that he attended upon Diti when she had perfected her ascetic penances. And the son of Ikṣvāku, O tiger among men, was supremely righteous."
1.046.011c Born of Alambuṣā, he was renowned as Viśāla. 1.046.012a By him, this city named Viśālā was established in this place. 1.046.013a O Rāma, the son of Viśāla was the mighty Hemacandra.
1.046.013c Sucandra, renowned by that name, followed after Hemacandra.
1.046.014a O Rāma, the son of Sucandra was celebrated as Dhūmrāśva;
1.046.014c and the son of Dhūmrāśva became Sṛñjaya.
The illustrious and powerful Sahadeva was the son of Sṛñjaya;
Kuśāśva, who was supremely righteous, was the son of Sahadeva;
and the highly energetic and powerful Somadatta was the son of Kuśāśva.
The son of Somadatta was renowned as Kākutstha;
his son, possessed of great splendor and resembling an immortal, named Sumati, is now dwelling in this city— he is invincible.
"By the grace of Ikṣvāku, all the kings of Vaiśālī are indeed long-lived, high-souled, heroic, and very righteous. O Rāma, we shall dwell here tonight in comfort."
"O best of men, tomorrow at dawn you shall see Janaka.
But the highly illustrious Sumati, the most excellent of the best of men, having heard that Viśvāmitra had arrived, went out to meet him.
Having performed the highest honors, together with his preceptors and kinsmen,
he joined his palms in reverence, inquired after Viśvāmitra’s welfare, and then spoke to him:
"O Sage, I am blessed and favored that you have come to my realm."
"He has come into my very sight; indeed, there is no one more fortunate than I.
Having exchanged greetings regarding each other's welfare upon their meeting, at the conclusion of their conversation, Sumati addressed these words to the great sage.
"May it be well with you; here are these two youths, whose prowess is equal to that of the gods,
who have the gait of elephants and lions, who are heroes resembling tigers and bulls,
and whose large eyes are like lotus petals, bearing swords, quivers, and bows."

"Resembling the Aśvins in beauty, with youth fully matured, they have arrived here by mere chance like two immortals from the world of the gods. O sage, how did they come here on foot, for what purpose, and to whom do they belong?"
Adorning this region like the sun and moon adorning the sky,
you two are equal to one another in stature, gestures, and movements. And for what purpose, O best of men, have you arrived upon this difficult path?
"I wish to hear in truth about those two heroes who bear excellent weapons.
Having heard those words of his, he related everything exactly as it had happened,
including their residence at Siddhāśrama and the slaughter of the Rākṣasas.

Having heard the words of Viśvāmitra, the king was filled with supreme joy; he honored those two mighty sons of Daśaratha— who had arrived as most excellent guests— according to the prescribed rites, for they were worthy of hospitality.

Then, having received the highest honors from Sumati, the two descendants of Raghu stayed there for one night and proceeded from there to Mithilā. Seeing that auspicious city of Janaka, all the sages [welcomed them].
"Excellent! Excellent! they exclaimed in praise, and thus honored him as he entered Mithilā.
There, in the grove of Mithilā, Rāghava beheld an ancient, secluded, and delightful hermitage, and questioned that bull among sages.
"O Blessed One, what is this place that resembles a glorious hermitage yet is devoid of sages?
I wish to hear, O Lord, whose hermitage was this in former times? Having heard those words spoken by Rāghava, he who was skilled in speech replied:
The great sage Viśvāmitra, endowed with immense splendor, replied:
"Ah, I shall tell you; listen to the truth of it, O Rāghava, as to whose hermitage this was cursed in anger by that high-souled one."

O best of men, formerly there was the hermitage of the high-souled Gautama, which resembled a celestial realm and was highly honored even by the gods. In ancient times, he performed austerities here together with Ahalyā.
O prince of great renown, for many countless series of years,
the thousand-eyed lord of Śacī, perceiving an opportunity,
assumed the guise of a sage and spoke these words to Ahalyā.
"O well-composed lady, those who seek their purpose do not wait for the arrival of the fertile season;
rather, O slender-waisted one, I desire union with you.
Recognizing the thousand-eyed Indra in the guise of a sage, the joy of the Raghus [spoke thus]."
1.047.019c Out of curiosity for the king of the gods, the evil-minded one formed a plan.
1.047.020a Then, with his inner self feeling its purpose already accomplished, he spoke to the best of the gods:
1.047.020c "Your purpose is achieved, O best of gods; go quickly from here, O Lord."
"O Lord of Gods, O bestower of honor, always protect both yourself and me.
Then Indra, laughing, spoke these words to Ahalyā:
"O woman of beautiful hips, I am well-pleased; I shall depart as I came."
Having thus united with her, he then emerged from the hut;
hurrying in agitation and apprehensive regarding Gautama, O Rāma,
he beheld the great sage Gautama entering.
He was unassailable by gods or demons, endowed with the power of asceticism,
his body moistened by the waters of sacred fords, blazing like a fire,
and there he stood as a bull among sages, holding sacrificial fuel and *kuśa* grass.
Seeing him, the lord of the gods was terrified and his face became dejected.
Then, seeing the thousand-eyed one disguised as a sage, the sage—
who was himself perfected in conduct— spoke these words in anger to that man of evil conduct.

"O evil-minded one, because you have committed this improper act by assuming my form, you shall become fruitless. When he had been addressed thus with anger by the high-souled Gautama, [the sage remained there].
At that very moment, the two testicles of the thousand-eyed one fell to the ground.
Having thus cursed Śakra, he also cursed his wife:
"You shall dwell here for many thousands of years."
Subsisting on air, taking no food, performing austerities, and lying upon ashes,
you shall dwell in this hermitage, invisible to all beings. And when Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, comes to this formidable forest—

"The invincible one will arrive; then you shall become purified. O woman of evil conduct, through his hospitality, you shall be freed from greed and delusion, and filled with joy in my presence, you shall regain your own true form."
Having spoken thus to the woman of wicked conduct, the immensely radiant Gautama abandoned this hermitage frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas and,
possessing great ascetic power, performed austerities on a beautiful peak of the Himalayas.
Then Śakra, his face pale with fear, spoke to the gods led by Agni, along with the hosts of ṛṣis and Cāraṇas,
saying: "By creating an obstacle to the asceticism of the high-souled Gautama..."
"Indeed, having given way to anger, I performed this work for the sake of the gods;
yet because of that anger, I have been rendered fruitless and she has been rejected. By the release of my curse, her great ascetic merit has been taken away by me."
"Therefore, O all you best of gods, together with the hosts of ṛṣis and the cāraṇas,
you ought to make my word fruitful by providing assistance to the gods.
Having heard the words of Śatakratu, the gods, led by Agni, [responded].
Having approached the ancestors and the gods together with all the hosts of Maruts, they said:
"This ram possesses testicles, whereas Śakra has been rendered castrated.
Seizing the testicles of the ram, give them to Śakra immediately."

"Though it has been rendered fruitless by me, this ram will grant supreme satisfaction for the sake of your joy, as well as for those men who shall offer it. Having heard these words of Agni, the ancestors and the gods assembled together.
Having extracted the testicles of the rams, they presented them to the Thousand-eyed One.
From that time forward, O descendant of Kakutstha, the ancestral gods, having assembled,
eat rams that are devoid of testicles, for they deprived those rams of their fruits.
"O Rāghava, from that time forward, Indra has possessed the testicles of a ram due to the power of Gautama’s asceticism and the greatness of that high-souled one. Therefore,
O one of great splendor, come now to the hermitage of that performer of meritorious deeds."
"Deliver this highly fortunate Ahalyā, who possesses a divine form.
Hearing Viśvāmitra’s words, Rāghava, together with Lakṣmaṇa and placing Viśvāmitra at their head, entered the hermitage.
And he beheld that highly fortunate lady, her radiance illuminated by asceticism;
though she was difficult even for the worlds, including gods and asuras, to gaze upon when assembled together,
she appeared like a divine illusion fashioned with great effort by the Creator.
Her limbs enveloped in smoke,
she was like the radiance of the full moon obscured by mist and clouds;
yet standing in the midst of the waters, she was invincible, blazing like the splendor of the sun.
Indeed, by the word of Gautama, she became difficult to behold for all the three worlds until the sight of Rāma. Then the two descendants of Raghu took hold of her feet.

Remembering the words of Gautama, she received them both; with great composure, she offered them water for their feet, the guest-offering, and hospitality. Kākutstha accepted these according to the prescribed rites.
A great rain of flowers fell amidst the sounding of celestial drums, and there was also a vast gathering of Gandharvas and Apsarases;
"Excellent! Excellent! the gods cried, as they honored Ahalyā.
Her limbs purified by the power of asceticism and remaining obedient to Gautama,
the highly effulgent Gautama, together with Ahalyā, lived happily;
having honored Rāma according to the prescribed rites, that great ascetic performed his penance.
1.048.022a Rāma, too, having received the highest honor from the great sage Gautama according to the prescribed rites, then departed for Mithilā.
1.049.001a Then, having gone toward the northeast together with the son of Sumitrā, Rāma—
Placing Viśvāmitra at their head, they approached the sacrificial enclosure.
Then Rāma, together with Lakṣmaṇa, said to that tiger among sages:
"Truly, the prosperity of the sacrifice of the high-souled Janaka is magnificent."
"O highly fortunate one, many thousands of Brāhmaṇas dwelling in various lands, distinguished by their study of the Vedas,
are here; and the hermitages of the sages are seen, crowded with hundreds of carts."
"O Brahmin, let a place be designated where we shall dwell. Having heard Rāma's words, the great sage Viśvāmitra chose a secluded spot abounding in water and established his camp there.
Having heard that Viśvāmitra was the best of sages,
the king then placed the blameless family priest Śatānanda at the forefront;
and the high-souled officiating priests also quickly took up the guest-offering (arghya).
In accordance with dharma, they gave [the daughter] to Viśvāmitra, preceded by sacred mantras. Having accepted that honor from the high-souled Janaka,
he inquired after the welfare of the king and the unimpeded progress of the sacrifice.
Having questioned those sages, along with the teachers and domestic priests,
according to custom, he then met with them all in great joy. Then the king, with palms joined in reverence, addressed the best of sages.
1.049.010c Let the Blessed One sit upon the seat together with these best of sages.
1.049.011a Having heard Janaka’s words, the great sage sat down; so too did the domestic priest, the officiating priests, and the king along with his ministers.
Seeing them all seated on their respective seats according to protocol, the king there then spoke to Viśvāmitra:
"Today, the success of my sacrifice has been made fruitful by the gods."

"Today, O Blessed One, the fruit of sacrifice has been attained by me through the sight of you. I am blessed and I am graced, O bull among sages, since you, O Brahmin, have arrived at my sacrificial assembly along with these other sages."
"O Brahmarṣi, the wise say that twelve days remain;
therefore, O Kauśika, you ought to see the gods who seek their shares.
Having spoken thus to the tiger among sages, he then spoke with a joyful countenance.
Once again, the king, restrained and with palms joined in reverence, questioned him:
"Blessings to you! These two youths possess prowess equal to the gods;
they have the gait of elephants and lions, and are heroes resembling tigers and bulls."
With eyes as broad as lotus petals, bearing swords, quivers, and bows,
they were like the two Aśvins in beauty, having reached their youth; they appeared as if two immortals had descended from the world of the gods to the earth by mere chance.
"How have they come here on foot? For what purpose and whose [sons] are they, O Sage?
Whose two sons are these heroes bearing excellent weapons, O Great Sage, who adorn this region like the sun and moon adorning the sky?"

"Those two heroes, who resemble one another in stature, gestures, and movements, and who still bear the side-locks of youth— I wish to hear the truth about them. Having heard those words of the high-souled Janaka, [Vasiṣṭha spoke].
They reported that those two high-souled sons of Daśaratha had dwelt at Siddhāśrama, had slain the Rākṣasas,
had returned without agitation, and had seen Viśālā.
The sight of Ahalyā, the meeting with Gautama,
and likewise the arrival for the purpose of testing his skill with the great bow—
all this [the sage of] great splendor related to the high-souled Janaka.
Having thus announced [the matter], the great sage Viśvāmitra then ceased speaking. Hearing those words of the wise Viśvāmitra,
the highly effulgent Śatānanda, a man of great asceticism, stood with his hair standing on end in joy.
The eldest son of Gautama, his splendor illuminated by asceticism,
was filled with supreme wonder at the very sight of Rāma.
Observing those two princes seated comfortably, he [approached].
Śatānanda then spoke to Viśvāmitra, the best of sages:
"O tiger among sages, was my illustrious mother,
who has practiced long austerities, shown to the prince?"
"Did my illustrious mother offer hospitality with forest-grown fruits to Rāma, who possesses great splendor and is worthy of worship by all embodied beings?
And was the ancient history related to Rāma exactly as it occurred?"
"O Kauśika, may you be blessed! My mother has been subjected to great suffering by the god through ill-treatment.
O best of sages, my mother has been reunited with her husband from this point on through the sight of Rāma."
"O son of Kuśika, has Rāma, who is endowed with great splendor, been honored by my preceptor upon his arrival here after receiving honor from that high-souled one?
O son of Kuśika, was my preceptor’s mind tranquil?"
"Having arrived here, Rāma has respectfully saluted me.
Hearing those words of his, the great sage Viśvāmitra,
who was skilled in speech, replied to Śatānanda, who was himself an expert in discourse.
"O best of sages, I have not transgressed; that which was to be done has been performed by me, just as Reṇukā was reunited with her husband by the sage Bhārgava.
Having heard those words of the wise Viśvāmitra, [the king spoke].
The immensely radiant Śatānanda spoke these words to Rāma:
"Welcome to you, O best of men! By good fortune you have arrived, O Rāghava, having placed the invincible great seer Viśvāmitra at your head."
"The Brahmarṣi Viśvāmitra, of inconceivable deeds, ascetic power, and immeasurable luster, and possessed of great majesty, will know him as the supreme goal.
O Rāma, there is no one else on earth more blessed than you."
"The son of Kuśika shall be your protector—he by whom great austerity was practiced. Listen, for I shall declare the history of the high-souled Kauśika;
hear it from me as I recount it according to his power and according to what occurred."
For a long time, this king was a righteous soul and a subduer of his enemies;
he was a knower of dharma, accomplished in learning, and devoted to the welfare of his subjects. Now, there was a lord of the earth named Kuśa, who was the son of Prajāpati.
Kuśa’s son was the powerful and highly righteous Kuśanābha. Kuśanābha’s son was the one renowned as Gādhi.
Gādhi’s son was the great sage Viśvāmitra, possessed of great splendor.
The immensely powerful Viśvāmitra protected the earth;
as king, he ruled the kingdom for many thousands of years.
On one occasion, however, that man of great splendor marshalled his army.
Surrounded by an *akṣauhiṇī* army, the king traversed the earth—
cities, kingdoms, rivers, and likewise mountains—
and as he journeyed through hermitages in due order, he arrived [at his destination].
The hermitage of Vasiṣṭha was filled with trees bearing various flowers and fruits, crowded with diverse herds of deer, frequented by siddhas and cāraṇas,
and graced by gods, dānavas, gandharvas, and kinnaras.
It was filled with peaceful deer and frequented by flocks of birds; it was crowded with throngs of Brahman-sages and served by hosts of celestial rishis,
and inhabited by high-souled ones who were like fires, perfected through the practice of austerity.
It was constantly crowded with majestic, high-souled beings who were like Brahmā himself—
those who subsisted on water, those who subsisted on air, and likewise those who fed on withered leaves;
those who ate fruits and roots, who were self-controlled, whose anger was conquered, and whose senses were mastered.

The immensely powerful Viśvāmitra, the best among victors, beheld the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha— which was like a second world of Brahmā— filled with the Vālakhilya rishis devoted to silent recitation and burnt offerings.
Seeing him, the mighty and heroic Viśvāmitra was filled with supreme joy; bowing with humility before Vasiṣṭha, the best of those who recite sacred prayers,
he was addressed by the high-souled Vasiṣṭha with the words, "Welcome to you."
The venerable Vasiṣṭha assigned a seat for him;
and when the wise Viśvāmitra had sat down,
that best of sages then offered him fruit and roots according to the prescribed custom.

Having accepted that worship from Vasiṣṭha, the best of kings inquired after the welfare of his austerities, his sacred fires, and his disciples; likewise, the immensely radiant Viśvāmitra inquired about the groves of trees.

Vasiṣṭha, the son of Brahmā and best among those who recite prayers, spoke auspicious words in every respect to that most excellent of kings; and when King Viśvāmitra was seated at ease, Vasiṣṭha, the son of Brahmā and greatest of ascetics, questioned him.
"O King, is all well with you? O righteous King, do you protect your subjects by delighting them through dharma, in accordance with the conduct of a king?
Are your servants well-supported, and do they abide by your command?"

"O slayer of enemies, have all your foes been conquered? O scorcher of the foe, O tiger among men, O sinless one, is all well with your army, your treasury, your friends, and likewise with your sons and grandsons?"
In every respect,
the highly effulgent Viśvāmitra, endowed with humility, addressed Vasiṣṭha with auspicious words; and both of those most righteous ones engaged in those auspicious conversations for a very long time.

Filled with supreme joy, may those two take delight in one another. Then, O descendant of Raghu, at the conclusion of the conversation, the venerable Vasiṣṭha spoke these words to Viśvāmitra as if smiling.

"O one of great strength, I wish to offer hospitality to this army and to you, O immeasurable one, according to your merit; please accept this from me. May you accept this honor that I have prepared."

"O King, you are the most excellent of guests and are worthy of being honored with every effort. When Vasiṣṭha had spoken thus, the high-minded Viśvāmitra said to him, "It is done; you have already honored me with your words."

"O Blessed One, whatever fruits and roots exist in your hermitage, along with water for the feet, water for sipping, and the very sight of you— by all these means, O one of great wisdom, you who are worthy of worship, we have been well-honored."
"I shall depart; let there be salutation to you; look upon me with a friendly eye.
To the king who was speaking thus, the righteous Vasiṣṭha, noble-minded, invited him once again and again.
"So be it," Gādheya replied to Vasiṣṭha.
"O best of sages, let it be exactly as the Blessed One desires.
Thus addressed, the highly effulgent Vasiṣṭha, the foremost of those who recite prayers, [consented].
Then, his impurities shaken off and filled with joy, he summoned Kalmāṣī:
"Come, come quickly, Śabalā! Listen also to my words;
I have resolved to do something for this royal seer Sabala."
"Provide for me a hospitable reception with most precious food;
whatever is desired by each person according to their wish among the six flavors— let all that rain down from this divine cow, which grants every desire, for my sake."
"O Śabalā, hasten and create an entire store of foods, provided with juices, solid food, drinks, and things to be licked and sucked. Thus addressed by Vasiṣṭha, O slayer of enemies, Śabalā—
The wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhuk) provided for each person whatever they desired, according to their wishes:
sugarcane, honey, parched grain, maireya wine, and excellent liquors;
as well as costly drinks and various kinds of foods.
There were also mountain-like heaps of rice enriched with heat,
as well as delicacies, soups, and even streams of curd; likewise,
there were various flavors and *ṣāḍava* preparations.
There were thousands of vessels filled with molasses-based sweets;
everything was perfectly satisfied, crowded with people who were joyful and well-nourished, O Rāma, as Viśvāmitra’s army was fully gratified by Vasiṣṭha.
The royal seer Viśvāmitra, too, was then filled with joy and well-being;
the king, together with his excellent inner apartments, his brahmins, and his domestic chaplain, as well as his ministers, counselors, and servants, was then honored.
Filled with supreme joy, he spoke these words to Vasiṣṭha:
"O Brahmin, I have been honored by you, who are yourself worthy of honor, and have been most hospitably received. O master of speech, listen as I speak these words."
"Let Śabalā be given to me in exchange for a hundred thousand cows;
for this, O Blessed One, is a jewel, and the king is a thief of jewels.
Therefore, give Śabalā to me; she belongs to me by right, O twice-born one."
Thus addressed by Viśvāmitra, the blessed Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages and soul of dharma, replied to the lord of the earth:
"I would not [accept] even a hundred thousand, nor even a hundred crores of cows."
"O King, I shall give you Śabalā, or else heaps of silver; O subduer of enemies, she should not be surrendered from my presence. To me, Śabalā is eternal, just as fame is to a man of self-mastery."
Upon her depend the offerings to the gods and the ancestors, as well as the sustenance of life;
likewise, the *agnihotra* sacrifice, the ritual oblation (*bali*), and the fire-offering (*homa*) are dependent on her.
So too are the utterances *svāhā* and *vaṣaṭ*, and the various branches of knowledge.
"O royal sage, all of this depends on you; of this there is no doubt. By truth, I shall always grant you my entire property; however, O King, for many reasons, I will not give Śabalā to you."
Thus addressed by Vasiṣṭha, Viśvāmitra,
who was skilled in speech, then spoke these words with even greater agitation:
"Horses adorned with golden girths and neck-chains, decorated with golden hooks— "
"I give you fourteen thousand elephants;
and I give you eight hundred golden chariots, each yoked to four white horses and adorned with tinkling bells."
"O you of noble vows, I give to you eleven thousand horses of great vigor, born in various lands and of noble lineage,
distinguished by their diverse colors and all in the prime of youth."
"I shall give you one crore of cows; let Śabalā be given to me.
Thus addressed by the wise Viśvāmitra, O King, the Blessed One replied, "I will not give up Śabalā under any circumstances."
For this alone is my jewel; for this alone is my wealth; for this alone is my entire possession; for this alone is my very life.
And the New Moon sacrifice, the Full Moon sacrifice, and sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees—these too are it.
"O King, it is for this very reason that my various ritual acts are likewise rooted in *adoman* (the cow);
all my rites, O King, have their source in her, without a doubt.
What is the use of much talk? I will not give away the wish-fulfilling cow."
1.053.001 When the sage Vasiṣṭha would not give up the wish-fulfilling cow,
O Rāma, Viśvāmitra then dragged away his Śabalā.
1.053.002 As Śabalā was being led away by the high-souled king, O Rāma, [she cried out].
Distressed, weeping, and emaciated by grief, she reflected:
"Have I been abandoned by the great-souled Vasiṣṭha?
For I, wretched and deeply afflicted, am being carried away by the king's servants."
"What wrong have I done to that great seer of purified soul, that the righteous man abandons me— innocent, devoted, and beloved? Thus she reflected, sighing again and again.
Then, O destroyer of enemies, having shaken off those hundreds of servants, he went with speed toward Vasiṣṭha of supreme luster;
with the velocity of the wind, he reached the feet of that high-souled one.
Weeping and crying out, Śabalā stood before Vasiṣṭha, her voice resonating like a cloud or a drum, and said this:
"O Blessed One, son of Brahmā, why have I been abandoned by you?"
"Because the king's servants are indeed leading me away from your presence.
Thus addressed, the Brahman-sage spoke these words to her who was as distressed as a sister, her heart tormented by grief.
"O Śabalā, I do not abandon you, nor have you done me any wrong;
yet this king, possessed of great strength, carries you away from me by force. For my strength is not equal to his, especially today."
King Bali was a Kṣatriya and indeed the lord of the earth;
he possessed this full Akṣauhiṇī army, crowded with horses and chariots and bristling with elephants and banners— therefore, he was more powerful.
Thus addressed by Vasiṣṭha, she who was skilled in speech replied with humility to that Brahmarṣi of immeasurable splendor:
"They say that the power of a Kṣatriya is not true power; a Brāhmaṇa is more powerful."
"O Brahmin, the divine power of a Brahmin is more powerful than the power of a Kshatriya. Your strength is immeasurable; no one is stronger than you.
Viśvāmitra is of great heroism, yet his splendor cannot withstand yours."
"O one of great splendor, employ me, who am empowered by the power of your *brahman*;
I shall destroy the pride and the strength of that evil-minded one. When she had spoken thus, O Rāma, the highly illustrious Vasiṣṭha—
"Create [an army]," he then said to Bala, the crusher of enemy forces.
From her lowing sound (*humbhā*), O King, hundreds of Pahlavas were released;
they destroyed the entire army while Viśvāmitra looked on.
1.053.019a That king, extremely enraged, his eyes wide with fury,
1.053.019c destroyed the Pahlavas with various kinds of weapons.
1.053.020a Seeing the Pahlavas then being slaughtered by the hundreds, afflicted by Viśvāmitra, [the king acted].
Furthermore, he created the terrible Śakas mixed with the Yavanas.
The earth was covered by those Śakas mixed with Yavanas—
men of great power and immense heroism, resembling the golden filaments of a lotus.
Carrying long swords and spears, and clad in golden-colored garments,
that entire army was consumed as if by blazing fires.
Then, the one of great splendor, Viśvāmitra, released his celestial weapons.
Then, seeing them agitated and bewildered by Viśvāmitra’s weapon,
Vasiṣṭha urged the wish-fulfilling cow, saying, "Create [beings] through yoga.
From her lowing sound (*humbhā-rava*), the Kāmbojas were born, radiant as the sun.
Then, from her udder were born the Pahlavas, armed with weapons;
from the region of her womb came the Yavanas, and from the region of her dung the Śakas; from the pores of her skin came the Mlecchas, the Haritas, and the Kirātas.

O descendant of Raghu, at that very moment, Viśvāmitra’s entire army— along with its foot soldiers, elephants, horses, and chariots— was slaughtered by those [sages]. Seeing his army thus destroyed by the high-souled Vasiṣṭha, [Viśvāmitra was overcome with grief].
The hundred sons of Viśvāmitra, bearing various kinds of weapons,
rushed in great fury toward Vasiṣṭha, the best of those who recite prayers. But the great Ṛṣi consumed them all with a mere sound of "hum."
Then, in a single moment, those sons of Viśvāmitra— along with their horses, chariots, and infantry— were reduced to ashes by the high-souled Vasiṣṭha.
Seeing his sons and his army thus destroyed, the highly illustrious [Viśvāmitra]...
Then Viśvāmitra became filled with shame and overcome by anxiety;
he was like a snake whose fangs have been broken, devoid of vigor,
or like the sun eclipsed, suddenly fallen into a state of lusterlessness.
His strength diminished by the loss of his sons, dejected like a bird with its wings clipped,
his pride shattered and his enthusiasm destroyed, he fell into despondency.
Having appointed his only remaining son to protect the kingdom, he said:
1.054.011c Having ruled the earth according to the duty of a kṣatriya, he retired to the forest.
1.054.012a Having gone to the slopes of the Himalayas, which are frequented by *kiṃnaras* and *uragas*,
that great ascetic performed austerities for the sake of propitiating Mahādeva.
Then, after some time, the Lord of the Gods, whose banner bears the bull, the granter of boons, revealed himself to the great sage Viśvāmitra.
"O King, for what purpose do you perform these austerities? Tell me what you wish to say."
"I am the granter of boons; let that boon which you desire be requested.
Thus addressed by the god, Viśvāmitra, of great asceticism, prostrated before Mahādeva and spoke these words.
"If you are pleased, O Mahādeva, O sinless one, let the science of archery be granted to me— with its limbs, sub-limbs, secret doctrines, and mysteries—
whatever weapons exist among the gods, the Dānavas, and the great ṛṣis."
"O sinless one, may [these mantras] manifest within me among the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas. O God of gods, by your grace, let my desire be fulfilled.
Having spoken these words, "So be it," the Lord of Gods departed for heaven.
Having obtained the weapons, the royal sage Viśvāmitra, possessed of great strength,
was then filled with immense pride and became full of arrogance;
increasing in prowess like the ocean during the full moon.
At that time, he considered the best of sages, Vasiṣṭha, as already slain.
Then, having gone to the hermitage, the king discharged his weapons,
by which the entire penance grove was consumed by the fiery energy of those missiles.
Seeing that weapon being discharged by the wise Viśvāmitra,
hundreds of terrified sages,
as well as the disciples of Vasiṣṭha and even the beasts and birds, fled in all directions.
Terrified by fear, they fled by the thousands in all directions. The hermitage of the high-souled Vasiṣṭha became empty;
for a moment, it was silent, resembling a barren wasteland.
"O Gādheya, do not fear," Vasiṣṭha said repeatedly as he spoke;
"I shall destroy you today, just as the sun destroys the mist.
Having spoken thus, the immensely radiant Vasiṣṭha, the best among those who recite prayers, [proceeded].
Then he spoke these words full of wrath to Viśvāmitra:
"Since you have destroyed this hermitage where we have grown for so long,
and since you are one of evil conduct, O fool, therefore you shall cease to exist."
Having spoken thus, extremely enraged, he quickly raised his staff like the smokeless fire of time, like a second staff of Yama. Thus addressed by Vasiṣṭha, the immensely powerful Viśvāmitra—
Raising the Āgneya weapon, he cried out, "Stay! Stay!
The venerable Vasiṣṭha, out of anger, spoke these words:
"O wretch of a Kṣatriya, here I stand; show whatever strength you possess!"
"O son of Gadhi, I shall destroy this pride of yours regarding your weapon.
Where is your kṣatriya strength, and where is the great power of a brāhmaṇa?
Behold, O disgrace to the kṣatriyas, my divine brāhmaṇa power!"
That terrible and supreme fiery weapon (*āgneya-astra*) of the son of Gādhi was quelled by the Brahma-staff (*brahmadaṇḍa*), like the force of fire by water.
And likewise, the Vāruṇa, Raudra, Aindra, and Pāśupata weapons [were neutralized].
And the enraged son of Gādhi also hurled the Aiṣīka weapon,
as well as the Mānava, the Mohana, the Gāndharva, and the Svāpana; likewise the Jṛmbhaṇa, the Mohana, the Saṃtāpana, and the Vilāpana.
The weapon Vajra, which is extremely difficult to conquer, as well as Śoṣaṇa and Dāraṇa;
the Brahma-pāśa, the Kāla-pāśa, and the Varuṇa-pāśa;
the beloved Pināka-weapon, and likewise the dry and wet thunderbolts (Aśanī).
Then the *daṇḍāstra*, the *paiśāca* weapon, and likewise the *krauñca* weapon;
the *dharmacakra*, the *kālacakra*, and likewise the *viṣṇucakra*;
the *vāyavya*, the *mathana*, and the *hayaśiras* weapon as well.
He hurled two spears, as well as a skeleton and a mace; then the great Vaidyādhara weapon and the terrible Kālāstra;
the formidable Triśūla weapon, and then the Kāpāla and the Kaṅkaṇa.
O descendant of Raghu, he discharged all these weapons at Vasiṣṭha, the best among those who recite prayers; that appeared truly wonderful. But the son of Brahmā swallowed them all with his staff.
When those [weapons] had been neutralized, the son of Gādhi discharged the Brahmā weapon.
Seeing that weapon raised, the gods led by Agni,
the celestial sages, the Gandharvas, and the great serpents were all thrown into agitation.
When the Brahmā-missile was discharged, the three worlds were struck with terror;
yet Vasiṣṭha, O Rāghava, swallowed that most terrible Brahmā-missile in its entirety by means of his own Brahmanic power and the staff of Brahmā.
As the high-souled Vasiṣṭha was swallowing the Brahmāstra,
his form became fierce and most terrible, enchanting the three worlds.
In every one of the pores of the high-souled Vasiṣṭha’s skin—
Like rays of light, flames mixed with smoke issued forth from the fire; and the staff of Brahmā, raised in Vasiṣṭha’s hand,
blazed like the smokeless fire of time, like a second staff of Yama.
Then the hosts of sages praised Vasiṣṭha, the best among those who recite prayers:
"O Brahmin, your power is unfailing; restrain your fiery energy with your own splendor! O Brahmin, Viśvāmitra of great asceticism has been subdued by you."
"Be gracious, O best of those who recite prayers; may the worlds be free from suffering.
Thus addressed, the one of great splendor and great asceticism attained peace.
But Viśvāmitra, feeling humiliated, sighed deeply and spoke this:
"Fie on the power of a Kṣatriya! The power of Brahmanic splendor is true power;
by a single staff of Brahman, all my weapons have been destroyed.
Having reflected upon this, I shall now remain with my senses and mind tranquil."

"I shall undertake great austerity that will surely bring about the state of Brahmanhood. Then, with a tormented heart, remembering his own defeat and sighing again and again, he harbored enmity toward the Great-Souled One.
Having gone to the southern direction with his queen, O Rāghava,
Viśvāmitra of great ascetic power performed most intense and formidable penance;
subsisting on fruits and roots and self-controlled, he practiced supreme austerity.
Then his sons were born, devoted to truth and righteousness:
Haviṣpanda, Madhuṣpanda, Dṛḍhanetra, and Mahāratha.
When a full thousand years had passed, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, [appeared].
He spoke these sweet words to Viśvāmitra, whose wealth is asceticism:
"O son of Kuśika, the worlds of the royal sages have been won by you through your penance;
indeed, because of this ascetic power, we know you as a royal sage."
Having spoken thus, the one of great splendor, the supreme lord of the worlds, departed for Triviṣṭapa, the realm of Brahmā, along with the deities.
Viśvāmitra, however, having heard that, stood with his face somewhat cast down in shame.
Overcome by great sorrow and filled with indignation, he spoke these words:
"I have performed very great austerities, and all the gods along with the hosts of sages know me as a royal seer (rājarṣi); yet I perceive no fruit of my asceticism."
Having thus resolved in his mind,
O descendant of Kakutstha, that great ascetic, possessed of the supreme self, once again performed supreme austerity.
At that very time, however, there was one who spoke the truth and had conquered his senses.
1.056.010c There was one renowned as Triśaṅku, the joy of the Ikṣvāku lineage.
1.056.011a O Rāghava, the thought arose in him: "I shall perform a sacrifice;
1.056.011c may I go to the supreme state of the gods in my own physical body."
Having summoned Vasiṣṭha, he related what he had contemplated;
but having been told by the high-souled Vasiṣṭha that it was impossible,
and being thus rejected by Vasiṣṭha, he departed toward the southern direction.

1.056.013c For it was there that the Vasiṣṭhas of long austerity performed their penance. 1.056.014a Triśaṅku, possessed of great splendor, beheld a hundred most radiant 1.056.014c sons of Vasiṣṭha, illustrious ones who were performing austerities.
Having approached all the high-souled sons of his preceptor and saluted them in due order, he— of great splendor and with his face somewhat downcast from shame—
spoke to them all with palms joined in reverence.
"I, who have come for refuge, seek your protection, O you who are worthy of providing refuge. I have been rejected by the high-souled Vasiṣṭha; may prosperity be yours.
Since I desire to perform a great sacrifice, you ought to grant me permission for it."
Having bowed down to all the sons of my preceptors, I seek their favor;
prostrating with my head, I entreat these brahmins established in asceticism: may you, being composed, officiate as priests for me for the sake of my success.
"O you whose wealth is asceticism, since I have been rejected by Vasiṣṭha, I see no other way at all to reach the world of the gods in my physical body,
except through the sons of my guru."
"For among all the Ikṣvākus, the family priest is indeed the supreme refuge;
therefore, you all are my deities immediately following him.
Then, having heard Triśaṅku’s words filled with anger, [the sages departed].
1.057.001c O Rāma, a hundred sons of sages said this to the king:
1.057.002a "O evil-minded one, you have been rejected by your truthful preceptor;
1.057.002c how is it that, bypassing him, you have gone to another branch?"
"For among all the Ikṣvākus, the family priest is the supreme refuge;
and it is not possible to transgress the word of one who speaks the truth.
Thus spoke the venerable seer Vasiṣṭha, saying, "It is impossible."
"How can we possibly be capable of performing that sacrifice for you?
O best of men, you are childish; please return to your own city. O King, the Blessed One is capable of officiating at a sacrifice even for the three worlds."
Having heard those words of theirs, spoken with syllables agitated by anger,
the king spoke these words to them once again:
"I have been rejected by my preceptor, and likewise by the sons of my preceptor."
"I shall go to another state; may it be well with you, O you whose wealth is asceticism.
But when the sons of the sages heard those words, which were intended to be so terrible, they became extremely enraged and cursed him, saying, "You shall become a Caṇḍāla!"
Having spoken thus, those great-souled ones entered their own hermitage.
Then, when the night had passed, the king became a caṇḍāla—
clad in blue garments, dark-complexioned, coarse, and with disheveled hair.
Wearing a garland and ointment, yet adorned with iron ornaments,
all the ministers saw him in the form of a Caṇḍāla and,
O Rāma, fled together, abandoning him, as did the citizens who were his followers.

1.057.011a For the king alone, O descendant of Kakutstha, being possessed of supreme self-control, went [to him] day and night while burning with grief; 1.057.011c [he went] to Viśvāmitra, whose wealth is asceticism.
1.057.012a But Viśvāmitra, seeing that king rendered unsuccessful, [spoke].
O Rāma, having come upon one in the form of a Caṇḍāla, the sage was moved by compassion.
Out of compassion, that most virtuous one of great splendor spoke these words to the king of terrible appearance: "May it be well with you."
"O mighty prince, O hero, lord of Ayodhyā who has fallen into the state of a Caṇḍāla due to a curse, what is the purpose of your coming? Then,
having heard those words, the king who had become a Caṇḍāla [spoke].
1.057.015c Skilled in speech, he addressed these words with joined palms to the one who was himself an expert in discourse:
1.057.016a "I have been rejected by my preceptor, and likewise by the sons of my preceptor;
1.057.016c having failed to obtain that desire, I have instead encountered its opposite."
"May I go to heaven in my physical body"—this was my gentle vision; yet though a hundred sacrifices were performed by me, their fruit has not been attained.
Never before have I spoken an untruth, nor shall I ever speak one at any time."
"O gentle one, even though I have fallen into hardships, I swear to you by the duty of a Kṣatriya:
sacrifices of many kinds have been performed, subjects have been protected according to dharma,
and high-souled elders have been gratified through my conduct and virtuous behavior."
"O bull among sages, though I strive in righteousness and desire to perform a sacrifice, my elders find no satisfaction;
I consider destiny alone to be supreme, while human effort is useless."

Everything is overcome by destiny, for destiny is indeed the supreme course. Therefore, may you grant favor to me, who am deeply distressed, who longs for your grace, and whose actions have been struck down by destiny; may prosperity be yours.
"I shall go to no other state; there is no other refuge for me.
You ought to turn back this destiny through human effort.
Having spoken these words to the king, the son of Kuśika, out of compassion, [responded].
He spoke these sweet words directly to the one in the form of a Caṇḍāla:
"O descendant of Ikṣvāku, welcome, my child! I know you to be a man of great righteousness.
I shall be your refuge; do not fear, O bull among kings."
"I address all you great seers of meritorious deeds:
O King, once you have secured the assistance for the sacrifice, you shall then perform it with a tranquil mind.
This form that now exists in you was brought about by the curse of your preceptor."
"With this very form, you shall go with your body intact.
O lord of men, I consider heaven already within your grasp,
since you have come to Kauśika, the protector, and sought refuge with him."
Having spoken thus to his sons, who were supremely righteous and possessed of great wisdom, the one of great splendor commanded them to prepare the materials for the sacrifice; then,
having summoned all his disciples, he addressed these words to them.
"O children, by my command, bring all the best of sages here,
along with their disciples, friends, officiating priests, and those of great learning.
Whatever else anyone might say, let it be prompted by the power of my word."
"All that which was to be told to me has been spoken in its entirety; it has not been disregarded. Having heard those words of his, they departed in all directions at his command.
Then, from every land, the exponents of the Veda arrived.
1.058.011a And those disciples, having assembled before the sage of blazing splendor, 1.058.011c all spoke these words to him, the teacher of all who discourse on Brahman:
1.058.012a "Having heard their words, all those twice-born ones are now arriving."
1.058.012c They came from all regions, with the exception of Mahodaya. 1.058.013a O bull among sages, hear all the words that entire hundred of Vasiṣṭha’s sons spoke, their voices agitated by anger.
"How can the celestial sages, or the high-souled brahmins, eat the sacrificial oblation (havis) in the assembly of one for whom a kṣatriya— especially a caṇḍāla— is the officiating priest,
after they have consumed the food of a caṇḍāla?"
"How will they go to heaven, protected by Viśvāmitra?"—
these harsh words,
O tiger among sages, did all those Vasiṣṭhas, together with Mahodaya, speak with eyes bloodshot with rage.
Having heard those words of them all, that bull among sages,
his eyes bloodshot with anger, spoke this in wrath:
"Since they defile me, though I am blameless and established in fierce asceticism..."
These evil-minded ones shall be reduced to ashes, of this there is no doubt.
Today they have been led by the noose of Time to the abode of Vaivasvata;
for seven hundred births, let them all be eaters of the dead.
Let the merciless ones known as Muṣṭikas, who subsist on a fixed diet of dog-meat,
deformed and misshapen, wander through these worlds. And let the evil-minded Mahodaya, who has defamed me though I am blameless, suffer likewise.
Contemned in all the worlds, he shall become a Niṣāda;
devoted to the taking of life and having reached a state of pitilessness,
he shall wander through miserable rebirths for a long time due to my wrath.
Having spoken these words, the great ascetic Viśvāmitra,
the sage of immense splendor, fell silent in the midst of the rishis.
Having struck down the sons of Vasiṣṭha along with Mahodaya by the power of his asceticism, he remained there.
In the midst of the sages, the highly effulgent Viśvāmitra addressed them:
"This son of Ikṣvāku, renowned as Triśaṅku,
is most righteous and generous, and he has come to me for refuge."
With this very body, out of a desire to conquer the world of the gods,
let the sacrifice be performed by you along with me, so that he may go to the world of the gods in his own body.

Having heard the words of Viśvāmitra, all the great seers, who were knowers of dharma, gathered together and spoke in unison regarding what was consistent with dharma: "This sage, the descendant of Kuśika, is exceedingly prone to anger."
"What he has said is correct; this must certainly be done, there is no doubt.
For the Blessed One is like fire; if provoked to anger, he will surely utter a curse.
Therefore, let the sacrifice be commenced so that he may go to heaven in his own body."
"Let the heir of Ikṣvāku go by the power of Viśvāmitra;
then let the sacrifice be commenced, for everyone is now ready.
Having spoken thus, the great seers then withdrew those ritual preparations.
And the immensely radiant Viśvāmitra became the chief officiating priest (*yājaka*) at the sacrifice;
and the other priests (*ṛtvij*), experts in the sacred formulas, performed all the rites in their proper sequence, according to the ritual manuals and according to rule, while reciting the mantras.
Then, after a long time, Viśvāmitra, the great ascetic,
performed an invocation there for the sake of the portions of all the gods.
Yet, though summoned for the sake of their portions, all the gods did not arrive.
Then the great sage Viśvāmitra, overcome with anger,
raised his sacrificial ladle and, full of wrath, spoke these words to Triśaṅku:
"O lord of men, behold the power of my ascetic merit, which I have earned by my own efforts!"
"By my own power, I shall lead you to heaven in your very body. Go to the celestial realm in your physical form, O lord of men,
for there is some fruit of my asceticism that I have earned for myself."

"O King, by his splendor, go to heaven in your physical body. When the sage had spoken these words, O descendant of Kakutstha, that lord of men went to heaven in his physical body while the sages were looking on.

Seeing Triśaṅku arrived in the world of the gods, the Subduer of Pāka (Indra), together with all the hosts of deities, spoke these words: "O Triśaṅku, go back; you have not earned a dwelling in heaven."
"O fool, struck by the curse of your guru, fall to the earth headlong! Thus addressed by Mahendra, Triśaṅku fell once more,
crying out for protection to Viśvāmitra, whose wealth is his asceticism.
Having heard those words of him who was crying out, Kauśika summoned a fierce rage and cried, "Stay! Stay!"—
that radiant one, like a second Prajāpati in the midst of the sages.
Creating another set of Seven Seers situated on the southern path,
he who was of great fame, standing in the midst of the sages and facing the southern direction, created another garland of constellations while overcome with rage.
Having created the lineage of the stars, he was clouded by anger and thought:
"I shall create another Indra, or the world shall be without an Indra.
Out of wrath, he then began to create even other deities.
Then, greatly agitated, the preeminent gods along with the hosts of sages spoke these conciliatory words to the high-souled Viśvāmitra:
"O illustrious one, this king has been struck down by his teacher’s curse."
"O one whose wealth is asceticism, he ought not to go to heaven with his physical body.
Having heard those words of the gods, Kauśika, the bull among sages, spoke these very significant words to all the deities:

"O blessed ones, having promised the ascent of this King Triśaṅku with his very body, I cannot bring myself to make that promise false. Let there be an eternal salvation for this Triśaṅku with his body."
"And let all the constellations belonging to me remain fixed as long as the worlds endure;
O gods, you ought to grant permission for all these things created by me."
Thus addressed, all the gods replied to that bull among sages:
"So be it; may prosperity be yours! Let these many [fires] remain on all sides in the sky, outside the path of Vaiśvānara."
"O best of sages, let Triśaṅku, blazing like a luminary among those stars and resembling an immortal, remain with his head turned downward;
for the righteous Viśvāmitra is praised by all the gods."
The great-spirited one said "So be it" to the deities and the seers.
Then, O best of men, at the conclusion of the sacrifice, all the high-souled gods and the sages whose wealth is asceticism departed as they had come.
Then the high-souled Viśvāmitra, seeing those sages ready to depart,
spoke to all those forest-dwellers, O tiger among men:
"A great obstacle has arisen, directed toward the southern quarter."
"Let us go to another direction; there we shall perform austerities.
In the western region, at the vast Puṣkaras, O high-souled ones, we shall practice penance with ease, for that is a supreme forest of asceticism."
Having spoken thus, the great sage of immense splendor performed fierce and invincible austerities at Puṣkara, subsisting on roots and fruits.
At that very time, however, there was a king who was the lord of Ayodhyā.
One renowned as Ambarīṣa began to perform a sacrifice.
While he was indeed performing that sacrifice, Indra carried off his sacrificial animal.
When the animal had vanished, the brahmin spoke thus to the king:
"O King, today an animal has been stolen; it was lost through your own misconduct. O Lord of Men, faults strike down a king who fails to protect.
For this is indeed a great expiation, O bull among men: either [the thief] must be surrendered, or a man [must be given]."
"Bring the sacrificial animal quickly, so that the ritual may proceed.
Hearing the words of his preceptor, O bull among men,
that king of great intelligence sought out an animal among thousands of cattle.
Seeking out various regions, provinces, cities, forests,
and sacred hermitages, that lord of the earth,
O dear one, [found] you, O descendant of Raghu, together with your wife and son.

He beheld Ṛcīka seated in the valley of Bhṛgu. Having bowed down and propitiated him, the royal sage of immeasurable splendor and great majesty addressed that brahmin seer who blazed with ascetic power.
Having inquired after his welfare in every respect, he spoke these words to Ṛcīka:
"O highly fortunate Bhārgava, if you would sell your son for a hundred thousand cows for the sake of the sacrificial animal, I shall have accomplished my purpose."
"I have wandered through all lands, yet I do not find a sacrificial animal to give.
You ought to give me one of your sons from here in exchange for a price.
Thus addressed, the highly effulgent Ṛcīka spoke these words:
"I would never, under any circumstances, sell my eldest, the best among men.
Having heard the words of Ṛcīka, the ascetic mother of those high-souled ones spoke to Ambarīṣa, that tiger among men.

"O King, know that my youngest son, Śunaka, is also dear to me. For generally, O best of men, the eldest sons are the favorites of their fathers, while the youngest are the favorites of their mothers; therefore, I protect the youngest."
When that sage had thus spoken, and the wife of the sage likewise,
O Rāma, Śunaḥśepa himself spoke these words as a mediator:
"The father said the eldest is not to be sold, and the mother said the youngest is not to be sold."
"O King, I consider my middle son to have been sold; take me [instead].
O descendant of Raghu, the lord of men, having taken Śunaḥśepa for a hundred thousand cows, departed in great joy.
1.060.022a But the royal sage Ambarīṣa, of great splendor and great fame, having quickly placed Śunaḥśepa upon his chariot, departed swiftly.
1.061.001a Having taken Śunaḥśepa with him, O best of men, the highly illustrious king proceeded.
At midday, O descendant of Raghu, the king rested at Puṣkara. While he was resting, the highly illustrious Śunaḥśepa arrived at the excellent Puṣkara and beheld Viśvāmitra.
With a dejected face, distressed by thirst and fatigue, he fell upon the lap of the sage, O Rāma, and spoke these words:
"I have no mother, no father; where indeed are my kinsmen or relatives?"
"O gentle one, O bull among sages, you ought to protect me in accordance with righteousness;
for you, O best of sages, are the protector and the sustainer of all. Thus the king shall have his purpose fulfilled, and I shall become long-lived and imperishable."

"Having performed unsurpassed austerity, may I attain the heavenly world. Therefore, with a noble heart, be the protector for me who am without a protector. O righteous-souled one, you ought to rescue me from this sin, just as a father rescues his son."
Having heard those words of his, Viśvāmitra, the great ascetic,
after consoling them in many ways, spoke thus to his sons: "For the sake of which fathers, seeking auspicious ends, procreate sons..."
"The time has now come for the sake of his welfare in the next world. This young son of a sage seeks refuge with me;
O dear sons, do what is pleasing to him by granting him merely his life."

"All of you, performers of good deeds and all devoted to dharma, become sacrificial animals for the lord of men and provide satisfaction to the fire. Thus Śunaḥśepa shall have a protector, and the sacrifice shall proceed without obstacle."
"The deities will be gratified, and my word shall have been fulfilled.
Having heard the words of the sage, O best of men, his sons Madhushyanda and the others spoke these words with pride and playfulness:
"O Lord, how is it that you abandon your own sons to protect the son of another?
We regard this as an improper act, like eating the flesh of a dog.
Having heard those words of his sons, the bull among sages—
With eyes bloodshot with anger, he began to speak:
"This which has been spoken is audacious and even censurable by the standards of dharma; it transgresses my command and is cruel and hair-raising."
"Like the Vasiṣṭhas among their own kind, you shall all eat the flesh of dogs;
for a full thousand years, you shall dwell upon this earth.
Having thus addressed his sons with these curses, the best of sages then [departed].
Having performed the protective rites for the distressed Śunaḥśepa so that he was free from harm,
[Viśvāmitra], bound with sacred cords and adorned with red garlands and unguents,
approached the sacrificial post dedicated to Viṣṇu and addressed Agni with these words:

"O son of a sage, you should sing these two divine verses at this sacrifice of Ambarīṣa; through them, you will then attain success. Having taken those two verses, Śunaḥśepa remained deeply concentrated.
With haste, he spoke to that lion among kings, Ambarīṣa:
"O lion among kings, O being of great courage, let us go quickly to the assembly hall. O Indra among kings, turn back and complete your consecration."
Having heard those words of the seer’s son, the king, filled with joy and eager anticipation,
went quickly and unweariedly to the sacrificial enclosure. With the approval of the assembly, the king [prepared] that which was marked by the purificatory rites.
Having made the sacrificial animal wear red garments, he bound it to the sacrificial post.
Bound there, that son of a sage duly praised the two gods, Indra and the younger brother of Indra (Viṣṇu), with the most excellent words.
Then, O Rāghava, the thousand-eyed Indra, pleased and gratified by that secret hymn of praise, granted a long life to Śunaḥśepa;
and that king, O best of men, completed his sacrifice.

"O Rāma, the fruit born of the grace of the Thousand-eyed One possesses manifold virtues. The righteous Viśvāmitra, a great ascetic, continued to perform intense penance at Puṣkara for a thousand years, O best of men."
When a full thousand years had passed, all the gods, desiring to bestow the fruit of his asceticism, approached the great sage who had completed his vow and bathed.
Then Brahmā, endowed with great splendor, spoke these most excellent words:
"You are a rishi; may prosperity be yours through your own well-earned auspicious deeds.
Having spoken thus to him, the Lord of the Gods returned once more to the third heaven.
Viśvāmitra, possessed of great luster, then performed even greater ascetic penance.
Then, after a long time, O best of men, the supreme Apsaras Menakā prepared to bathe at Puṣkara. The son of Kuśika, possessed of great splendor, beheld her.
Seeing her there, peerless in beauty like lightning within a cloud, the sage, falling under the sway of Kandarpa, said this to her:
"Welcome, O Apsaras; dwell here in my hermitage."
"May prosperity be yours; show favor to me, who am utterly deluded by passion.
Having been addressed thus, that woman of excellent limbs then made her dwelling there, for a great obstacle to his asceticism had come upon Viśvāmitra.
While she was dwelling there, O gentle Rāghava,
ten years passed happily in the hermitage of Viśvāmitra.
Then, when that time had elapsed, the great sage Viśvāmitra—
As if overcome with shame, he became devoted to anxiety and grief. O descendant of Raghu, indignation arose in the sage’s mind;
he realized that all this was the work of the gods, a great theft of his ascetic power.
"Ten years have passed under the guise of days and nights;
this obstacle has presented itself for one overcome by the delusion of desire.
Sighing, the best of sages was thereafter distressed with remorse.
Seeing the terrified Apsaras Menakā trembling and standing with palms joined in reverence,
the son of Kuśika dismissed her with sweet words,
O Rāma, and Viśvāmitra departed for the northern mountain.

Having formed a resolute determination and desiring victory, that highly illustrious one reached the bank of the Kauśikī and performed most rigorous austerities. As he practiced those terrible austerities for a thousand years, [the gods were moved].
On the northern mountain, O Rāma, fear arose among the deities. All the gods, together with the hosts of ṛṣis, having assembled, consulted one another:
"May this son of Kuśika truly receive the title of 'Great Ṛṣi'."

Having heard the words of the deities, the Grandfather of all the worlds spoke these sweet words to Viśvāmitra, whose wealth is asceticism: "O Great Seer, welcome, my child; I am gratified by your fierce austerity."
"I grant you greatness and the status of a preeminent rishi, O Kauśika.
Having heard these words of Brahmā, Viśvāmitra, whose wealth is his asceticism,
bowed with palms joined in reverence and replied to the Grandfather.
"If the Blessed One says that I have attained the incomparable title of *brahmarṣi* through my own well-performed auspicious deeds, then I am one who has conquered his senses.
Then Brahmā said to him, "You have not yet conquered your senses."
"Exert yourself, O tiger among sages! Having said this, he departed for heaven.
When the gods had departed, the great sage Viśvāmitra, with arms upraised and without support, subsisting on air, practiced asceticism.
Practicing the five-fold heat as his dharma during the rains, he took shelter in the open air;
during the cold season, that one whose wealth is austerity remained in the water day and night.
In this manner, he indeed performed terrible asceticism for a thousand years.
While that great sage Viśvāmitra was thus performing his penance,
a very great agitation arose among the gods and Vāsava;
Śakra, together with all the hosts of Maruts, [prepared for action] against the Apsaras Rambhā.
She spoke words that were for her own benefit and to the detriment of Kauśika:
"O Rambhā, this very great task of the gods must be performed by you here—
the seduction of Kauśika, filled with the delusion of desire."
1.063.002a Thus addressed by the wise thousand-eyed one, O Rāma, that Apsaras,
feeling ashamed, joined her palms in reverence and replied to the Lord of the Gods:
1.063.003a "O Lord of the Gods, this great sage Viśvāmitra is formidable."
"O Lord, he will undoubtedly unleash a terrible wrath upon me;
therefore, O God, I am afraid of him, and you ought to show me favor.
To her, as she stood trembling with palms joined in reverence, the thousand-eyed one spoke.
"Do not fear, Rambhā; may it be well with you. Carry out my command.
In the month of Mādhava, amidst the beautiful trees, there dwells a heart-captivating cuckoo;
accompanied by Kandarpa, I shall stand by your side."
"O Rambhā, having assumed a form of many qualities and supreme brilliance,
you must seduce that ascetic seer Kauśika.
Having heard his words, she assumed an unsurpassed form.
Lalitā, with her pure smile, sought to entice Viśvāmitra;
she heard the sweet sound of a cuckoo singing,
and with a joyful heart, she then gazed up at him.
Then, by that sound, by her incomparable song,
and by the sight of Rambhā, the sage fell into doubt.
Having understood that deed of the Thousand-Eyed One, that bull among sages—
Overcome with anger, the son of Kuśika cursed Rambhā:
"Since you, O Rambhā, seek to seduce me who am striving for mastery over desire and wrath,
you shall remain as stone for ten thousand years, O unfortunate woman!"
"O Rambhā, a Brāhmaṇa of great splendor, endowed with the power of asceticism, shall deliver you from being defiled by my wrath. Having spoken thus, the great sage Viśvāmitra of immense luster—
Unable to restrain his anger, he was overcome with distress;
by his great curse, Rambhā then became like stone.
And having heard the words of the great seer, Kandarpa departed.
1.063.015a When his ascetic power had been stolen away by anger, O Rāma, that man of great splendor, with his senses unsubdued, found no peace within himself.
1.064.001a Then, O Rāma, the great sage, having abandoned the direction of the Himalayas, departed.
