Having reached the eastern direction, he performed most severe asceticism. Having undertaken the unsurpassed vow of silence for a thousand years, O Rāma, he performed incomparable penance that was exceedingly difficult to accomplish.
When a full thousand years had passed, though the great sage was shaken by many obstacles and had become like a piece of wood, anger did not enter within him.
Then the gods, along with the gandharvas, pannagas, asuras, and rākṣasas—
Bewildered by his splendor, their rays dimmed by his ascetic power,
and all overcome by dejection, they then spoke to the Grandfather:
"O God, for many reasons, the great sage Viśvāmitra..."
Whether provoked by greed or incensed by anger, he increases further through his ascetic power;
for not even the slightest trace of sin is seen in him,
even though that which his mind desires is not given to him.
By his ascetic power, he destroys the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile;
all the quarters are agitated, and nothing at all is visible. All the oceans are turbulent, and the mountains are crumbling.
The earth trembles and the wind blows with violent agitation;
as long as the great sage does not set his mind upon destruction, O Lord,
so long must the Blessed One of great splendor, who is like fire, be propitiated.
"Just as in former times the entire triple world was consumed by the fire of time (kālāgni), so too [this one] desires to exercise the sovereignty of the gods; let that which is his will be granted.
Thereupon, all the hosts of gods, led by the Grandfather (Brahmā), [spoke].
They spoke these sweet words to the high-souled Viśvāmitra:
"O Brahmarṣi, welcome to you! We have been well-pleased by your asceticism.
O Kauśika, you have attained the status of a Brāhmaṇa through your fierce penance."
"O Brahmin, I, together with the hosts of Maruts, grant you long life.
May you attain well-being; may it be auspicious for you; go, gentle one, as you please.
Having heard these words of the Grandfather and of all the inhabitants of heaven, [he departed].
Having offered his salutation, the great sage spoke joyfully:
"If I have attained the status of a Brahmin and likewise long life,
then let the syllable *oṃ*, the *vaṣaṭ* call, and the Vedas choose me."
"O deities, let Vasiṣṭha— the son of Brahmā, the best among those who know the Kṣatra-veda and also the best among those who know the Brahma-veda— speak thus to me:
'If this supreme desire has been fulfilled, then let the bulls among the gods depart.'"
Then, propitiated by the gods, Vasiṣṭha, the best of those who recite prayers, established friendship [with Viśvāmitra] and said, "So be it.
"There is no doubt that you shall attain the status of a Brahmarṣi; everything shall be accomplished for you."

Having spoken thus, all the deities also departed as they had come. Viśvāmitra, the righteous-souled one, having attained supreme Brahminhood, honored the Brahmarṣi Vasiṣṭha, the best among those who recite prayers.
Having accomplished his desire, he wandered over the entire earth, established in austerity.
Thus, O Rāma, did that great-souled one attain the status of a Brāhmaṇa.
This, O Rāma, is the best of sages; this is austerity incarnate.
"This is the eternal, supreme dharma; this is the ultimate resort of valor.
Having heard these words of Śatānanda in the presence of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, Janaka, with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words to the son of Kuśika.
"I am blessed, I am favored, O bull among sages,
that you, O righteous descendant of Kakutstha, have come together with me to this sacrifice.
O Brahmin, O great sage, I have been purified by the very sight of you."

"O Brahmin, through the sight of you, many kinds of virtues have been attained by me. Furthermore, O one of great splendor, I have heard in detail your great asceticism being recounted, as has the high-souled Rāma."
Having reached the assembly hall with the members of the council, they heard of your many virtues:
"Immeasurable is your asceticism, immeasurable is your strength,
and your virtues, O son of Kuśika, are likewise eternally immeasurable."
"O Lord, I am never satiated with these wonderful stories. O best of sages, the time for my ritual duties is at hand as the solar disc is hanging low.
You may see me again tomorrow morning, O one of great splendor."
"Welcome, O best of ascetics; you should grant me leave to depart.
Having spoken thus to the best of sages, the King of Mithilā, the ruler of Videha, quickly performed a circumambulation along with his preceptors and kinsmen.
The righteous Viśvāmitra, together with Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa,
proceeded toward his own hermitage while being honored by the great seers.
Then, at the clear dawn, the lord of men, having performed his morning rites, [set out].
He summoned the high-souled Viśvāmitra along with the descendant of Raghu.
Having honored him according to the rites prescribed in the scriptures,
the righteous-souled one then addressed these words to the two high-souled descendants of Raghu.
"O Blessed One, welcome to you! What may I do for you, O sinless one?
May your lordship command me, for I am indeed to be commanded by you.
Thus was that righteous-souled one addressed by the high-souled Janaka.
The sage, skilled in speech, replied to the hero with these words:
"These two sons of Daśaratha are Kṣatriyas renowned throughout the world;
they desire to see this preeminent bow which rests with you."
"Show this to them— blessings upon you— so that the two princes, their desire fulfilled,
may depart as they wish upon seeing this bow.
Thus addressed, Janaka replied to the great sage.
"Listen to the purpose for which this bow remains here:
There was a lord of the earth known as Devarāta, the sixth in descent from Nimi.
O Blessed One, this [bow] was placed as a trust in his hands by that high-souled one."
Formerly, at the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice,
the valiant Rudra, having drawn his bow in anger toward the gods, spoke these words to them:
"Since you gods, seeking your own portions, did not allot a portion for me,"
"I shall sever your precious limbs with my bow.
Then, O bull among sages, all the gods became despondent;
they propitiated the Lord of Gods, and Bhava became pleased with them.
Filled with affection, he gave it to all those great-souled ones.
This very jewel of a bow belonging to the high-souled God of gods was then deposited as a trust with our ancestors, O Lord.
Then, as I was plowing the field with a plow, she rose from my field while I was clearing it; having been found, she became renowned by the name Sītā.
Having risen from the surface of the earth, she grew up as my own daughter.

"O bull among sages, this daughter of mine, born not from a womb, was established by me with valor as her bride-price. Kings came and sought the hand of my daughter, who had risen from the earth and was growing in stature."
"O Blessed One, as all those lords of the earth were seeking my daughter, I said, 'Her bride-price is valor,' and thus I did not give her away.
Then, O bull among sages, all those kings gathered together."

Having arrived at Mithilā, they then sought to test his prowess. While they were thus desiring to test his strength, the bow was brought forth; yet they were unable either to grasp that bow or even to lift it.

"O great sage, having perceived that the vigor of those powerful kings was slight, they were rejected; learn of this, O ascetic rich in austerity. Thereupon, O bull among sages, the kings [acted] with supreme wrath."
Having come to Mithilā with their prowess in doubt, they all besieged it;
O bull among sages, perceiving themselves as humiliated,
they were overcome by great rage and oppressed the city of Mithilā.

Then, when a full year had passed, all my provisions were completely exhausted; O best of sages, I was consequently deeply distressed. Thereupon, I sought to propitiate all the hosts of gods through my ascetic penance.
And the gods, exceedingly pleased, bestowed upon him an army of four divisions.
Then the kings, being broken and struck down, fled in all directions— those evildoers, devoid of prowess, their valor eclipsed, along with their ministers.
"O tiger among sages, O observer of noble vows, I shall show this most radiant bow to Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa as well. O sage, if Rāma should succeed in stringing this bow,"
"I shall give my daughter Sītā, born not from a womb, to the son of Daśaratha.
Having heard Janaka’s words, the great sage Viśvāmitra said to the king, "Show the bow to Rāma."
Then King Janaka commanded his ministers:
"Let the divine bow, adorned with perfumes and garlands, be brought here. Thus instructed by Janaka, the ministers entered the city.
Placing that bow before them, they departed by the king’s command;
fifty thousand mighty kings of great stature somehow managed to carry that eight-wheeled chest.
Having taken that long casket in which that bow was kept,
the ministers said to King Janaka, who was like a god:
"O King, this is the excellent bow, honored by all kings."
"O lord of Mithilā, O Indra among kings, if you desire to see that which is worthy of being seen," [said they].
Having heard their words, the king, with palms joined in reverence,
addressed the high-souled Viśvāmitra and both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
"O Brahmin, this excellent bow was honored by the Janakas;
it could not then be strung even by kings of great heroism.
Neither all the hosts of gods, nor the asuras, nor the rakshasas [could do so]."
Where is the scope for the foremost of Gandharvas and Yakṣas, along with the Kinnaras and Mahoragas,
or even for humans, in the drawing of this bow, or in its stringing, its joining, its vibration, or even its lifting?
"O bull among sages, this most excellent of bows has been brought;
O illustrious one, show it to these two princes.
Hearing these words spoken by Janaka, the righteous-souled Viśvāmitra—
"Child Rāma, behold the bow," he said to the descendant of Raghu.
At the word of the great seer, Rāma went to where that bow stood;
having opened the casket and seen the bow, he then spoke.
"O Brahmin, I shall touch this excellent bow here with my hand; I will exert myself in both lifting it and drawing it.
"So be it," the king and the sage replied to him.
At the word of the sage,
that delight of the Raghus, in the sight of many thousands of men, took up the bow at its middle with ease; and that righteous-souled one strung it as if in sport.
Having strung the bowstring, the heroic one drew it to his ear;
then that best of men, possessed of great fame, broke the bow in the middle.
Its sound was immense, like the roar of a thunderclap.
There was a great earthquake, as if a mountain were splitting apart;
and all the men fell down, stupefied by that sound. Having left the best of sages, the king, and those two Raghavas, they fled.
When those people had recovered their breath, the king, his fear dispelled,
spoke these words with joined palms to that bull among sages, for he was skilled in speech:
"O Blessed One, I have witnessed the prowess of Rāma, the son of Daśaratha."
"This is most wonderful, inconceivable, and beyond my imagination. My daughter Sītā, having obtained as her husband Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, will bring glory to the lineage of the Janakas."
"O Kauśika, my vow is true:
that her dowry is valor. My daughter Sītā, who is dearer to me than life itself, shall be given to Rāma with your consent, O Brahmin; let the ministers go at once."
"O Kauśika, may prosperity be yours; let them swiftly bring the king to my city by means of chariots with humble words,
and let them announce in every way that the hand of my daughter is to be given away, for which valor is the bride-price."
"Let the two descendants of Kakutstha, while hidden by the sage, indeed tell the king;
let those who travel with great speed bring the king here, for he is longing [to see them]. And Kauśika said, "So be it," after addressing the ministers.
1.066.027c The righteous-souled one, having issued his command, sent [messengers] to Ayodhyā.
1.067.001a Those messengers, commanded by Janaka, with their mounts exhausted,
1.067.001c having stayed on the road for three nights, entered the city of Ayodhyā.
By the king's command, those messengers were ushered into the royal palace;
there they beheld the aged King Daśaratha, who resembled a god.
With their palms joined in reverence, all the messengers were freed from their trepidation.
With purified minds, they addressed the king in sweet-sounding words:
"King Janaka of Mithilā, accompanied by his sacred fires,
enquires after your welfare and well-being, as does his teacher and domestic priest."
"O Great King, Janaka, the lord of Mithilā and ruler of Videha, repeatedly asks after you with a sweet voice full of affection, along with your attendants;
having calmly inquired after your welfare."
With the consent of Kauśika, he addressed these words to you:
"It was previously known that my daughter’s bride-price is valor;
and the kings, having become indignant, were rendered powerless and turned away."
"O King, this daughter of mine has been won by these heroic sons of yours, who arrived by chance with Viśvāmitra at their head.
And that divine bow, O King, was broken in the midst of the assembly by that high-souled one."

"For by Rāma, O Great King, in the presence of a vast assembly of people, it was vowed: 'Sītā shall be given to this high-souled one as her bride-price is valor. I wish to fulfill that promise; therefore, you ought to grant me your permission."
"O Great King, accompanied by your teacher and preceded by your domestic priest,
come quickly— blessings be upon you— you ought to see the two Raghavas. And you,
O Indra among kings, ought to fulfill my desire."
"You too shall obtain joy from both of your sons.
Thus did the Lord of Videha speak these sweet words,
having been authorized by Viśvāmitra and remaining steadfast in the opinion of Śatānanda.
Having heard those words of the messenger, the king was filled with supreme joy;
he spoke to Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, and his other ministers:
"The enhancer of Kausalyā’s delight is being protected by the son of Kuśika."
He dwells among the Videhas together with his brother Lakṣmaṇa. Having witnessed the prowess of that descendant of Kakutstha, the high-souled Janaka desires to bestow his daughter upon Rāghava.
"If the conduct of the high-souled Janaka pleases you,
let us go quickly to the city so that there may be no lapse of time.
"Very well," the ministers replied, together with all the great seers.
The king, being well-pleased, said to his ministers, "We shall depart tomorrow.
The ministers of the lord of men, having been treated with the highest honor, spent that night delighted, endowed as they were with every virtue.
Then, when the night had passed, King Daśaratha, together with his preceptor and his kinsmen, spoke joyfully to Sumantra as follows:
"Today, let all the treasurers take abundant wealth."
"Let well-prepared [forces], endowed with various jewels, go ahead; let the fourfold army also set out quickly from all sides,
and at the same time as my command, let the unsurpassed vehicles and draft animals depart."
"Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, Jābāli, and Kāśyapa,
as well as the long-lived seer Mārkaṇḍeya and Kātyāyana—
let these twice-born ones go ahead; yoke my chariot."
"1.068.005c For the messengers indeed urge me on so that there may be no delay.
1.068.006a And by the command of the lord of men, that fourfold army 1.068.006c followed behind the king as he proceeded together with the sages."
Having traveled for four days on the road, he arrived in the kingdom of Videha.
Upon hearing of his arrival, the illustrious King Janaka prepared a formal reception.
Then, having approached the aged King Daśaratha, the monarch...
King Janaka was delighted and attained supreme joy.
That best of men spoke with gladness to that other best of men:
"Welcome to you, O great king; by good fortune have you arrived, O Rāghava."
"You shall obtain the joy of both your sons, won through their prowess.
By good fortune, the illustrious and highly energetic seer Vasiṣṭha has arrived,
together with all the best of the twice-born, like Śatakratu with the gods."

"By good fortune my obstacles have been overcome; by good fortune my lineage has been honored through this alliance with the Raghavas—those high-souled ones who are preeminent in valor. O Indra among kings, you ought to perform the wedding ceremony tomorrow at dawn."
"At the conclusion of the sacrifice, O best of men, there shall be a marriage approved by the sages.
Having heard those words of his in the midst of the sages, the lord of men—
the best among those skilled in speech— replied to the king.
"Acceptance of gifts is dependent upon the giver; this I have heard long ago.
O knower of dharma, we shall do exactly as you say. These were the most righteous and glorious words of that speaker of truth.
1.068.015c Upon hearing this, the lord of Videha was filled with supreme wonder.
1.068.016a Then all the hosts of sages, gathered together with one another, 1.068.016c being endowed with great joy, dwelt happily through that night.

1.068.017a And King Janaka, having beheld his two sons, the descendants of Raghu, was filled with supreme joy; 1.068.017c he dwelt there, highly gratified and well-honored by Janaka. 1.068.018a Janaka too, of great splendor and a knower of the truth, performed his religious rites according to dharma.
Having performed the rites for the sacrifice and the two Soma-pressings, he spent the night there.
Then, at dawn, Janaka, who was skilled in speech, having completed his duties with the great seers, addressed these words to his family priest, Śatānanda.
My younger brother, possessed of great splendor and exceedingly righteous,
is known as Kuśadhvaja; he dwells in an auspicious city that borders the Vāryāphalaka region and drinks from the river Ikṣumatī.

In Sāṃkāśyā, which is as auspicious as a holy sight and resembles the Puṣpaka celestial chariot, I desire to see him; he is, in my opinion, the protector of the sacrifice. That one of great splendor shall also enjoy this pleasure together with me.
By the command of the lord of men, they set out on swift horses to bring that tiger among men, just as Viṣṇu was brought by the order of Indra.
And at the command of the lord of men, Kuśadhvaja arrived.
He beheld the high-souled Janaka, who is devoted to righteousness. Having saluted Śatānanda and the righteous king,
he ascended a supreme, divine throne worthy of a monarch.
When those two brothers of immeasurable splendor were seated,
the two heroes dispatched Sudāmana, the best of ministers, saying:
"Go quickly, O lord of ministers, to the descendant of Ikṣvāku of boundless luster."
"Bring the invincible one, together with his sons and his ministers. Having gone to the royal pavilion, he beheld that enhancer of the Raghu dynasty and,
saluting him with his head bowed, spoke as follows.
"O hero, lord of Ayodhyā, the King of Videha, the ruler of Mithilā,
has resolved to see you, together with your teachers and domestic priests.
Having heard these words of the best of ministers, the king, accompanied by the assembly of sages, then [prepared to depart].
Accompanied by his kinsmen, Janaka went to the place where he was; that king, together with his ministers, his preceptors, and his relatives—
the best among those skilled in speech— spoke these words to the King of Videha.
"O Great King, it is known to you that the venerable seer Vasiṣṭha is the tutelary deity of the Ikṣvāku lineage and the one who speaks on all matters of duty;
he has been authorized by Viśvāmitra along with all the great seers."
"This righteous-souled Vasiṣṭha will explain everything to me in due order.
When Daśaratha had become silent, the venerable sage Vasiṣṭha,
skilled in speech, addressed these words to the King of Videha and his domestic priest.
Brahmā, whose origin is unmanifest, is eternal, perpetual, and immutable. From him Marīci was born; Marīci’s son was Kaśyapa.
Vivasvat was born from Kaśyapa, and he is remembered as Vaivasvata Manu.
In former times, Manu was the Prajāpati, and Ikṣvāku was the son of Manu. Know that Ikṣvāku was the first king in Ayodhyā;
and from Ikṣvāku was born the illustrious Vikukṣi.
The son of Vikukṣi was the highly energetic and majestic Bāṇa;
the son of Bāṇa was the highly energetic and majestic Anaraṇya;
from Anaraṇya was born Pṛthu, and Triśaṅku was the son of Pṛthu.

To Triśaṅku was born a son of great fame, Dhundhumāra. From Dhundhumāra came the highly resplendent Yuvanāśva, a great chariot-warrior. The illustrious Māndhātā, lord of the earth, was the son of Yuvanāśva.
To Māndhātṛ was born a glorious son named Susaṃdhi.
Susaṃdhi also had two sons: Dhruvasaṃdhi and Prasenajit. From Dhruvasaṃdhi was born a renowned son known by the name Bharata.
From Bharata was born a son of great splendor named Asita; because he was born with that very poison, he became known as Sagara. Sagara’s son was Asamañja, and from Asamañja came Aṃśumat.
Dilīpa was the son of Aṃśumat; Dilīpa’s son was Bhagīratha;
from Bhagīratha came Kakutstha, and Kakutstha’s son was Raghu. The son of Raghu was the radiant Pravṛddha, also known as Puruṣādaka.
From him was born Kalmāṣapāda, and from him Śaṅkhaṇa;
Sudarśana was the son of Śaṅkhaṇa, Agnivarṇa was the son of Sudarśana, Śīghraga was the son of Agnivarṇa, and Maru was the son of Śīghraga.
Maru’s son was Praśuśruka, and from Praśuśruka came Ambarīṣa.
Ambarīṣa’s son was Nahuṣa, the lord of the earth. Nahuṣa’s son was Yayāti, and Nābhāga was born of Yayāti.
From Nābhāga was born Aja, and from Aja was born Daśaratha;
from that Daśaratha were born two brothers, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa—
kings of supreme righteousness, whose lineage was pure from the very beginning.

"O King, for the sake of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa— heroes born of the Ikṣvāku lineage who are speakers of truth— I request your two daughters. O best of men, it is fitting that you should give these two worthy maidens to these two worthy suitors."
To him who was speaking thus, Janaka replied with palms joined in reverence:
"May you be blessed; you ought to hear our supreme lineage as it is proclaimed.
For, O best of sages, when giving [in marriage], one must recount the family in its entirety."
"O great sage, listen to that which must be said by one born of noble lineage:
There was a king, renowned throughout the three worlds for his own deeds,
Nimi, whose soul was supremely devoted to dharma and who was the best among all those endowed with living beings."
His son was named Mithi, whose son was Janaka; the first [of the line] was named Janaka, and from Janaka came Udāvasu. From Udāvasu was born the righteous-souled Nandivardhana.
The son of Nandivardhana was named Suketu by name;
the son of Suketu was the righteous and mighty Devarāta;
and the son of the royal sage Devarāta was known as Bṛhadratha.
To Bṛhadratha was born Śūra, a great hero and a man of prowess.
To Mahāvīra was born Dhṛtimān, who was Sudhṛti and possessed of true valor.
From Sudhṛti also came Dhṛṣṭaketu, whose soul was righteous and who was exceedingly virtuous.
The son of the royal seer Dhṛṣṭaketu was the renowned Haryaśva;
Haryaśva’s son was Maru, and Maru’s son was Pratīndhaka. The son of Pratīndhaka was the righteous King Kīrtiratha.
The son of Kīrtiratha was known as Devamīḍha; the son of Devamīḍha was Vibudha, and the son of Vibudha was Mahīdhraka. The son of Mahīdhraka was the mighty king Kīrtirāta.
From the royal sage Kīrtirāta was born Mahāroma;
from Mahāroma, the righteous-souled Svarṇaroma was born;
and from the royal sage Svarṇaroma was born Hrasvaroma.
Two sons were born to that high-souled knower of dharma:
I am the elder, and my younger brother is the heroic Kuśadhvaja.
Having consecrated me as the eldest in the kingdom, that lord of men, my father—
Having entrusted Kuśadhvaja with the kingdom and taken the burden upon myself, I departed for the forest.
When my aged father had ascended to heaven, I bore the yoke of sovereignty according to dharma,
while looking after my godlike brother Kuśadhvaja with affection.
Then, after some time had passed, the heroic King Sudhanvan came from the city of Sāṃkāśya to besiege Mithilā;
he sent to me that unsurpassed bow of Śiva.
"Let Sītā, the lotus-eyed maiden, be given to me.
O Brahman-sage, because she was not given to him, there was a war between him and me;
that King Sudhanvan was slain by me in battle while facing me directly.
O best of sages, having slain that king Sudhanvan, I consecrated my heroic brother Kuśadhvaja as ruler in Sāṃkāśya. O great sage, this is my younger brother; I am the elder.
"O bull among sages, being exceedingly pleased, I give you these two daughters-in-law—blessings upon you:
Sītā to Rāma and Ūrmilā to Lakṣmaṇa. My daughter Sītā, who is like a daughter of the gods, has valor as her bride-price."

"I speak three times without doubt: I give even the second daughter, Ūrmilā, to you, O descendant of Raghu; being exceedingly pleased, I give these two daughters-in-law to you, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa. O King, have the godāna ceremony performed for them."
"May you be blessed; perform the rites for the ancestors first, and then perform the wedding ceremony.
For today, O mighty-armed lord, is the constellation Maghā; on the third day, O King, when the constellation is Uttaraphalgunī, perform the wedding."
"For the sake of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, a gift that results in happiness must be made.
To the King of Videha who had spoken thus, the great sage Viśvāmitra,
together with Vasiṣṭha, addressed these words to the heroic monarch.

"O bull among men, the lineages of the Ikṣvākus and the Videhas are inconceivable and immeasurable; there is no one who is their equal. Their connection through dharma is worthy, as is their excellence of form."
"O King, Sītā is with Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, along with Urmilā.
O best of men, you must not speak [harshly]; listen to my words.
This King Kuśadhvaja is his younger brother and a knower of dharma."
"O King, O best of men, we seek two daughters for our sons— Bharata and the wise Śatrughna— from this righteous-souled one whose beauty is peerless on earth."
"O King, let us choose [a bride] for the sake of those two high-souled ones among your daughters. These sons of Daśaratha are endowed with beauty and youth;
they are all like the world-protectors and equal to the gods in prowess."

"O Indra among kings, let the Ikṣvāku lineage, which is free from anxiety, be bound to you through this alliance with both families, for you are a performer of meritorious deeds. Having heard the words of Viśvāmitra, [Rāma] then acted according to the opinion of Vasiṣṭha.
Janaka, with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words to the two bulls among sages:
"Since you yourselves have commanded this alliance between our families as being worthy, let it be so; may prosperity be yours. These two daughters of Kuśadhvaja—"
"Let both Śatrughna and Bharata together take their two wives. O great sage, on a single day, let the four mighty princes take the hands of the four princesses."
"On the following day, O Brahmin, during the Phalgunī constellation, the wise praise the performance of marriage, for it was there that Bhaga, the Lord of Progeny,
was wedded. Having spoken these gentle words, he rose up with palms joined in reverence.
King Janaka spoke these words to both excellent sages:
"The highest dharma has been performed for me; I am forever your disciple. O bulls among sages, please sit upon these preeminent seats."
"Just as this city of Ayodhyā belongs to Daśaratha, so does it belong to me; there is no doubt regarding my sovereignty. You ought to act as is appropriate.
While Janaka, the King of Videha, was speaking thus, the joy of the Raghus [Rāma]—
King Daśaratha, delighted, replied to the lord of the earth:
"O lords of Mithilā, you two brothers possess innumerable virtues;
both sages and hosts of kings have been honored by you."

"May you attain well-being; may prosperity be yours. I shall depart for my own abode," he said, "and I shall perform all the ancestral rites (*śrāddha-karmāṇi*). Then King Daśaratha took leave of that lord of men.

Placing those two lords of sages at the forefront, the highly illustrious king departed quickly. Having returned to his residence and performed the *śrāddha* ceremony according to the prescribed rites,
the king rose early at dawn and made an excellent gift of cows.

The king, the lord of men, gave hundreds of thousands of cows to the Brahmins, one by one, in accordance with dharma, intending them for his sons. They were endowed with golden horns, accompanied by their calves, and possessed bronze milking vessels.
That bull among men, the joy of the Raghus, who was deeply affectionate toward his sons, gave four hundred thousand cows and a vast amount of other wealth to the twice-born,
dedicating it as a gift of cattle for the sake of his sons.
Surrounded then by his sons who had performed the *godāna* ceremony,
the gentle king shone like Prajāpati surrounded by the world-protectors (*lokapālas*).
On the very day that the king performed that supreme *godāna*, [the auspicious signs appeared].
On that very day, however, the heroic Yudhājit arrived—
he who was the son of the King of Kekaya and the biological maternal uncle of Bharata.
Having seen the king and inquired after his welfare, he spoke these words.

The king, the lord of Kekaya, out of affection, inquired after their welfare: "O Indra among kings, O lord of the earth, those for whom you desire well-being are now free from ailment; I am desirous of seeing my sister's son."

"For that purpose, O descendant of Raghu, I have come to Ayodhyā. Having heard, O lord of the earth, that those two sons of yours had gone to Mithilā with you for the sake of marriage, I have arrived."
"I have come in haste, desiring to see the son of my sister. Then King Daśaratha, seeing that dear guest who had arrived, honored him with the highest hospitality, for he was worthy of worship.
Then, having spent that night with his high-souled sons,
he approached the sacrificial enclosure, placing the sages at the forefront,
at the auspicious moment called Vijaya, while they were adorned with all their ornaments.
Accompanied by his brothers, Rāma— having performed the auspicious marriage rites and having placed Vasiṣṭha and other great sages at the front— King Daśaratha,
O King, likewise performed the auspicious marriage rites.

"O best among the foremost of men, through sons one desires a giver; for indeed, all purposes arise from both the giver and the receiver. Therefore, perform an excellent marriage and fulfill your own duty."
Thus addressed by the high-souled Vasiṣṭha, the immensely radiant one, who knew the supreme dharma, replied with these words:
"Who is my gatekeeper standing there? Whose command is being awaited?"

"What deliberation can there be regarding one's own home, just as this kingdom is yours? O best of sages, my daughter, having performed all the auspicious rites, has arrived at the base of the altar, radiant like the flames of fire."
"I am ready and waiting for you, stationed upon this sacrificial altar. Let the King ensure there is no obstacle; for what reason is there such delay?
Having heard those words spoken by Janaka, Daśaratha then—
He caused all his sons and the hosts of sages to enter. King Janaka spoke to the one who increases the joy of Kausalyā:
"This Sītā, my daughter, shall be your partner in dharma."
"Accept her; may prosperity be yours! Take her hand with your own hand.
O Lakṣmaṇa, come; may prosperity be yours! Accept Urmilā, who is offered by me; take her hand, lest there be a lapse of time."
Having spoken thus to him, Janaka addressed Bharata:
"O descendant of Raghu, take the hand of Māṇḍavī with your own hand.
Then the righteous lord of the Janakas also spoke to Śatrughna.
"O mighty-armed one, take Śrutakīrti’s hand with your own hand.
May all of you, being united and all having well-performed vows, be joined with your wives, O descendants of Kakutstha; let there be no further delay."
Having heard the words of Janaka, those four, abiding by the counsel of Vasiṣṭha, touched their hands together with their hands;
they then circumambulated the fire, the altar, and the king.
The high-souled best of the Raghus, together with their wives,
performed the marriage according to the prescribed rites and as previously instructed.
A great shower of radiant flowers fell from the sky.
With the sounds of divine drums and the resonance of songs and musical instruments,
throngs of apsarases danced and the gandharvas sang melodiously;
at the wedding of the foremost of the Raghus, it was like a marvel.

While such a scene was unfolding, resounding with the blare of musical instruments, those of great prowess circumambulated the fire three times and led their wives away. Then, O descendant of Raghu, they went to the royal pavilion together with their wives.
The king also followed along, watching him, accompanied by the assembly of sages and his kinsmen.
Then, when the night had passed, the great sage Viśvāmitra took leave of those two kings and departed for the Northern Mountains.
1.073.002 When Viśvāmitra had departed, King Daśaratha took leave of the Vaideha, the lord of Mithilā,
and quickly returned to his own city. 1.073.003 Then the king of the Videhas gave a great dowry for the maiden.
The Lord of Mithilā gave many hundreds of thousands of cows, as well as the finest blankets, ten million silken garments,
and an army of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, all of divine appearance and well-adorned.
The father of those maidens gave them excellent female and male servants;
being exceedingly joyful, he gave unsurpassed bridal wealth consisting of silver, gold, pearls, and coral.
Having bestowed much wealth and taken leave of the king, the lord of Mithilā entered his own abode, Mithilā. And the king,
the sovereign of Ayodhyā, together with his high-souled sons, [entered his city].
Placing all the sages at his head, he departed with his army and followers.
As that tiger among men proceeded together with the host of sages and the Rāghavas,
terrible birds uttered ominous cries from every direction.
All the terrestrial animals were moving in a clockwise direction.
Seeing them, that tiger among kings questioned Vasiṣṭha:
"The birds are inauspicious and terrible, yet the beasts are moving clockwise."
"Why does my heart tremble and my mind despond?
Having heard these words of King Daśaratha, the great seer spoke in a sweet voice: 'Listen to what its consequence shall be.'"
"A terrible and divine danger has arrived, fallen from the mouth of a bird;
these deer are pacifying it, so let this distress be abandoned. While they were conversing there, a wind suddenly appeared.
Making the entire earth tremble and felling the auspicious trees,
the sun was shrouded in darkness and all the directions ceased to shine;
everything was covered in ash, and that army became as if utterly bewildered.

Then Vasiṣṭha, the other ṛṣis, and the king along with his sons, remained there as if they alone possessed consciousness, while everyone else was unconscious. In that terrible darkness, the entire army was as if shrouded in ashes.
He beheld one of terrifying appearance, wearing a mass of matted locks;
as unassailable as Mount Kailāsa and as unbearable as the fire of cosmic destruction,
he was blazing with splendors and difficult for ordinary people to look upon.
Having placed the axe upon his shoulder and grasping a bow resembling a flash of lightning, he took up a preeminent arrow like Hara, the destroyer of Tripura;
seeing him of terrifying appearance, blazing like a fire.
Led by Vasiṣṭha, the Brahmins were devoted to silent recitation and burnt offerings;
all the sages gathered together and then conversed with one another:
"Will he, incensed by the slaughter of his father, not utterly destroy the Kṣatriyas?"
"Having previously committed the slaughter of the Kṣatriyas, his anger has subsided and his fever has passed;
indeed, he no longer intends to carry out the further extermination of the Kṣatriyas. Having spoken thus, [the king] took the water of honor (*arghya*) for the Bhārgava of fearsome appearance.
The sages addressed him with sweet words, saying, "O Rāma! O Rāma!
Having accepted that worship offered by the sages, the powerful Rāma, son of Jamadagni, spoke to Rāma, the son of Daśaratha.
"O hero Rāma, son of Daśaratha, your extraordinary valor is being heard of;
indeed, I have heard in its entirety about the breaking of the bow.
That breaking of the bow by you was truly wonderful and inconceivable."
Having heard that, I arrived, taking up another beautiful bow.
This is that great bow of Jamadagni’s son, of terrible appearance;
string it with an arrow and display your own strength.
"Having seen your strength in drawing this bow,
I shall grant you a duel that will bring glory to your prowess.
Having heard those words of his, King Daśaratha then—
With a dejected face and despondent, he spoke these words with palms joined in reverence:
"O highly illustrious one, you have been pacified by the anger of a brahmin;
you ought to grant safety to my young sons."
Born in the lineage of the Bhārgavas, who are distinguished by their Vedic study and vows,
you laid down your weapons after making a promise to the Thousand-eyed One. Having become devoted to dharma, you [gave] the earth to Kāśyapa.
"O great sage, having given [the kingdom] and retired to the forest, you have come here with Mahendra as your banner for my total destruction. Yet,
if Rāma alone is killed, none of us shall remain alive."
While Daśaratha was speaking thus, the powerful son of Jamadagni,
disregarding those words, addressed Rāma:
"These two excellent divine bows are world-renowned."

O best of men, O descendant of Kakutstha, that single weapon— firm, powerful, preeminent, and well-crafted by Viśvakarman— which was bestowed upon the three-eyed Lord for his desire to fight, and which was the destroyer of Tripura, has been shattered by you.

"O descendant of Kakutstha, this second bow, invincible and equal in strength to the Raudra bow, was given to Viṣṇu by the foremost of the gods. At that time, all the deities questioned the Grandfather."
Out of a desire to observe the relative strength and weakness of Śitikaṇṭha and Viṣṇu,
the Grandfather, the best among those who speak the truth, perceived the intention of the deities and instigated a conflict between the two.

In that conflict, there occurred a great battle that caused the hair to stand on end between Śitikaṇṭha and Viṣṇu, both desiring victory over the other. Then, that bow of Śiva, possessed of terrifying prowess, was made to yawn open.
Then, by the sound of "huṃ," the three-eyed Mahādeva was paralyzed.
Thereupon, the gods, together with the hosts of sages and the Cāraṇas, approached and entreated them; thus those two supreme deities attained peace.
Seeing that bow of Śiva strung by the prowess of Viṣṇu,
the gods along with the hosts of sages then held Viṣṇu in even higher esteem. But Rudra, the highly illustrious one, became enraged at the Videhas regarding the bow.
He placed it, along with the arrow, into the hand of the royal sage Devarāta. And this bow of Viṣṇu, O Rāma, which conquers the cities of enemies, Viṣṇu gave as a supreme trust to Ṛcīka Bhārgava.

But the immensely powerful Ṛcīka gave to my father, the high-souled Jamadagni, who was of matchless deeds, a divine [bow] from the great-souled Jamadagni. When my father, endowed with the power of asceticism, had laid down his weapons, [the enemy attacked].
Arjuna, relying on his ordinary intellect, ordained death [for them];
having heard of the most terrible and unworthy slaughter of his father,
he repeatedly destroyed the Kṣatriyas as they were born, out of rage.
O Rāma, having obtained the entire earth as a sacrificial fee at the conclusion of the sacrifice for the high-souled Kaśyapa of meritorious deeds, he—
endowed with the power of asceticism— then made his abode on Mount Mahendra.

"Having heard of the breaking of the bow, I have come here in haste. O Rāma, honoring the duty of a Kṣatriya, take up this great and supreme bow of Viṣṇu, which has been passed down through your father and grandfather."
"Fix an arrow capable of conquering enemy cities upon your excellent bow, O descendant of Kakutstha; if you are able, I shall then grant you a duel.
Having heard those words of the son of Jamadagni, the son of Daśaratha then—
Restraining his speech out of respect for his father, he then spoke to Rāma:
"O Bhārgava, I have heard of the deed you have performed.
O Brahmin, we shall follow you, established in the fulfillment of our debt to our father."
"O Bhārgava, you treat me as if I were devoid of vigor and incapable according to the duty of a Kṣatriya; you despise my splendor. Behold today my prowess!
Having spoken thus, the enraged Rāghava [seized] the excellent weapon of Bhārgava.
Quickly taking an arrow from his hand,
Rāma of swift prowess strung his bow and fixed the arrow upon it.
Then the enraged Rāma spoke these words to Paraśurāma, the son of Jamadagni:
"Because you are a Brahmin, O Rāma, you are worthy of my honor on account of Viśvāmitra;
therefore, I am not able to release at you this life-taking arrow. Or else, O Rāma, [take] this [bow], which was acquired through the power of asceticism, as your means of departure."
"Even if you wish to destroy incomparable worlds, I shall do so;
for this divine arrow of Viṣṇu, the conqueror of enemy cities, which destroys the pride of strength by its prowess, never falls in vain."
To behold Rāma bearing his excellent weapons, the gods together with the hosts of ṛṣis assembled there in throngs, placing the Grandfather at their head;
likewise, the gandharvas, apsarases, siddhas, cāraṇas, and kiṃnaras gathered there.
Then, while the world was rendered motionless and Rāma held his excellent bow, the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Nāgas came to behold that great marvel;
and that son of Jamadagni, rendered powerless, gazed up at Rāma.
His prowess struck down by the splendors [of Paraśurāma], the son of Jamadagni was rendered motionless;
he spoke very softly to Rāma, whose eyes were like lotus petals:
"In the past, when the earth was given by me to Kāśyapa..."

"‘You must not dwell within my domain,’ so Kāśyapa said to me. Therefore, O descendant of Kakutstha, honoring the word of my guru, I have made this vow: I shall not dwell on the earth for a single night. Thus was the promise indeed made to Kāśyapa.
"Therefore, O hero Rāghava, you ought not to destroy this state of mine. With the speed of thought, I shall go to Mahendra, the best of mountains.
For incomparable worlds have been won by me through ascetic penance, O Rāma."
"Kill him with your foremost arrow; let there be no delay.
I know you to be the slayer of Madhu, the imperishable Lord of the Gods. By the mere touch of this bow, may it be well with you, O scorcher of foes."
All these hosts of gods have assembled here to gaze upon you,
whose deeds are incomparable and who have no rival in battle.
And yet, O descendant of Kakutstha, this shame of mine ought not to exist.

"O Rāma of noble vows, since I have been turned away by you, the lord of the three worlds, you ought to discharge that peerless arrow. Upon the release of the arrow, I shall go to Mahendra, the best of mountains."
While the son of Jamadagni, Rāma, was speaking thus, the powerful and glorious Rāma,
son of Daśaratha, discharged a supreme arrow. Thereupon, all the cardinal and intermediate directions were freed from darkness.
The gods, together with the hosts of sages, praised Rāma as he stood with his weapon raised.
Having praised Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, the lord Rāma, the son of Jamadagni,
circumambulated him and departed for his own destination.
When Rāma had departed, the self-composed Rāma, son of Daśaratha, placed the bow together with the arrow into the hand of the immeasurable Varuṇa.
Then, having offered salutations to the sages headed by Vasiṣṭha, Rāma [departed].
Seeing his father distressed, the joy of the Raghus spoke:
"Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, has departed; let the fourfold army, protected by you as its lord, set out toward Ayodhyā."
Having heard Rāma’s words, King Daśaratha embraced his son with both arms and smelled the crown of Rāghava’s head;
hearing that Rāma had departed, the king was thrilled and overjoyed.
He urged on that army, and it quickly proceeded toward the city—
charming with its banners and flags, resounding with the blare of trumpets,
its royal roads sprinkled with water and strewn with heaps of scattered flowers.

The king entered the city, which was filled with throngs of people and beautifully adorned by the citizens, who were cheerful at his arrival and uttering auspicious greetings. Kausalyā, Sumitrā, and Kaikeyī of slender waist [also entered].
Those royal women who were engaged in receiving the brides, as well as the other queens,
then took hold of the highly fortunate Sītā, the illustrious Ūrmilā,
and both daughters of Kuśadhvaja.
Adorned with auspicious greetings and dressed in silken garments,
they all quickly paid homage to the temples of the gods;
then all those princesses offered salutations to everyone worthy of their salutation.
1.076.011c All of them, filled with joy, gazed upon [him] in private together with their husbands.
1.076.012a Having taken wives, mastered weapons, and possessing wealth along with their circle of friends,
those bulls among men 1.076.012c dwell while serving their father.
Among them, Rāma, whose valor was true, became the most illustrious in the world;
like the Self-Existent One among all beings, he was preeminent in virtue.
And Rāma sported with Sītā for many seasons.
The wise one was intent upon her, his mind perpetually surrendered to her heart;
for Sītā was Rāma’s beloved wife, bestowed by his father,
and his affection increased even further because of her virtues and her beauty.
And her husband dwells doubly within her heart;
though it be born within, the heart makes manifest to the heart what is hidden. This is especially true for him regarding Maithilī, the daughter of Janaka.

In beauty, Sītā was equal to the goddesses, like Śrī herself in embodied form. Having been united with that most excellent princess, who was so exceedingly lovely, the son of the royal seer [found his fulfillment].
Rāma shone exceedingly with his beloved,
like the all-pervading Lord Viṣṇu, the sovereign of the immortals, with his divine splendor.
